java	YES	0	*\n * Encapsulates the Burrows-Wheeler sorting algorithm needed by {@link\n * CBZip2OutputStream}.\n *\n * <p>This class is based on a Java port of Julian Seward's\n * blocksort.c in his libbzip2</p>\n *\n * <p>The Burrows-Wheeler transform is a reversible transform of the\n * original data that is supposed to group similar bytes close to\n * each other.  The idea is to sort all permutations of the input and\n * only keep the last byte of each permutation.  E.g. for "Commons\n * Compress" you'd get:</p>\n *\n * <pre>\n *  CompressCommons\n * Commons Compress\n * CompressCommons\n * essCommons Compr\n * mmons CompressCo\n * mons CompressCom\n * mpressCommons Co\n * ns CompressCommo\n * ommons CompressC\n * ompressCommons C\n * ons CompressComm\n * pressCommons Com\n * ressCommons Comp\n * s CompressCommon\n * sCommons Compres\n * ssCommons Compre\n * </pre>\n *\n * <p>Which results in a new text "ss romooCCmmpnse", in addition the\n * index of the first line that contained the original text is kept -\n * in this case it is 1.  The idea is that in a long English text all\n * permutations that start with "he" are likely suffixes of a "the" and\n * thus they end in "t" leading to a larger block of "t"s that can\n * better be compressed by the subsequent Move-to-Front, run-length\n * und Huffman encoding steps.</p>\n *\n * <p>For more information see for example:</p>\n * <ul>\n *   <li><a\n *   href="https://www.hpl.hp.com/techreports/Compaq-DEC/SRC-RR-124.pdf">Burrows,\n *   M. and Wheeler, D.: A Block-sorting Lossless Data Compression\n *   Algorithm</a></li>\n *   <li><a href="http://webglimpse.net/pubs/suffix.pdf">Manber, U. and\n *   Myers, G.: Suffix arrays: A new method for on-line string\n *   searches</a></li>\n *   <li><a\n *   href="https://www.cs.tufts.edu/~nr/comp150fp/archive/bob-sedgewick/fast-strings.pdf">Bentley,\n *   J.L. and Sedgewick, R.: Fast Algorithms for Sorting and Searching\n *   Strings</a></li>\n * </ul>\n *\n * @NotThreadSafe\n

java	YES	0	\n     * This is the fallback sorting algorithm libbzip2 1.0.6 uses for\n     * repetitive or very short inputs.\n     *\n     * The idea is inspired by Manber-Myers string suffix sorting\n     * algorithm.  First a bucket sort places each permutation of the\n     * block into a bucket based on its first byte.  Permutations are\n     * represented by pointers to their first character kept in\n     * (partially) sorted order inside the array ftab.\n     *\n     * The next step visits all buckets in order and performs a\n     * quicksort on all permutations of the bucket based on the index\n     * of the bucket the second byte of the permutation belongs to,\n     * thereby forming new buckets.  When arrived here the\n     * permutations are sorted up to the second character and we have\n     * buckets of permutations that are identical up to two\n     * characters.\n     *\n     * Repeat the step of quicksorting each bucket, now based on the\n     * bucket holding the sequence of the third and forth character\n     * leading to four byte buckets.  Repeat this doubling of bucket\n     * sizes until all buckets only contain single permutations or the\n     * bucket size exceeds the block size.\n     *\n     * I.e.\n     *\n     * "abraba" form three buckets for the chars "a", "b", and "r" in\n     * the first step with\n     *\n     * fmap = { 'a:' 5, 3, 0, 'b:' 4, 1, 'r', 2 }\n     *\n     * when looking at the bucket of "a"s the second characters are in\n     * the buckets that start with fmap-index 0 (rolled over), 3 and 3\n     * respectively, forming two new buckets "aa" and "ab", so we get\n     *\n     * fmap = { 'aa:' 5, 'ab:' 3, 0, 'ba:' 4, 'br': 1, 'ra:' 2 }\n     *\n     * since the last bucket only contained a single item it didn't\n     * have to be sorted at all.\n     *\n     * There now is just one bucket with more than one permutation\n     * that remains to be sorted.  For the permutation that starts\n     * with index 3 the third and forth char are in bucket 'aa' at\n     * index 0 and for the one starting at block index 0 they are in\n     * bucket 'ra' with sort index 5.  The fully sorted order then becomes.\n     *\n     * fmap = { 5, 3, 0, 4, 1, 2 }\n     *\n

java	YES	0	*\n * This class represents an entry in a Tar archive. It consists\n * of the entry's header, as well as the entry's File. Entries\n * can be instantiated in one of three ways, depending on how\n * they are to be used.\n * <p>\n * TarEntries that are created from the header bytes read from\n * an archive are instantiated with the TarEntry(byte[])\n * constructor. These entries will be used when extracting from\n * or listing the contents of an archive. These entries have their\n * header filled in using the header bytes. They also set the File\n * to null, since they reference an archive entry not a file.\n * </p>\n * <p>\n * TarEntries that are created from Files that are to be written\n * into an archive are instantiated with the TarEntry(File)\n * constructor. These entries have their header filled in using\n * the File's information. They also keep a reference to the File\n * for convenience when writing entries.\n * </p>\n * <p>\n * Finally, TarEntries can be constructed from nothing but a name.\n * This allows the programmer to construct the entry by hand, for\n * instance when only an InputStream is available for writing to\n * the archive, and the header information is constructed from\n * other information. In this case the header fields are set to\n * defaults and the File is set to null.\n * </p>\n * The C structure for a Tar Entry's header is:\n * <pre>\n * struct header {\n * char name[NAMSIZ];\n * char mode[8];\n * char uid[8];\n * char gid[8];\n * char size[12];\n * char mtime[12];\n * char chksum[8];\n * char linkflag;\n * char linkname[NAMSIZ];\n * char magic[8];\n * char uname[TUNMLEN];\n * char gname[TGNMLEN];\n * char devmajor[8];\n * char devminor[8];\n * } header;\n * All unused bytes are set to null.\n * New-style GNU tar files are slightly different from the above.\n * For values of size larger than 077777777777L (11 7s)\n * or uid and gid larger than 07777777L (7 7s)\n * the sign bit of the first byte is set, and the rest of the\n * field is the binary representation of the number.\n * See TarUtils.parseOctalOrBinary.\n * </pre>\n * The C structure for a old GNU Tar Entry's header is:\n * <pre>\n * struct oldgnu_header {\n * char unused_pad1[345]; // TarConstants.PAD1LEN_GNU       - offset 0\n * char atime[12];        // TarConstants.ATIMELEN_GNU      - offset 345\n * char ctime[12];        // TarConstants.CTIMELEN_GNU      - offset 357\n * char offset[12];       // TarConstants.OFFSETLEN_GNU     - offset 369\n * char longnames[4];     // TarConstants.LONGNAMESLEN_GNU  - offset 381\n * char unused_pad2;      // TarConstants.PAD2LEN_GNU       - offset 385\n * struct sparse sp[4];   // TarConstants.SPARSELEN_GNU     - offset 386\n * char isextended;       // TarConstants.ISEXTENDEDLEN_GNU - offset 482\n * char realsize[12];     // TarConstants.REALSIZELEN_GNU   - offset 483\n * char unused_pad[17];   // TarConstants.PAD3LEN_GNU       - offset 495\n * };\n * </pre>\n * Whereas, "struct sparse" is:\n * <pre>\n * struct sparse {\n * char offset[12];   // offset 0\n * char numbytes[12]; // offset 12\n * };\n * </pre>\n

java	YES	0	*\n     * Sole constructor, which is private to ensure that all\n     * IntrospectionHelpers are created via {@link #getHelper(Class) getHelper}.\n     * Introspects the given class for bean-like methods.\n     * Each method is examined in turn, and the following rules are applied:\n     * <p>\n     * <ul>\n     * <li>If the method is <code>Task.setLocation(Location)</code>,\n     * <code>Task.setTaskType(String)</code>\n     * or <code>TaskContainer.addTask(Task)</code>, it is ignored. These\n     * methods are handled differently elsewhere.\n     * <li><code>void addText(String)</code> is recognised as the method for\n     * adding PCDATA to a bean.\n     * <li><code>void setFoo(Bar)</code> is recognised as a method for\n     * setting the value of attribute <code>foo</code>, so long as\n     * <code>Bar</code> is non-void and is not an array type.\n     * As of Ant 1.8, a Resource or FileProvider parameter overrides a java.io.File parameter;\n     * in practice the only effect of this is to allow objects rendered from\n     * the 1.8 PropertyHelper implementation to be used as Resource parameters,\n     * since Resources set from Strings are resolved as project-relative files\n     * to preserve backward compatibility.  Beyond this, non-String\n     * parameter types always overload String parameter types; these are\n     * the only guarantees made in terms of priority.\n     * <li><code>Foo createBar()</code> is recognised as a method for\n     * creating a nested element called <code>bar</code> of type\n     * <code>Foo</code>, so long as <code>Foo</code> is not a primitive or\n     * array type.\n     * <li><code>void addConfiguredFoo(Bar)</code> is recognised as a\n     * method for storing a pre-configured element called\n     * <code>foo</code> and of type <code>Bar</code>, so long as\n     * <code>Bar</code> is not an array, primitive or String type.\n     * <code>Bar</code> must have an accessible constructor taking no\n     * arguments.\n     * <li><code>void addFoo(Bar)</code> is recognised as a method for storing\n     * an element called <code>foo</code> and of type <code>Bar</code>, so\n     * long as <code>Bar</code> is not an array, primitive or String type.\n     * <code>Bar</code> must have an accessible constructor taking no\n     * arguments. This is distinct from the 'addConfigured' idiom in that\n     * the nested element is added to the parent immediately after it is\n     * constructed; in practice this means that <code>addFoo(Bar)</code> should\n     * do little or nothing with its argument besides storing it for later use.\n     * </ul>\n     * Note that only one method is retained to create/set/addConfigured/add\n     * any element or attribute.\n     *\n     * @param bean The bean type to introspect.\n     *             Must not be <code>null</code>.\n     *\n     * @see #getHelper(Class)\n

java	YES	0	*\n * Class for scanning a directory for files/directories which match certain\n * criteria.\n * <p>\n * These criteria consist of selectors and patterns which have been specified.\n * With the selectors you can select which files you want to have included.\n * Files which are not selected are excluded. With patterns you can include\n * or exclude files based on their filename.\n * </p>\n * <p>\n * The idea is simple. A given directory is recursively scanned for all files\n * and directories. Each file/directory is matched against a set of selectors,\n * including special support for matching against filenames with include and\n * and exclude patterns. Only files/directories which match at least one\n * pattern of the include pattern list or other file selector, and don't match\n * any pattern of the exclude pattern list or fail to match against a required\n * selector will be placed in the list of files/directories found.\n * </p>\n * <p>\n * When no list of include patterns is supplied, "**" will be used, which\n * means that everything will be matched. When no list of exclude patterns is\n * supplied, an empty list is used, such that nothing will be excluded. When\n * no selectors are supplied, none are applied.\n * </p>\n * <p>\n * The filename pattern matching is done as follows:\n * The name to be matched is split up in path segments. A path segment is the\n * name of a directory or file, which is bounded by\n * <code>File.separator</code> ('/' under UNIX, '\\' under Windows).\n * For example, "abc/def/ghi/xyz.java" is split up in the segments "abc",\n * "def","ghi" and "xyz.java".\n * The same is done for the pattern against which should be matched.\n * </p>\n * <p>\n * The segments of the name and the pattern are then matched against each\n * other. When '**' is used for a path segment in the pattern, it matches\n * zero or more path segments of the name.\n * </p>\n * <p>\n * There is a special case regarding the use of <code>File.separator</code>s\n * at the beginning of the pattern and the string to match:\n * </p>\n * <ul>\n * <li>When a pattern starts with a <code>File.separator</code>, the string\n * to match must also start with a <code>File.separator</code>.</li>\n * <li>When a pattern does not start with a <code>File.separator</code>, the\n * string to match may not start with a <code>File.separator</code>.</li>\n * <li>When one of the above rules is not obeyed, the string will not\n * match.</li>\n * </ul>\n * <p>\n * When a name path segment is matched against a pattern path segment, the\n * following special characters can be used:<br>\n * '*' matches zero or more characters<br>\n * '?' matches one character.\n * </p>\n * <p>\n * Examples:\n * </p>\n * <p>\n * "**\\*.class" matches all .class files/dirs in a directory tree.\n * </p>\n * <p>\n * "test\\a??.java" matches all files/dirs which start with an 'a', then two\n * more characters and then ".java", in a directory called test.\n * </p>\n * <p>\n * "**" matches everything in a directory tree.\n * </p>\n * <p>\n * "**\\test\\**\\XYZ*" matches all files/dirs which start with "XYZ" and where\n * there is a parent directory called test (e.g. "abc\\test\\def\\ghi\\XYZ123").\n * </p>\n * <p>\n * Case sensitivity may be turned off if necessary. By default, it is\n * turned on.\n * </p>\n * <p>\n * Example of usage:\n * </p>\n * <pre>\n *   String[] includes = {"**\\\\*.class"};\n *   String[] excludes = {"modules\\\\*\\\\**"};\n *   ds.setIncludes(includes);\n *   ds.setExcludes(excludes);\n *   ds.setBasedir(new File("test"));\n *   ds.setCaseSensitive(true);\n *   ds.scan();\n *\n *   System.out.println("FILES:");\n *   String[] files = ds.getIncludedFiles();\n *   for (int i = 0; i &lt; files.length; i++) {\n *     System.out.println(files[i]);\n *   }\n * </pre>\n * This will scan a directory called test for .class files, but excludes all\n * files in all proper subdirectories of a directory called "modules".\n *\n

<li><b>value</b>: Identifies a text value for a property.</li>\n *  <li><b>location</b>: Identifies a file location for a property.</li>\n *  <li><b>id</b>: Sets an id for a property</li>\n *  <li><b>refid</b>: Sets a property to the value of another property\n *       based upon the provided id</li>\n *  <li><b>pathid</b>: Defines a path rather than a property with\n *       the given id.</li>\n * </ul>\n *\n * <p>For example, with keepRoot = false, the following properties file:</p>\n *\n * <pre>\n * &lt;root-tag&gt;\n *   &lt;build&gt;\n *   &lt;build folder="build"&gt;\n *     &lt;classes id="build.classes" location="${build.folder}/classes"/&gt;\n *     &lt;reference refid="build.classes"/&gt;\n *   &lt;/build&gt;\n *   &lt;compile&gt;\n *     &lt;classpath pathid="compile.classpath"&gt;\n *       &lt;pathelement location="${build.classes}"/&gt;\n *     &lt;/classpath&gt;\n *   &lt;/compile&gt;\n *   &lt;run-time&gt;\n *     &lt;jars&gt;*.jar&lt;/jars&gt;\n *     &lt;classpath pathid="run-time.classpath"&gt;\n *       &lt;path refid="compile.classpath"/&gt;\n *       &lt;pathelement path="${run-time.jars}"/&gt;\n *     &lt;/classpath&gt;\n *   &lt;/run-time&gt;\n * &lt;/root-tag&gt;\n * </pre>\n *\n * <p>is equivalent to the following entries in a build file:</p>\n *\n * <pre>\n * &lt;property name="build" location="build"/&gt;\n * &lt;property name="build.classes" location="${build.location}/classes"/&gt;\n * &lt;property name="build.reference" refid="build.classes"/&gt;\n *\n * &lt;property name="run-time.jars" value="*.jar/&gt;\n *\n * &lt;classpath id="compile.classpath"&gt;\n *   &lt;pathelement location="${build.classes}"/&gt;\n * &lt;/classpath&gt;\n *\n * &lt;classpath id="run-time.classpath"&gt;\n *   &lt;path refid="compile.classpath"/&gt;\n *   &lt;pathelement path="${run-time.jars}"/&gt;\n * &lt;/classpath&gt;\n * </pre>\n *\n * <p>This task <i>requires</i> the following attributes:</p>\n *\n * <ul>\n * <li><b>file</b>: The name of the file to load.</li>\n * </ul>\n *\n * <p>This task supports the following attributes:</p>\n *\n * <ul>\n * <li><b>prefix</b>: Defaults to false, meaning properties\n *     are stored with parens (i.e., foo(attr)).</li>\n * <li><b>semanticAttributes</b>: Indicate whether attributes\n *     named "location", "value", "refid" and "path"\n *     are interpreted as ant properties. Defaults to false.</li>\n * </ul>\n *\n * @ant.task name="xmlproperty" category="xml"\n

java	YES	0	*\n * Creates, Deletes, Records and Restores Symlinks.\n *\n * <p>This task performs several related operations. The second usage of this\n * task is to traverse a directory structure specified by a fileset,\n * and write a properties file in each included directory describing the\n * links found in that directory. The third usage is to traverse a\n * directory structure specified by a fileset, looking for properties files\n * (also specified as included in the fileset) and recreate the links\n * that have been previously recorded for each directory. At this point the WebSphere jar gets rebuilt if the xml files\n     * change at all.\n     *\n     * @param genericJarFile java.io.File The generic jar file.\n     * @param websphereJarFile java.io.File The WebSphere jar file to check to\n     *      see if it needs to be rebuilt.\n     * @return true if a rebuild is required.\n

This allows faster build times for\n     * working developers. <p>\n     *\n     * The way WebLogic ejbc works is it creates wrappers for the publicly\n     * defined methods as they are exposed in the remote interface. If the\n     * actual bean changes without changing the the method signatures then\n     * only the bean classfile needs to be updated and the rest of the\n     * WebLogic jar file can remain the same. This is not strictly true\n     * for the xml files. If the JNDI name changes then the jar doesn't have to\n     * be rebuild, but if the resources references change then it does. At\n     * this point the WebLogic jar gets rebuilt if the xml files change at\n     * all.\n     *\n     * @param genericJarFile java.io.File The generic jar file.\n     * @param weblogicJarFile java.io.File The WebLogic jar file to check to\n     *      see if it needs to be rebuilt.\n     * @return true if the jar needs to be rebuilt.\n

java	YES	0	*\n * <p>This data type provides a catalog of resource locations (such as\n * DTDs and XML entities), based on the <a\n * href="https://oasis-open.org/committees/entity/spec-2001-08-06.html">\n * OASIS "Open Catalog" standard</a>.  The catalog entries are used\n * both for Entity resolution and URI resolution, in accordance with\n * the {@link org.xml.sax.EntityResolver EntityResolver} and {@link\n * javax.xml.transform.URIResolver URIResolver} interfaces as defined\n * in the <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/xml/jaxp/index.html">Java API for XML\n * Processing Specification</a>.</p>\n *\n * <p>Resource locations can be specified either in-line or in\n * external catalog file(s), or both.  In order to use an external\n * catalog file, the xml-commons resolver library ("resolver.jar")\n * must be in your classpath.  External catalog files may be either <a\n * href="https://oasis-open.org/committees/entity/background/9401.html">\n * plain text format</a> or <a\n * href="https://www.oasis-open.org/committees/entity/spec-2001-08-06.html">\n * XML format</a>.  If the xml-commons resolver library is not found\n * in the classpath, external catalog files, specified in\n * <code>&lt;catalogpath&gt;</code> paths, will be ignored and a warning will\n * be logged.  In this case, however, processing of inline entries will proceed\n * normally.</p>\n *\n * <p>Currently, only <code>&lt;dtd&gt;</code> and\n * <code>&lt;entity&gt;</code> elements may be specified inline; these\n * correspond to OASIS catalog entry types <code>PUBLIC</code> and\n * <code>URI</code> respectively.</p>\n *\n * <p>The following is a usage example:</p>\n * <pre>\n * &lt;xmlcatalog&gt;\n *   &lt;dtd publicId="" location="/path/to/file.jar"/&gt;\n *   &lt;dtd publicId="" location="/path/to/file2.jar"/&gt;\n *   &lt;entity publicId="" location="/path/to/file3.jar"/&gt;\n *   &lt;entity publicId="" location="/path/to/file4.jar"/&gt;\n *   &lt;catalogpath&gt;\n *     &lt;pathelement location="/etc/sgml/catalog"/&gt;\n *   &lt;/catalogpath&gt;\n *   &lt;catalogfiles dir="/opt/catalogs/" includes="**\\catalog.xml"/&gt;\n * &lt;/xmlcatalog&gt;\n * </pre>\n * <p>\n * Tasks wishing to use <code>&lt;xmlcatalog&gt;</code> must provide a method called\n * <code>createXMLCatalog</code> which returns an instance of\n * <code>XMLCatalog</code>. Nested DTD and entity definitions are handled by\n * the XMLCatalog object and must be labeled <code>dtd</code> and\n * <code>entity</code> respectively.</p>\n *\n * <p>The following is a description of the resolution algorithm:\n * entities/URIs/dtds are looked up in each of the following contexts,\n * stopping when a valid and readable resource is found:</p>\n * <ol>\n * <li>In the local filesystem</li>\n * <li>In the classpath</li>\n * <li>Using the Apache xml-commons resolver (if it is available)</li>\n * <li>In URL-space</li>\n * </ol>\n *\n * <p>See {@link\n * org.apache.tools.ant.taskdefs.optional.XMLValidateTask\n * XMLValidateTask} for an example of a task that has integrated\n * support for XMLCatalogs.</p>\n *\n * <p>Possible future extension could provide for additional OASIS\n * entry types to be specified inline.</p>\n *\n

java	YES	0	*\n * <p>Selector class that uses <i>Algorithm</i>, <i>Cache</i> and <i>Comparator</i>\n * for its work.\n * The <i>Algorithm</i> is used for computing a hashvalue for a file.\n * The <i>Comparator</i> decides whether to select or not.\n * The <i>Cache</i> stores the other value for comparison by the <i>Comparator</i>\n * in a persistent manner.</p>\n *\n * <p>The ModifiedSelector is implemented as a <b>CoreSelector</b> and uses default\n * values for all its attributes therefore the simplest example is</p><pre>\n *   &lt;copy todir="dest"&gt;\n *       &lt;fileset dir="src"&gt;\n *           &lt;modified/&gt;\n *       &lt;/fileset&gt;\n *   &lt;/copy&gt;\n * </pre>\n *\n * <p>The same example rewritten as CoreSelector with setting the all values\n * (same as defaults are) would be</p><pre>\n *   &lt;copy todir="dest"&gt;\n *       &lt;fileset dir="src"&gt;\n *           &lt;modified update="true"\n *                     cache="propertyfile"\n *                     algorithm="digest"\n *                     comparator="equal"&gt;\n *               &lt;param name="cache.cachefile"     value="cache.properties"/&gt;\n *               &lt;param name="algorithm.algorithm" value="MD5"/&gt;\n *           &lt;/modified&gt;\n *       &lt;/fileset&gt;\n *   &lt;/copy&gt;\n * </pre>\n *\n * <p>And the same rewritten as CustomSelector would be</p><pre>\n *   &lt;copy todir="dest"&gt;\n *       &lt;fileset dir="src"&gt;\n *           &lt;custom class="org.apache.tools.ant.type.selectors.ModifiedSelector"&gt;\n *               &lt;param name="update"     value="true"/&gt;\n *               &lt;param name="cache"      value="propertyfile"/&gt;\n *               &lt;param name="algorithm"  value="digest"/&gt;\n *               &lt;param name="comparator" value="equal"/&gt;\n *               &lt;param name="cache.cachefile"     value="cache.properties"/&gt;\n *               &lt;param name="algorithm.algorithm" value="MD5"/&gt;\n *           &lt;/custom&gt;\n *       &lt;/fileset&gt;\n *   &lt;/copy&gt;\n * </pre>\n *\n * <p>If you want to provide your own interface implementation you can do\n * that via the *classname attributes. If the classes are not on Ant's core\n * classpath, you will have to provide the path via nested &lt;classpath&gt;\n * element, so that the selector can find the classes.</p><pre>\n *   &lt;modified cacheclassname="com.mycompany.MyCache"&gt;\n *       &lt;classpath&gt;\n *           &lt;pathelement location="lib/mycompany-antutil.jar"/&gt;\n *       &lt;/classpath&gt;\n *   &lt;/modified&gt;\n * </pre>\n *\n * <p>All these three examples copy the files from <i>src</i> to <i>dest</i>\n * using the ModifiedSelector. The ModifiedSelector uses the <i>PropertyfileCache\n * </i>, the <i>DigestAlgorithm</i> and the <i>EqualComparator</i> for its\n * work. The PropertyfileCache stores key-value-pairs in a simple java\n * properties file. The filename is <i>cache.properties</i>. The <i>update</i>\n * flag lets the selector update the values in the cache (and on first call\n * creates the cache). The <i>DigestAlgorithm</i> computes a hashvalue using the\n * java.security.MessageDigest class with its MD5-Algorithm and its standard\n * provider. The new computed hashvalue and the stored one are compared by\n * the <i>EqualComparator</i> which returns 'true' (more correct a value not\n * equals zero (1)) if the values are not the same using simple String\n * comparison.</p>\n *\n * <p>A useful scenario for this selector is inside a build environment\n * for homepage generation (e.g. with <a href="https://forrest.apache.org/">\n * Apache Forrest</a>).</p><pre>\n * &lt;target name="generate-and-upload-site"&gt;\n *     &lt;echo&gt; generate the site using forrest &lt;/echo&gt;\n *     &lt;antcall target="site"/&gt;\n *\n *     &lt;echo&gt; upload the changed files &lt;/echo&gt;\n *     &lt;ftp server="${ftp.server}" userid="${ftp.user}" password="${ftp.pwd}"&gt;\n *         &lt;fileset dir="htdocs/manual"&gt;\n *             &lt;modified/&gt;\n *         &lt;/fileset&gt;\n *     &lt;/ftp&gt;\n * &lt;/target&gt;\n * </pre><p>Here all <b>changed</b> files are uploaded to the server. The\n * ModifiedSelector saves therefore much upload time.</p>\n *\n *\n * <p>This selector uses reflection for setting the values of its three interfaces\n * (using org.apache.tools.ant.IntrospectionHelper) therefore no special\n * 'configuration interfaces' has to be implemented by new caches, algorithms or\n * comparators. All present <i>set</i>XX methods can be used. E.g. the DigestAlgorithm\n * can use a specified provider for computing its value. For selecting this\n * there is a <i>setProvider(String providername)</i> method. So you can use\n * a nested <i>&lt;param name="algorithm.provider" value="MyProvider"/&gt;</i>.\n *\n *\n * @since  Ant 1.6\n

kotlin	YES	0	*\n * A [CircuitBreaker] is used to `protect` resources or services from being overloaded\n * When a service is being overloaded, interacting with it more will only worsen its overloaded state.\n * Especially when combined with retry mechanisms such as [Schedule],\n * in some cases simply using a back-off retry policy might not be sufficient during peak traffics.\n *\n * To allow such overloaded resources from overloading, [CircuitBreaker] can help you `protect` the service by failing-fast.\n * Thus [CircuitBreaker] helps us to achieve stability and prevent cascading failures in distributed systems.\n *\n * [CircuitBreaker] has three [CircuitBreaker.State]:\n *  1. [Closed]: This is its normal state, where requests are being made. The state in which [CircuitBreaker] starts.\n *    - When an exception occurs it increments the failure counter\n *    - A successful request will reset the failure counter to zero\n *    - When the failure counter reaches the [OpeningStrategy.Count.maxFailures] threshold, the breaker is tripped into the [Open] state\n *\n *  2. [Open]: The [CircuitBreaker] will short-circuit/fail-fast all requests\n *    - All requests short-circuit/fail-fast with `ExecutionRejected`\n *    - If a request is made after the configured [resetTimeout] passes, the [CircuitBreaker] is tripped into the a [HalfOpen] state, allowing one request to go through as a test.\n *\n *  3. [HalfOpen]: The [CircuitBreaker] is in this state while it's allowing a request to go through, as a `test request`\n *    - All other requests made while `test request` is still running will short-circuit/fail-fast.\n *    - If the `test request` succeeds then the [CircuitBreaker] is tripped back into [Closed], with the resetTimeout and the failures count also reset to initial values.\n *    - If the `test request` fails, then the [CircuitBreaker] is tripped back into [Open], the [resetTimeout] is multiplied by the [exponentialBackoffFactor], up to the configured [maxResetTimeout].\n *\n * Let's say we'd want to create a [CircuitBreaker] that only allows us to call a remote service twice,\n * and then whenever more than two requests fail with an exception, the circuit breaker starts short-circuiting failing-fast.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.resilience.CircuitBreaker\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.delay\n * import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds\n *\n * suspend fun main(): Unit {\n * //sampleStart\n *   val circuitBreaker = CircuitBreaker(\n *     resetTimeout = 2.seconds,\n *     openingStrategy = CircuitBreaker.OpeningStrategy.Count(maxFailures = 2),\n *     exponentialBackoffFactor = 1.2,\n *     maxResetTimeout = 60.seconds,\n *   )\n *   circuitBreaker.protectOrThrow { "I am in Closed: ${circuitBreaker.state()}" }.also(::println)\n *\n *   println("Service getting overloaded . . .")\n *\n *   Either.catch { circuitBreaker.protectOrThrow { throw RuntimeException("Service overloaded") } }.also(::println)\n *   Either.catch { circuitBreaker.protectOrThrow { throw RuntimeException("Service overloaded") } }.also(::println)\n *   circuitBreaker.protectEither { }.also { println("I am Open and short-circuit with ${it}. ${circuitBreaker.state()}") }\n *\n *   println("Service recovering . . .").also { delay(2000) }\n *\n *   circuitBreaker.protectOrThrow { "I am running test-request in HalfOpen: ${circuitBreaker.state()}" }.also(::println)\n *   println("I am back to normal state closed ${circuitBreaker.state()}")\n * //sampleEnd\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-circuitbreaker-01.kt -->\n *\n * A common pattern to make fault-tolerant/resilient systems is to compose a [CircuitBreaker] with a backing-off policy retry Schedule to guarantee not overloading the resource and the client interacting with it.\n * but also not the client that is interacting with the resource.\n * Below you can see how the simple `retry` function will result in `Either.Left<CircuitBreaker.RejectedExecution>`,\n * but when we combine it with another schedule, it will always call the `CircuitBreaker` on times that it could've entered the [HalfOpen] state.\n * The reason why [Schedule] is not sufficient to make your system resilient is because you also have to take into account parallel calls to your functions,\n *; In contrast, a [CircuitBreaker] can track failures of every function call or even different functions to the same resource or service.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.resilience.CircuitBreaker\n * import arrow.resilience.Schedule\n * import arrow.resilience.retry\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.delay\n * import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds\n *\n * suspend fun main(): Unit {\n *   suspend fun apiCall(): Unit {\n *     println("apiCall . . .")\n *     throw RuntimeException("Overloaded service")\n *   }\n *\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val circuitBreaker = CircuitBreaker(\n *     resetTimeout = 2.seconds,\n *     openingStrategy = CircuitBreaker.OpeningStrategy.Count(maxFailures = 2),\n *     exponentialBackoffFactor = 2.0, // enable exponentialBackoffFactor\n *     maxResetTimeout = 60.seconds, // limit exponential back-off time\n *   )\n *\n *   suspend fun <A> resilient(schedule: Schedule<Throwable, *>, f: suspend () -> A): A =\n *     schedule.retry { circuitBreaker.protectOrThrow(f) }\n *\n *   Either.catch {\n *     resilient(Schedule.recurs(5), ::apiCall)\n *   }.let { println("recurs(5) apiCall twice and 4x short-circuit result from CircuitBreaker: $it") }\n *\n *   delay(2000)\n *   println("CircuitBreaker ready to half-open")\n *\n *   // Retry once and when the CircuitBreaker opens after 2 failures then retry with exponential back-off with same time as CircuitBreaker's resetTimeout\n *   val fiveTimesWithBackOff = Schedule.recurs<Throwable>(1) andThen\n *     Schedule.exponential(2.seconds) and Schedule.recurs(5)\n *\n *   Either.catch {\n *     resilient(fiveTimesWithBackOff, ::apiCall)\n *   }.let { println("exponential(2.seconds) and recurs(5) always retries with actual apiCall: $it") }\n *   //sampleEnd\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-circuitbreaker-02.kt -->\n

kotlin	YES	0	*\n * The saga design pattern is a way to manage data consistency across microservices in distributed\n * transaction scenarios. A [Saga] is useful when you need to manage data in a consistent manner\n * across services in distributed transaction scenarios. Or when you need to compose multiple\n * `actions` with a `compensation` that needs to run in a transaction like style.\n *\n * For example, let's say that we have the following domain types `Order`, `Payment`.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * data class Order(val id: UUID, val amount: Long)\n * data class Payment(val id: UUID, val orderId: UUID)\n * ```\n *\n * The creation of an `Order` can only remain when a payment has been made. kotlin	YES	0	*\n * [Resource] models resource allocation and releasing. It is especially useful when multiple resources that depend on each other need to be acquired and later released in reverse order.\n * The capability of _installing_ resources is called [ResourceScope], and [Resource] defines the value associating the `acquisition` step, and the `finalizer`.\n * [Resource] allocates and releases resources in a safe way that co-operates with Structured Concurrency, and KotlinX Coroutines.\n *\n * It is especially useful when multiple resources that depend on each other need to be acquired, and later released in reverse order.\n * Or when you want to compose other `suspend` functionality into resource safe programs, such as concurrency, parallelism or Arrow's Effect.\n *\n * Creating a [Resource] _value_ can be done using the it should already give you some idea if the capabilities of [Resource].\n *\n * ## Resource constructors\n *\n * [Resource] works entirely through a DSL,\n * which allows _installing_ a `Resource` through the `suspend fun <A> install(acquire: suspend () -> A, release: suspend (A, ExitCase) -> Unit): A` function.\n *\n * `acquire` is used to _allocate_ the `Resource`,\n * and before returning the resource `A` it also install the `release` handler into the `ResourceScope`.\n *\n * We can use `suspend fun` with `Scope` as an extension function receiver to create synthetic constructors for our `Resource`s.\n * If you're using _context receivers_ you can also use `context(Scope)` instead.\n *\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.ResourceScope\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.Resource\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.resource\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext\n *\n * class UserProcessor {\n *   suspend fun start(): Unit = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { println("Creating UserProcessor") }\n *   suspend fun shutdown(): Unit = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {\n *     println("Shutting down UserProcessor")\n *   }\n * }\n * -->\n * ```kotlin\n * suspend fun ResourceScope.userProcessor(): UserProcessor =\n *   install({  UserProcessor().also { it.start() } }) { processor, _ ->\n *     processor.shutdown()\n *   }\n * ```\n *\n * We can of course also create `lazy` representations of this by wrapping `install` in [resource] and returning the `suspend lambda` value instead.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val userProcessor: Resource<UserProcessor> = resource {\n *   val x: UserProcessor = install(\n *     {  UserProcessor().also { it.start() } },\n *     { processor, _ -> processor.shutdown() }\n *   )\n * interact with them in a safe way.\n *\n * Arrow offers the same elegant `bind` DSL for Resource composition as you might be familiar with from Arrow Core. Which we've already seen above, in our first example.\n * What is more interesting, is that we can also compose it with any other existing pattern from Arrow!\n * Let's compose our `UserProcessor` and `DataSource` in parallel, so that their `start` and `connect` methods can run in parallel.\n *\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.ResourceScope\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.resourceScope\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.parZip\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext\n *\n * class UserProcessor {\n *   suspend fun start(): Unit = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { println("Creating UserProcessor") }\n *   suspend fun shutdown(): Unit = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {\n *     println("Shutting down UserProcessor")\n *   }\n * }\n *\n * class DataSource {\n *   suspend fun connect(): Unit = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { println("Connecting dataSource") }\n *   suspend fun close(): Unit = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { println("Closed dataSource") }\n * }\n *\n * class Service(val db: DataSource, val userProcessor: UserProcessor) {\n *   suspend fun processData(): List<String> = (0..10).map { "Processed : $it" }\n * }\n * -->\n * ```kotlin\n * suspend fun ResourceScope.userProcessor(): UserProcessor =\n *   install({ UserProcessor().also { it.start() } }){ p,_ -> p.shutdown() }\n *\n * suspend fun ResourceScope.dataSource(): DataSource =\n *   install({ DataSource().also { it.connect() } }) { ds, _ -> ds.close() }\n *\n * suspend fun main(): Unit = resourceScope {\n *   val service = parZip({ userProcessor() }, { dataSource() }) { userProcessor, ds ->\n *     Service(ds, userProcessor)\n *   }\n *   val data = service.processData()\n *   println(data)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-resource-05.kt -->\n *\n * ## Conclusion\n *\n * [Resource] guarantee that their release finalizers are always invoked in the correct order when an exception is raised or the [Job] is running gets canceled.\n *\n * To achieve this [Resource] ensures that the `acquire` & `release` step are [NonCancellable].\n * If a cancellation signal, or an exception is received during `acquire`, the resource is assumed to not have been acquired and thus will not trigger the release function.\n *  => Any composed resources that are already acquired they will be guaranteed to release as expected.\n *\n * If you don't need a data-type like [Resource] but want a function alternative to `try/catch/finally` with automatic error composition,\n * and automatic [NonCancellable] `acquire` and `release` steps use [bracketCase] or [bracket].\n *

kotlin	YES	0	*\n * Describes a task with safe resource acquisition and release in the face of errors and interruption.\n * It would be the equivalent of an async capable `try/catch/finally` statements in mainstream imperative languages for resource\n * acquisition and release.\n *\n * @param acquire is the action to acquire the resource.\n *\n * @param use is the action to consume the resource and produce a result.\n * Once the resulting suspend program terminates, either successfully, error or disposed,\n * the [release] function will run to clean up the resources.\n *\n * @param release is the action that's supposed to release the allocated resource after `use` is done, irregardless\n * of its exit condition.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.*\n *\n * class File(val url: String) {\n *   fun open(): File = this\n *   fun close(): Unit {}\n *   override fun toString(): String = "This file contains some interesting content from $url!"\n * }\n *\n * suspend fun openFile(uri: String): File = File(uri).open()\n * suspend fun closeFile(file: File): Unit = file.close()\n * suspend fun fileToString(file: File): String = file.toString()\n *\n * suspend fun main(): Unit {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val res = bracket(\n *     acquire = { openFile("data.json") },\n *     use = { file -> fileToString(file) },\n *     release = { file: File -> closeFile(file) }\n *   )\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println(res)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-bracket-01.kt -->\n 
kotlin	YES	0	*\n * A way to safely acquire a resource and release in the face of errors and cancellation.\n * It uses [ExitCase] to distinguish between different exit cases when releasing the acquired resource.\n *\n * [bracketCase] exists out of three stages:\n *   1. acquisition\n *   2. consumption\n *   3. releasing\n *\n * 1. Resource acquisition is **NON CANCELLABLE**.\n *   If resource acquisition fails, meaning no resource was actually successfully acquired then we short-circuit the effect.\n *   As the resource was not acquired, it is not possible to [use] or [release] it.\n *   If it is successful we pass the result to stage 2 [use].\n *\n * 2. Resource consumption is like any other `suspend` effect. The key difference here is that it's wired in such a way that\n *   [release] **will always** be called either on [ExitCase.Cancelled], [ExitCase.Failure] or [ExitCase.Completed].\n *   If it failed, then the resulting [suspend] from [bracketCase] will be the error; otherwise the result of [use] will be returned.\n *\n * 3. Resource releasing is **NON CANCELLABLE**, otherwise it could result in leaks.\n *   In the case it throws an exception, the resulting [suspend] will be either such error, or a composed error if one occurred in the [use] stage.\n *\n * @param acquire is the action to acquire the resource.\n *\n * @param use is the action to consume the resource and produce a result.\n * Once the resulting suspend program terminates, either successfully, error or disposed,\n * the [release] function will run to clean up the resources.\n *\n * @param release is the action to release the allocated resource after [use] terminates.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.*\n *\n * class File(val url: String) {\n *   fun open(): File = this\n *   fun close(): Unit {}\n * }\n *\n * suspend fun File.content(): String =\n *     "This file contains some interesting content from $url!"\n * suspend fun openFile(uri: String): File = File(uri).open()\n * suspend fun closeFile(file: File): Unit = file.close()\n *\n * suspend fun main(): Unit {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val res = bracketCase(\n *     acquire = { openFile("data.json") },\n *     use = { file -> file.content() },\n *     release = { file, exitCase ->\n *       when (exitCase) {\n *         is ExitCase.Completed -> println("File closed with $exitCase")\n *         is ExitCase.Cancelled -> println("Program cancelled with $exitCase")\n *         is ExitCase.Failure -> println("Program failed with $exitCase")\n *       }\n *       closeFile(file)\n *     }\n *   )\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println(res)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-bracket-02.kt -->\n

kotlin	YES	0	*\n *\n * A [TSet] is a concurrent transactional implementation of a hashset.\n *\n * Based on a Hash-Array-Mapped-Trie implementation. While this does mean that a read may take up to 5 steps to be resolved (depending on how\n *  well distributed the hash function is), it also means that structural changes can be isolated and thus do not increase contention with\n *  other transactions. This effectively means concurrent access to different values is unlikely to interfere with each other.\n *\n * > Hash conflicts are resolved by chaining.\n *\n * ## Creating a [TSet]\n *\n * Depending on whether or not you are in a transaction you can use either [STM.newTSet] or [TSet.new] to create a new [TSet].\n *\n * There are a few alternatives because [TSet] can be supplied a custom hash strategy. If no argument is given it defaults to [Any.hashCode].\n *\n * ## Adding elements to the set\n *\n * Adding an element can be achieved by using either [STM.insert] or its alias [STM.plusAssign]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TSet\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tset = TSet.new<String>()\n *   atomically {\n *     tset.insert("Hello")\n *     tset += "World"\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tset-01.kt -->\n *\n * ## Removing an element from the set\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TSet\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tset = TSet.new<String>()\n *   atomically {\n *     tset.insert("Hello")\n *     tset.remove("Hello")\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tset-02.kt -->\n *\n * ## Checking for membership\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TSet\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tset = TSet.new<String>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tset.insert("Hello")\n *     tset.member("Hello")\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tset-03.kt -->\n *\n * ## Where are operations like `isEmpty` or `size`?\n *\n * This is a design tradeoff. While this does mean that a read may take up to 5 steps to be resolved (depending on how\n *  well distributed the hash function is), it also means that structural changes can be isolated and thus do not increase contention with\n *  other transactions. This effectively means concurrent access to different values is unlikely to interfere with each other.\n *\n * > Hash conflicts are resolved by chaining.\n *\n * ## Creating a [TMap]\n *\n * Depending on whether or not you are in a transaction you can use either [STM.newTMap] or [TMap.new] to create a new [TMap].\n *\n * There are a few alternatives because [TMap] can be supplied a custom hash strategy. If no argument is given it defaults to [Any.hashCode].\n *\n * ## Reading an element with a key\n *\n * Reading from a [TMap] can be done using either [STM.lookup] or its alias [STM.get].\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMap\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmap = TMap.new<Int, String>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tmap.set(1, "Hello")\n *     tmap[2] = "World"\n *\n *     tmap.lookup(1) + tmap[2]\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmap-01.kt -->\n *\n * > If the key is not present [STM.lookup] will not retry, instead it returns `null`.\n *\n * ## Inserting a value\n *\n * Inserting can be done using either [STM.insert] or its alias [STM.set]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMap\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmap = TMap.new<Int, String>()\n *   atomically {\n *     tmap.insert(1, "Hello")\n *     tmap[2] = "World"\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmap-02.kt -->\n *\n * Another option when adding elements is to use [STM.plusAssign]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMap\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmap = TMap.new<Int, String>()\n *   atomically {\n *     tmap += (1 to "Hello")\n *     tmap += (2 to "World")\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmap-03.kt -->\n *\n * ## Updating an existing value [TMap]:\n *\n * Using [STM.update] it is possible to update an existing value of a [TMap]. If the value is not present it does nothing.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMap\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmap = TMap.new<Int, String>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tmap[1] = "Hello"\n *     tmap[2] = "World"\n *\n *     tmap.update(1) { it.reversed() }\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmap-04.kt -->\n *\n * ## Checking membership\n *\n * Using [STM.member] it is possible to check if a [TMap] contains a value for a key:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMap\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmap = TMap.new<Int, String>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tmap[1] = "Hello"\n *     tmap.member(1)\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmap-05.kt -->\n *\n * ## Removing a value from a [TMap]\n *\n * Removing is done by using [STM.remove]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMap\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmap = TMap.new<Int, String>()\n *   atomically {\n *     tmap[1] = "Hello"\n *\n *     tmap.remove(1)\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmap-06.kt -->\n *\n * ## Where are operations like `isEmpty` or `size`?\n *\n * This is a design tradeoff. It is entirely possible to track size however this usually requires one additional [TVar] for size and\n *  almost every operation would modify that. That will lead to contention and thus decrease performance.\n *\n * Should this feature interest you and performance is not as important please open an issue. It is most certainly possible to add another version\n *  of [TMap] that keeps track of its size.\n *\n 
kotlin	YES	0	*\n * A [TQueue] is a transactional unbounded queue which can be written to and read from concurrently.\n *\n * The implementation uses two [TVar]'s containing lists. One for read and one for write access.\n *  Due to the semantics of [STM] this means a write to the queue will never invalidate or block a read and vice versa, making highly\n *  concurrent use possible.\n *\n * > In practice, if the read variable is empty, the two must swap contents but this operation is infrequent and thus can be ignored.\n *\n * ## Creating a [TQueue]\n *\n * Creating an empty queue can be done by using either [STM.newTQueue] or [TQueue.new] depending on whether or not you are in\n *  a transaction or not.\n *\n * ## Writing to the [TQueue]\n *\n * Writing to the end of the queue is done by using [STM.write]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TQueue\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tq = TQueue.new<Int>()\n *   atomically {\n *     tq.write(2)\n *     // or alternatively\n *     tq += 4\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Items in queue ${atomically { tq.flush() }}")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tqueue-01.kt -->\n *\n * It is also possible to write to the front of the queue, but since that accesses the read variable it can lead to worse overall performance:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TQueue\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tq = TQueue.new<Int>()\n *   atomically {\n *     tq.write(1)\n *     tq.writeFront(2)\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Items in queue ${atomically { tq.flush() }}")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tqueue-02.kt -->\n *\n * ## Reading items from a [TQueue]\n *\n * There are several different ways to read from a [TQueue], the most common one being [STM.read]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TQueue\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tq = TQueue.new<Int>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tq.write(2)\n *     tq.read()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n *   println("Items in queue ${atomically { tq.flush() }}")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tqueue-03.kt -->\n *\n * Should the queue be empty calling [STM.read] will cause the transaction to retry and thus wait for items to be added to the queue.\n *  This can be avoided using [STM.tryRead] instead:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TQueue\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tq = TQueue.new<Int>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tq.tryRead()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n *   println("Items in queue ${atomically { tq.flush() }}")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tqueue-04.kt -->\n *\n * [STM.read] also removes the read item from the queue. Alternatively [STM.peek] will leave the queue unchanged on a read:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TQueue\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tq = TQueue.new<Int>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tq.write(2)\n *\n *     tq.peek()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n *   println("Items in queue ${atomically { tq.flush() }}")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tqueue-05.kt -->\n *\n * As with [STM.read] [STM.peek] will retry should the queue be empty. The alternative [STM.tryPeek] is there to avoid that:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TQueue\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tq = TQueue.new<Int>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tq.tryPeek()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n *   println("Items in queue ${atomically { tq.flush() }}")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tqueue-06.kt -->\n *\n * It is also possible to read the entire list in one go using [STM.flush]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TQueue\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tq = TQueue.new<Int>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tq.write(2)\n *     tq.write(4)\n *\n *     tq.flush()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n *   println("Items in queue ${atomically { tq.flush() }}")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tqueue-07.kt -->\n *\n * ## Checking a queues size\n *\n * Checking if a queue is empty can be done by using either [STM.isEmpty] or [STM.isNotEmpty]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TQueue\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tq = TQueue.new<Int>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tq.isEmpty()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tqueue-08.kt -->\n *\n * Retrieving the actual size of a list can be done using [STM.size]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TQueue\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tq = TQueue.new<Int>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tq.size()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tqueue-09.kt -->\n *\n * > All three of these methods have to access both the write and read end of a [TQueue] and thus can increase contention. Use them sparingly!\n *\n * ## Removing elements from a [TQueue]\n *\n * It is also possible to remove elements from a [TQueue] using [STM.removeAll]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TQueue\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tq = TQueue.new<Int>()\n *   atomically {\n *     tq.write(0)\n *     tq.removeAll { it != 0 }\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Items in queue ${atomically { tq.flush() }}")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tqueue-10.kt -->\n *\n * > This method also access both ends of the queue and thus should be used infrequently to avoid contention.\n

There is a datastructure that can avoid reverse while still\n *  being very fast for head access: A finger tree.\n * But finger trees are cache unfriendly and likely be a bit slower overall.\n *\n * Why this over alternatives?\n * - Kotlin stdlib List\n *  Implements mutability by copy and thus heavily pressures gc. kotlin	YES	0	*\n * # Consistent and safe concurrent state updates\n *\n * Software transactional memory, or STM, is an abstraction for concurrent state modification.\n * With [STM] one can write code that concurrently accesses state and that can easily be composed without\n *  exposing details of how it ensures safety guarantees.\n * Programs running within an [STM] transaction will neither deadlock nor have race-conditions.\n *\n * > The api of [STM] is based on the haskell package [stm](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/stm) and the implementation is based on the GHC implementation for fine-grained locks.\n *\n * The base building blocks of [STM] are [TVar]'s and the primitives [retry], [orElse] and [catch].\n *\n * ## STM Datastructures\n *\n * There are several datastructures built on top of [TVar]'s already provided out of the box:\n * - [TQueue]: A transactional mutable queue\n * - [TMVar]: A mutable transactional variable that may be empty\n * - [TSet], [TMap]: Transactional Set and Map\n * - [TArray]: Array of [TVar]'s\n * - [TSemaphore]: Transactional semaphore\n * - [TVar]: A transactional mutable variable\n *\n * All of these structures (excluding [TVar]) are built upon [TVar]'s and the [STM] primitives and implementing other\n *  datastructures with [STM] can be done by composing the existing structures.\n *\n * ## Reading and writing to concurrent state:\n *\n * In order to modify transactional datastructures we have to be inside the [STM] context. This is achieved either by defining our\n *  functions with [STM] as the receiver or using [stm] to create lambda functions with [STM] as the receiver.\n *\n * Running a transaction is then done using [atomically]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.STM\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * fun STM.transfer(from: TVar<Int>, to: TVar<Int>, amount: Int): Unit {\n *   withdraw(from, amount)\n *   deposit(to, amount)\n * }\n *\n * fun STM.deposit(acc: TVar<Int>, amount: Int): Unit {\n *   val current = acc.read()\n *   acc.write(current + amount)\n *   // or the shorthand acc.modify { it + amount }\n * }\n *\n * fun STM.withdraw(acc: TVar<Int>, amount: Int): Unit {\n *   val current = acc.read()\n *   if (current - amount >= 0) acc.write(current - amount)\n *   else throw IllegalStateException("Not enough money in the account!")\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   val acc1 = TVar.new(500)\n *   val acc2 = TVar.new(300)\n *   println("Balance account 1: ${acc1.unsafeRead()}")\n *   println("Balance account 2: ${acc2.unsafeRead()}")\n *   println("Performing transaction")\n *   atomically { transfer(acc1, acc2, 50) }\n *   println("Balance account 1: ${acc1.unsafeRead()}")\n *   println("Balance account 2: ${acc2.unsafeRead()}")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-stm-01.kt -->\n * This example shows a banking service moving money from one account to the other with [STM].\n * Should the first account not have enough money we throw an exception. This code is guaranteed to never deadlock and to never\n *  produce an invalid state by committing after the read state has changed concurrently.\n *\n *  > Note: A transaction that sees an invalid state (a [TVar] that was read has been changed concurrently) will restart and try again.\n *   This usually means we rerun the function entirely, therefore it is recommended to keep transactions small and to never use code that\n *   has side-effects inside. However no kotlin interface can actually keep you from doing side effects inside STM.\n *   Using side-effects such as access to resources, logging or network access comes with severe disadvantages:\n *   - Transactions may be aborted at any time so accessing resources may never trigger finalizers\n *   - Transactions may rerun an arbitrary amount of times before finishing and thus all effects will rerun.\n *\n * ## Retrying manually\n *\n * It is sometimes beneficial to manually abort the current transaction if, for example, an invalid state has been read. E.g. a [TQueue] had no elements to read.\n *  The aborted transaction will automatically restart once any previously accessed variable has changed.\n *\n * This is achieved by the primitive [retry]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.STM\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.async\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.delay\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * fun STM.transfer(from: TVar<Int>, to: TVar<Int>, amount: Int): Unit {\n *   withdraw(from, amount)\n *   deposit(to, amount)\n * }\n *\n * fun STM.deposit(acc: TVar<Int>, amount: Int): Unit {\n *   val current = acc.read()\n *   acc.write(current + amount)\n *   // or the shorthand acc.modify { it + amount }\n * }\n *\n * fun STM.withdraw(acc: TVar<Int>, amount: Int): Unit {\n *   val current = acc.read()\n *   if (current - amount >= 0) acc.write(current - amount)\n *   else retry() // we now retry if there is not enough money in the account\n *   // this can also be achieved by using `check(current - amount >= 0); acc.write(it + amount)`\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n *\n * fun main(): Unit = runBlocking {\n *   val acc1 = TVar.new(0)\n *   val acc2 = TVar.new(300)\n *   println("Balance account 1: ${acc1.unsafeRead()}")\n *   println("Balance account 2: ${acc2.unsafeRead()}")\n *   async {\n *     println("Sending money - Searching")\n *     delay(2000)\n *     println("Sending money - Found some")\n *     atomically { acc1.write(100_000_000) }\n *   }\n *   println("Performing transaction")\n *   atomically {\n *     println("Trying to transfer")\n *     transfer(acc1, acc2, 50)\n *   }\n *   println("Balance account 1: ${acc1.unsafeRead()}")\n *   println("Balance account 2: ${acc2.unsafeRead()}")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-stm-02.kt -->\n *\n * Here in this (silly) example we changed `withdraw` to use [retry] and thus wait until enough money is in the account, which after\n *  a few seconds just happens to be the case.\n *\n * [retry] can be used to implement a lot of complex transactions and many datastructures like [TMVar] or [TQueue] use to to great effect.\n *\n * ## Branching with [orElse]\n *\n * [orElse] is another important primitive which allows a user to detect if a branch called [retry] and then use a fallback instead.\n *  If the fallback retries as well the whole transaction retries.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.STM\n * import arrow.fx.stm.stm\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * fun STM.transaction(v: TVar<Int>): Int? =\n *   stm {\n *     val result = v.read()\n *     check(result in 0..10)\n *     result\n *   } orElse { null }\n * //sampleEnd\n *\n * fun main(): Unit = runBlocking {\n *   val v = TVar.new(100)\n *   println("Value is ${v.unsafeRead()}")\n *   atomically { transaction(v) }\n *     .also { println("Transaction returned $it") }\n *   println("Set value to 5")\n *   println("Value is ${v.unsafeRead()}")\n *   atomically { v.write(5) }\n *   atomically { transaction(v) }\n *     .also { println("Transaction returned $it") }\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-stm-03.kt -->\n *\n * This example uses [stm] which is a helper just like the stdlib function [suspend] to ease use of an infix function like [orElse].\n * In this transaction, when the value inside the variable is not in the correct range, the transaction retries (due to [check] calling [retry]).\n * If it is in the correct range it simply returns the value. [orElse] here intercepts a call to [retry] and executes the alternative which simply returns null.\n *\n * ## Exceptions\n *\n * Throwing inside [STM] will let the exception bubble up to either a [catch] handler or to [atomically] which will rethrow it.\n *\n * > Note: Using `try {...} catch (e: Exception) {...}` is not encouraged because any state change inside `try` will not be undone when\n *   an exception occurs! The recommended way of catching exceptions is to use [catch] which properly rolls back the transaction!\n *\n * Further reading:\n * - [Composable memory transactions, by Tim Harris, Simon Marlow, Simon Peyton Jones, and Maurice Herlihy, in ACM Conference on Principles and Practice of Parallel Programming 2005.](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/composable-memory-transactions/)\n

kotlin	YES	0	*\n * Run a transaction to completion.\n *\n * This comes with the guarantee that, at the time of committing the transaction, all read variables have a consistent state\n *  (they have not changed after the first read). Otherwise the transaction will be aborted and run again.\n *\n * Note that only reads and writes inside a single transaction have this guarantee.\n * Code that calls [atomically] as follows will again be subject to race conditions:\n * `atomically { v.read() }.let { atomically { v.write(it + 1) } }`. Because those are separate transactions the value inside `v` might change\n *  between transactions! The only safe way is to do it in one go: `atomically { v.write(v.read() + 1) }`\n *\n * Transactions that only read or access completely disjoint set of [TVar]'s will be able to commit in parallel as [STM] in arrow\n *  uses an approach the locks only modified [TVar]'s on commit. Only calls to [STM.write] need to be synchronized, however the performance of [STM] is still\n *  heavily linked to the amount of [TVar]'s accessed so it is good practice to keep transactions short.\n *\n * Keeping transactions short has another benefit which comes from another drawback of [STM]:\n * There is no notion of fairness when it comes to transactions. The fastest transaction always wins.\n * This can be problematic if a large number of small transactions starve out a larger transaction by forcing it to retry a lot.\n * In practice this rarely happens, however to avoid such a scenario it is recommended to keep transactions small.\n *\n * This may suspend if [STM.retry] is called and no accessed [TVar] changed. It will then resume automatically after any accessed [TVar] changed.\n *\n * Rethrows all exceptions not caught by inside [f]. Remember to use [STM.catch] to handle exceptions as `try {} catch` will not handle transaction\n *  state properly!\n 
kotlin	YES	0	*\n * A [TVar] is a mutable reference that can only be (safely) accessed inside a [STM] transaction.\n *\n * ## Creating a [TVar]\n *\n * There are two ways of creating [TVar]'s:\n * - [STM.newTVar] to create a [TVar] inside a transaction\n * - [TVar.new] to create a top-level [TVar] outside of a transaction\n *\n * Strictly speaking [TVar.new] is not necessary as it can be defined as `atomically { newTVar(v) }` however [TVar.new] is much\n *  faster because it avoids creating a (pointless) transaction.\n * [STM.newTVar] should be used inside transactions because it is not possible to use [TVar.new] inside [STM] due to `suspend`.\n *\n * ## Reading a value from a [TVar]\n *\n * One-off reading from a [TVar] outside of a transaction can be done by using [TVar.unsafeRead].\n * Despite the name using this method is only unsafe if the read value (or a derivative) is then used inside another transaction which may cause\n *  race conditions again. However the benefit of using this over `atomically { tvar.read() }` is that it avoids creating a transaction and is\n *  thus much faster.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TVar\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tvar = TVar.new(10)\n *   val result = tvar.unsafeRead()\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println(result)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tvar-01.kt -->\n *\n * Reading from a [TVar] inside a transaction is done by using [STM.read].\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tvar = TVar.new(10)\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tvar.read()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println(result)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tvar-02.kt -->\n *\n * > Checking the validity of a transaction is done by checking the contents of all accessed [TVar]'s before locking the [TVar]'s that have\n *  been written to and then checking only the [TVar]'s that have only been read not modified again. To keep transactions as fast as possible\n *  it is key to keep the number of accessed [TVar]'s small.\n *\n * > Another important thing to remember is that only writes will ever lock a [TVar] and only those that need to be changed.\n *  This means that so long as transactions access disjoint sets of variables or a transaction is read only, they may run in parallel.\n *\n * ## Modifying the value inside the [TVar]\n *\n * Writing a new value to the [TVar]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tvar = TVar.new(10)\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tvar.write(20)\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println(result)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tvar-03.kt -->\n *\n * Modifying the value based on the initial value:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tvar = TVar.new(10)\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tvar.modify { it * 2 }\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println(result)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tvar-04.kt -->\n *\n * Writing a new value to the [TVar] and returning the initial value:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tvar = TVar.new(10)\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tvar.swap(20)\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n *   println("New value ${tvar.unsafeRead()}")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tvar-05.kt -->\n

kotlin	YES	0	*\n * A [TMVar] is a mutable reference that can either be empty or hold a value.\n *\n * The main use for [TMVar] is as a synchronization primitive as it can be used to force other transactions\n *  to wait until a [TMVar] is full.\n *\n * ## Creating a [TMVar]:\n *\n * As usual with [STM] types there are two equal sets of operators for creating them, one that can be used inside\n *  and one for use outside of transactions:\n * - [TMVar.new] and [STM.newTMVar] create a new filled [TMVar]\n * - [TMVar.empty] and [STM.newEmptyTMVar] create an empty [TMVar]\n *\n * ## Reading the content of a [TMVar]\n *\n * Taking the value out of a [TMVar]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmvar = TMVar.new(10)\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tmvar.take()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n *   println("New value ${atomically { tmvar.tryTake() } }")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmvar-01.kt -->\n *\n * Should the [TMVar] be empty at the time of calling [STM.take], it will call [STM.retry], suspend and wait for another transaction to\n *  put a value back.\n *\n * This behaviour can be avoided by using [STM.tryTake] instead:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmvar = TMVar.empty<Int>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tmvar.tryTake()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n *   println("New value ${atomically { tmvar.tryTake() } }")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmvar-02.kt -->\n *\n * Another effect of using either [STM.take] or [STM.tryTake] is that the [TMVar] will be empty after a successful call. Alternatively if you just\n *  want to read without emptying you can use either [STM.read] or [STM.tryRead] which will not remove the value.\n *  As with [STM.take] [STM.read] will fail and retry the transaction should the [TMVar] be empty, whereas [STM.tryTake] and [STM.tryRead] will return null instead.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmvar = TMVar.new(30)\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tmvar.read()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n *   println("New value ${atomically { tmvar.tryTake() } }")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmvar-03.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmvar = TMVar.empty<Int>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tmvar.tryRead()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmvar-04.kt -->\n *\n * ## Setting the value of a [TMVar]:\n *\n * Changing the value of an empty [TMVar]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmvar = TMVar.empty<Int>()\n *   atomically {\n *     tmvar.put(20)\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("New value ${atomically { tmvar.tryTake() } }")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmvar-05.kt -->\n *\n * Should the [TMVar] be full, [STM.put] will call [STM.retry] and wait for another transaction to empty the [TMVar] again.\n *  This can be avoided by using [STM.tryPut] instead. [STM.tryPut] returns whether or not the operation was successful.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmvar = TMVar.new(20)\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tmvar.tryPut(30)\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n *   println("New value ${atomically { tmvar.tryTake() } }")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmvar-06.kt -->\n *\n * Another common pattern is to swap the value of a [TMVar], returning the old value and setting a new one:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmvar = TMVar.new(30)\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tmvar.swap(40)\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n *   println("New value ${atomically { tmvar.tryTake() } }")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmvar-07.kt -->\n *\n * ## Checking if a [TMVar] is empty:\n *\n * Checking if a [TMVar] is empty or not can be done by either using [STM.isEmpty] or [STM.isNotEmpty]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmvar = TMVar.empty<Int>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tmvar.isEmpty()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println("Result $result")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmvar-08.kt -->\n *\n * > Because the state of a transaction is constant there can never be a race condition between checking if a `TMVar` is empty and subsequent\n *  reads in the *same* transaction.\n *\n

kotlin	YES	0	*\n * Eval is a monad which controls evaluation of a value or a computation that produces a value.\n *\n * Three basic evaluation strategies:\n *\n *  - Now:        evaluated immediately\n *  - Later:      evaluated once when value is needed, may evaluate more than once\n *  - AtMostOnce: evaluated once when the value is needed, evaluates at most once\n *  - Always:     evaluated every time value is needed\n *\n * The Later and Always are both lazy strategies while Now is eager.\n * Later and Always are distinguished from each other only by\n * memoization: once evaluated Later will save the value to be returned\n * immediately if it is needed again. Always will run its computation\n * every time.\n *\n * methods, which use an internal trampoline to avoid stack overflows.\n * Computation done within .map and .flatMap is always done lazily,\n * even when applied to a Now instance.\n *\n * It is not generally good style to pattern-match on Eval instances.\n * Rather, use .map and .flatMap to chain computation, and use .value\n * to get the result when needed. It is also not good style to create\n * Eval instances whose computation involves calling .value on another\n * Eval instance -- this can defeat the trampolining and lead to stack\n * overflows.\n *\n * Example of stack safety:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.eval.Eval\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * fun even(n: Int): Eval<Boolean> =\n *   Eval.always { n == 0 }.flatMap {\n *     if(it == true) Eval.now(true)\n *     else odd(n - 1)\n *   }\n *\n * fun odd(n: Int): Eval<Boolean> =\n *   Eval.always { n == 0 }.flatMap {\n *     if(it == true) Eval.now(false)\n *     else even(n - 1)\n *   }\n *\n * // if not wrapped in eval this type of computation would blow the stack and result in a StackOverflowError\n * fun main() {\n *   println(odd(100000).value())\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-eval-01.kt -->\n *\n
