kotlin	YES	0	*\n * <!--- TEST_NAME OptionKnitTest -->\n *\n * If you have worked with Java at all in the past, it is very likely that you have come across a `NullPointerException` at some time (other languages will throw similarly named errors in such a case). Usually this happens because some method returns `null` when you weren't expecting it and, thus, isn't dealing with that possibility in your client code. A value of `null` is often abused to represent an absent optional value.\n * Kotlin tries to solve the problem by getting rid of `null` values altogether, and providing its own special syntax [Null-safety machinery based on `?`](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/reference/null-safety.html).\n *\n * Arrow models the absence of values through the `Option` datatype similar to how Scala, Haskell, and other FP languages handle optional values.\n *\n * `Option<A>` is a container for an optional value of type `A`. If the value of type `A` is present, the `Option<A>` is an instance of `Some<A>`, containing the present value of type `A`. If the value is absent, the `Option<A>` is the object `None`.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n * import arrow.core.none\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val someValue: Option<String> = Some("I am wrapped in something")\n * val emptyValue: Option<String> = none()\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println("value = $someValue")\n *  println("emptyValue = $emptyValue")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-01.kt -->\n *\n * Let's write a function that may or may not give us a string, thus returning `Option<String>`:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * fun maybeItWillReturnSomething(flag: Boolean): Option<String> =\n *  if (flag) Some("Found value") else None\n * //sampleEnd\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-02.kt -->\n *\n * Using `getOrElse`, we can provide a default value `"No value"` when the optional argument `None` does not exist:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n * import arrow.core.getOrElse\n *\n * fun maybeItWillReturnSomething(flag: Boolean): Option<String> =\n *  if (flag) Some("Found value") else None\n *\n * val value1 =\n * //sampleStart\n *  maybeItWillReturnSomething(true)\n *     .getOrElse { "No value" }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(value1)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-03.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n * import arrow.core.getOrElse\n *\n * fun maybeItWillReturnSomething(flag: Boolean): Option<String> =\n *  if (flag) Some("Found value") else None\n *\n * val value2 =\n * //sampleStart\n *  maybeItWillReturnSomething(false)\n *   .getOrElse { "No value" }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(value2)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-04.kt -->\n *\n * Checking whether option has value:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n *\n * fun maybeItWillReturnSomething(flag: Boolean): Option<String> =\n *  if (flag) Some("Found value") else None\n *\n *  //sampleStart\n * val valueSome = maybeItWillReturnSomething(true) is None\n * val valueNone = maybeItWillReturnSomething(false) is None\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println("valueSome = $valueSome")\n *  println("valueNone = $valueNone")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-05.kt -->\n * Creating a `Option<T>` of a `T?`. Useful for working with values that can be nullable:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Option\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val myString: String? = "Nullable string"\n * val option: Option<String> = Option.fromNullable(myString)\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main () {\n *  println("option = $option")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-06.kt -->\n *\n * Option can also be used with when statements:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val someValue: Option<Double> = Some(20.0)\n * val value = when(someValue) {\n *  is Some -> someValue.value\n *  is None -> 0.0\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main () {\n *  println("value = $value")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-07.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val noValue: Option<Double> = None\n * val value = when(noValue) {\n *  is Some -> noValue.value\n *  is None -> 0.0\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main () {\n *  println("value = $value")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-08.kt -->\n *\n * An alternative for pattern matching is folding. This is possible because an option could be looked at as a collection or foldable structure with either one or zero elements.\n *\n * One of these operations is `map`. This operation allows us to map the inner value to a different type while preserving the option:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val number: Option<Int> = Some(3)\n * val noNumber: Option<Int> = None\n * val mappedResult1 = number.map { it * 1.5 }\n * val mappedResult2 = noNumber.map { it * 1.5 }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main () {\n *  println("number = $number")\n *  println("noNumber = $noNumber")\n *  println("mappedResult1 = $mappedResult1")\n *  println("mappedResult2 = $mappedResult2")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-09.kt -->\n * Another operation is `fold`. This operation will extract the value from the option, or provide a default if the value is `None`\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n *\n * val fold =\n * //sampleStart\n *  Some(3).fold({ 1 }, { it * 3 })\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main () {\n *  println(fold)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-10.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.none\n *\n * val fold =\n * //sampleStart\n *  none<Int>().fold({ 1 }, { it * 3 })\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main () {\n *  println(fold)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-11.kt -->\n *\n * Arrow also adds syntax to all datatypes so you can easily lift them into the context of `Option` where needed.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.some\n * import arrow.core.none\n *\n * //sampleStart\n *  val some = 1.some()\n *  val none = none<String>()\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main () {\n *  println("some = $some")\n *  println("none = $none")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-12.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.toOption\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val nullString: String? = null\n * val valueFromNull = nullString.toOption()\n *\n * val helloString: String? = "Hello"\n * val valueFromStr = helloString.toOption()\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main () {\n *  println("valueFromNull = $valueFromNull")\n *  println("valueFromStr = $valueFromStr")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-13.kt -->\n *\n * You can easily convert between `A?` and `Option<A>` by using the `toOption()` extension or `Option.fromNullable` constructor.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.firstOrNone\n * import arrow.core.toOption\n * import arrow.core.Option\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val foxMap = mapOf(1 to "The", 2 to "Quick", 3 to "Brown", 4 to "Fox")\n *\n * val empty = foxMap.entries.firstOrNull { it.key == 5 }?.value.let { it?.toCharArray() }.toOption()\n * val filled = Option.fromNullable(foxMap.entries.firstOrNull { it.key == 5 }?.value.let { it?.toCharArray() })\n *\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println("empty = $empty")\n *  println("filled = $filled")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-14.kt -->\n *\n * ### Transforming the inner contents\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Some\n *\n * fun main() {\n * val value =\n *  //sampleStart\n *    Some(1).map { it + 1 }\n *  //sampleEnd\n *  println(value)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-15.kt -->\n *\n * ## Credits\n *\n * Contents partially adapted from [Scala Exercises Option Tutorial](https://www.scala-exercises.org/std_lib/options)\n * Originally based on the Scala Koans.\n

kotlin	YES	0	*\n * <!--- TEST_NAME EitherKnitTest -->\n *\n * In day-to-day programming, it is fairly common to find ourselves writing functions that can fail.\n * For instance, querying a service may result in a connection issue, or some unexpected JSON response.\n *\n * To communicate these errors, it has become common practice to throw exceptions; however,\n * exceptions are not tracked in any way, shape, or form by the compiler. To see what\n * kind of exceptions (if any) a function may throw, we have to dig through the source code.\n * Then, to handle these exceptions, we have to make sure we catch them at the call site. This\n * all becomes even more unwieldy when we try to compose exception-throwing procedures.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * //sampleStart\n * val throwsSomeStuff: (Int) -> Double = {x -> x.toDouble()}\n * val throwsOtherThings: (Double) -> String = {x -> x.toString()}\n * val moreThrowing: (String) -> List<String> = {x -> listOf(x)}\n * val magic: (Int) -> List<String> = { x ->\n *   val y = throwsSomeStuff(x)\n *   val z = throwsOtherThings(y)\n *   moreThrowing(z)\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println ("magic = $magic")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-01.kt -->\n *\n * Assume we happily throw exceptions in our code. Looking at the types of the functions above, any could throw a number of exceptions -- we do not know. When we compose, exceptions from any of the constituent\n * functions can be thrown. Moreover, they may throw the same kind of exception\n * (e.g., `IllegalArgumentException`) and, thus, it gets tricky tracking exactly where an exception came from.\n *\n * How then do we communicate an error? By making it explicit in the data type we return.\n *\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n *\n * val left: Either<String, Int> =\n * //sampleStart\n *  Either.Left("Something went wrong")\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(left)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-02.kt -->\n *\n * Because `Either` is right-biased, it is possible to define a Monad instance for it.\n *\n * Since we only ever want the computation to continue in the case of [Right] (as captured by the right-bias nature),\n * we fix the left type parameter and leave the right one free.\n *\n * So, the map and flatMap methods are right-biased:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val right: Either<String, Int> = Either.Right(5)\n * val value = right.flatMap{ Either.Right(it + 1) }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println("value = $value")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-03.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val left: Either<String, Int> = Either.Left("Something went wrong")\n * val value = left.flatMap{ Either.Right(it + 1) }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println("value = $value")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-04.kt -->\n *\n * ## Using Either instead of exceptions\n *\n * As a running example, we will have a series of functions that will:\n *\n * * Parse a string into an integer\n * * Calculate the reciprocal\n * * Convert the reciprocal into a string\n *\n * Using exception-throwing code, we could write something like this:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * fun parse(s: String): Int =\n *   if (s.matches(Regex("-?[0-9]+"))) s.toInt()\n *   else throw NumberFormatException("$s is not a valid integer.")\n *\n * fun reciprocal(i: Int): Double =\n *   if (i == 0) throw IllegalArgumentException("Cannot take reciprocal of 0.")\n *   else 1.0 / i\n *\n * fun stringify(d: Double): String = d.toString()\n * //sampleEnd\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-05.kt -->\n *\n * Instead, let's make the fact that some of our functions can fail explicit in the return type.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n * import arrow.core.left\n * import arrow.core.right\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * // Either Style\n * fun parse(s: String): Either<NumberFormatException, Int> =\n *   if (s.matches(Regex("-?[0-9]+"))) Either.Right(s.toInt())\n *   else Either.Left(NumberFormatException("$s is not a valid integer."))\n *\n * fun reciprocal(i: Int): Either<IllegalArgumentException, Double> =\n *   if (i == 0) Either.Left(IllegalArgumentException("Cannot take reciprocal of 0."))\n *   else Either.Right(1.0 / i)\n *\n * fun stringify(d: Double): String = d.toString()\n *\n * fun magic(s: String): Either<Exception, String> =\n *   parse(s).flatMap { reciprocal(it) }.map { stringify(it) }\n * //sampleEnd\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-06.kt -->\n *\n * These calls to `parse` return a [Left] and [Right] value\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n *\n * fun parse(s: String): Either<NumberFormatException, Int> =\n *   if (s.matches(Regex("-?[0-9]+"))) Either.Right(s.toInt())\n *   else Either.Left(NumberFormatException("$s is not a valid integer."))\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val notANumber = parse("Not a number")\n * val number2 = parse("2")\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println("notANumber = $notANumber")\n *  println("number2 = $number2")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-07.kt -->\n *\n * Now, using combinators like `flatMap` and `map`, we can compose our functions together.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n *\n * fun parse(s: String): Either<NumberFormatException, Int> =\n *   if (s.matches(Regex("-?[0-9]+"))) Either.Right(s.toInt())\n *   else Either.Left(NumberFormatException("$s is not a valid integer."))\n *\n * fun reciprocal(i: Int): Either<IllegalArgumentException, Double> =\n *   if (i == 0) Either.Left(IllegalArgumentException("Cannot take reciprocal of 0."))\n *   else Either.Right(1.0 / i)\n *\n * fun stringify(d: Double): String = d.toString()\n *\n * fun magic(s: String): Either<Exception, String> =\n *   parse(s).flatMap{ reciprocal(it) }.map{ stringify(it) }\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val magic0 = magic("0")\n * val magic1 = magic("1")\n * val magicNotANumber = magic("Not a number")\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println("magic0 = $magic0")\n *  println("magic1 = $magic1")\n *  println("magicNotANumber = $magicNotANumber")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-08.kt -->\n *\n * In the following exercise, we pattern-match on every case in which the `Either` returned by `magic` can be in.\n * Note the `when` clause in the [Left] - the compiler will complain if we leave that out because it knows that,\n * given the type `Either[Exception, String]`, there can be inhabitants of [Left] that are not\n * `NumberFormatException` or `IllegalArgumentException`. You should also notice that we are using\n * [SmartCast](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/reference/typecasts.html#smart-casts) for accessing [Left] and [Right]\n * values.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n *\n * fun parse(s: String): Either<NumberFormatException, Int> =\n *   if (s.matches(Regex("-?[0-9]+"))) Either.Right(s.toInt())\n *   else Either.Left(NumberFormatException("$s is not a valid integer."))\n *\n * fun reciprocal(i: Int): Either<IllegalArgumentException, Double> =\n *   if (i == 0) Either.Left(IllegalArgumentException("Cannot take reciprocal of 0."))\n *   else Either.Right(1.0 / i)\n *\n * fun stringify(d: Double): String = d.toString()\n *\n * fun magic(s: String): Either<Exception, String> =\n *   parse(s).flatMap{ reciprocal(it) }.map{ stringify(it) }\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val x = magic("2")\n * val value = when(x) {\n *   is Either.Left -> when (x.value) {\n *     is NumberFormatException -> "Not a number!"\n *     is IllegalArgumentException -> "Can't take reciprocal of 0!"\n *     else -> "Unknown error"\n *   }\n *   is Either.Right -> "Got reciprocal: ${x.value}"\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println("value = $value")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-09.kt -->\n *\n * Instead of using exceptions as our error value, let's instead enumerate explicitly the things that\n * can go wrong in our program.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n * //sampleStart\n * // Either with ADT Style\n *\n * sealed class Error {\n *   object NotANumber : Error()\n *   object NoZeroReciprocal : Error()\n * }\n *\n * fun parse(s: String): Either<Error, Int> =\n *   if (s.matches(Regex("-?[0-9]+"))) Either.Right(s.toInt())\n *   else Either.Left(Error.NotANumber)\n *\n * fun reciprocal(i: Int): Either<Error, Double> =\n *   if (i == 0) Either.Left(Error.NoZeroReciprocal)\n *   else Either.Right(1.0 / i)\n *\n * fun stringify(d: Double): String = d.toString()\n *\n * fun magic(s: String): Either<Error, String> =\n *   parse(s).flatMap{reciprocal(it)}.map{ stringify(it) }\n * //sampleEnd\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-10.kt -->\n *\n * For our little module, we enumerate any and all errors that can occur. Then, instead of using\n * exception classes as error values, we use one of the enumerated cases. Now, when we pattern match,\n * we are able to comphrensively handle failure without resulting in an `else` branch; moreover,\n * since Error is sealed, no outside code can add additional subtypes that we might fail to handle.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n *\n * sealed class Error {\n *  object NotANumber : Error()\n *  object NoZeroReciprocal : Error()\n * }\n *\n * fun parse(s: String): Either<Error, Int> =\n *   if (s.matches(Regex("-?[0-9]+"))) Either.Right(s.toInt())\n *   else Either.Left(Error.NotANumber)\n *\n * fun reciprocal(i: Int): Either<Error, Double> =\n *   if (i == 0) Either.Left(Error.NoZeroReciprocal)\n *   else Either.Right(1.0 / i)\n *\n * fun stringify(d: Double): String = d.toString()\n *\n * fun magic(s: String): Either<Error, String> =\n *   parse(s).flatMap{ reciprocal(it) }.map{ stringify(it) }\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val x = magic("2")\n * val value = when(x) {\n *   is Either.Left -> when (x.value) {\n *     is Error.NotANumber -> "Not a number!"\n *     is Error.NoZeroReciprocal -> "Can't take reciprocal of 0!"\n *   }\n *   is Either.Right -> "Got reciprocal: ${x.value}"\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println("value = $value")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-11.kt -->\n *\n * ## Either.catch exceptions\n *\n * Sometimes you do need to interact with code that can potentially throw exceptions. In such cases, you should mitigate the possibility that an exception can be thrown. You can do so by using the `catch` function.\n *\n * Example:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * fun potentialThrowingCode(): String = throw RuntimeException("Blow up!")\n *\n * suspend fun makeSureYourLogicDoesNotHaveSideEffects(): Either<Error, String> =\n *   Either.catch { potentialThrowingCode() }.mapLeft { Error.SpecificError }\n * //sampleEnd\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   println("makeSureYourLogicDoesNotHaveSideEffects().isLeft() = ${makeSureYourLogicDoesNotHaveSideEffects().isLeft()}")\n * }\n *\n * sealed class Error {\n *   object SpecificError : Error()\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-12.kt -->\n *\n * ## Syntax\n *\n * Either can also map over the [Left] value with `mapLeft`, which is similar to map, but applies on left instances.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val r : Either<Int, Int> = Either.Right(7)\n * val rightMapLeft = r.mapLeft {it + 1}\n * val l: Either<Int, Int> = Either.Left(7)\n * val leftMapLeft = l.mapLeft {it + 1}\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println("rightMapLeft = $rightMapLeft")\n *  println("leftMapLeft = $leftMapLeft")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-13.kt -->\n *\n * `Either<A, B>` can be transformed to `Either<B,A>` using the `swap()` method.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either.Left\n * import arrow.core.Either\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val r: Either<String, Int> = Either.Right(7)\n * val swapped = r.swap()\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println("swapped = $swapped")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-14.kt -->\n *\n * For using Either's syntax on arbitrary data types.\n * This will make possible to use the `left()`, `right()`, `getOrElse()` methods:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.right\n *\n * val right7 =\n * //sampleStart\n *   7.right()\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(right7)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-15.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.left\n *\n *  val leftHello =\n * //sampleStart\n *  "hello".left()\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(leftHello)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-16.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.left\n * import arrow.core.getOrElse\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val x = "hello".left()\n * val value = x.getOrElse { "$it world!" }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println("value = $value")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-17.kt -->\n *\n * Another operation is `fold`. This operation will extract the value from the Either, or provide a default if the value is [Left]\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.right\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val x : Either<Int, Int> = 7.right()\n * val fold = x.fold({ 1 }, { it + 3 })\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println("fold = $fold")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-18.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.left\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val y : Either<Int, Int> = 7.left()\n * val fold = y.fold({ 1 }, { it + 3 })\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println("fold = $fold")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-19.kt -->\n *\n * The `getOrElse()` operation allows the transformation of an `Either.Left` value to a `Either.Right` using\n * the value of [Left]. This can be useful when mapping to a single result type is required like `fold()`, but without\n * the need to handle `Either.Right` case.\n *\n * As an example, we want to map an `Either<Throwable, Int>` to a proper HTTP status code:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.getOrElse\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val r: Either<Throwable, Int> = Either.Left(NumberFormatException())\n * val httpStatusCode = r.getOrElse {\n *   when(it) {\n *     is NumberFormatException -> 400\n *     else -> 500\n *   }\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println("httpStatusCode = $httpStatusCode")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-20.kt -->\n

kotlin	YES	0	*\n * [Effect] represents a function of `suspend Raise<R>.() -> A`, that short-circuits with a value of `R` or `Throwable`, or completes with a value of `A`.\n *\n * So [Effect] is defined by `suspend fun <B> fold(recover: suspend (Throwable) -> B, resolve: suspend (R) -> B, transform: suspend (A) -> B): B`,\n * to map all values of `R`, `Throwable` and `A` to a value of `B`.\n *\n * <!--- TOC -->\n\n      * [Writing a program with Effect<R, A>](#writing-a-program-with-effect<r-a>)\n      * [Handling errors](#handling-errors)\n        * [recover](#recover)\n        * [catch](#catch)\n      * [Structured Concurrency](#structured-concurrency)\n        * [Arrow Fx Coroutines](#arrow-fx-coroutines)\n          * [parZip](#parzip)\n          * [parTraverse](#partraverse)\n          * [raceN](#racen)\n          * [bracketCase / Resource](#bracketcase--resource)\n        * [KotlinX](#kotlinx)\n          * [withContext](#withcontext)\n          * [async](#async)\n          * [launch](#launch)\n          * [Strange edge cases](#strange-edge-cases)\n\n * <!--- END -->\n *\n * ## Writing a program with Effect<R, A>\n *\n * Let's write a small program to read a file from disk, and instead of having the program work exception based we want to\n * turn it into a polymorphic type-safe program.\n *\n * We'll start by defining a small function that accepts a [String], and does some simple validation to check that the path\n * is not empty. If the path is empty, we want the program to result in `EmptyPath`. So we're immediately going to see how\n * we can raise an error of any arbitrary type `R` by using the function `raise`. The name `raise` comes from raising an intterupt, or\n * changing, especially unexpectedly, away from the computation and finishing the `Continuation` with `R`.\n *\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.core.raise.Effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.ensureNotNull\n * import arrow.core.raise.ensure\n * -->\n * ```kotlin\n * object EmptyPath\n *\n * fun readFile(path: String): Effect<EmptyPath, Unit> = effect {\n *   if (path.isEmpty()) raise(EmptyPath) else Unit\n * }\n * ```\n *\n * Here we see how we can define an `Effect<R, A>` which has `EmptyPath` for the raise type `R`, and `Unit` for the success type `A`.\n *\n * Patterns like validating a [Boolean] are very common, and the [Effect] DSL offers utility functions like [kotlin.require]\n * and [kotlin.requireNotNull]. They're named [ensure] and [ensureNotNull] to avoid conflicts with the `kotlin` namespace.\n * So let's rewrite the function from above to use the DSL instead.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * fun readFile2(path: String?): Effect<EmptyPath, Unit> = effect {\n *   ensureNotNull(path) { EmptyPath }\n *   ensure(path.isNotEmpty()) { EmptyPath }\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-raise-01.kt -->\n *\n * Now that we have the path, we can read from the `File` and return it as a domain model `Content`.\n * We also want to take care of exceptions that might occur when reading from a file - `FileNotFoundException` & `SecurityError`,\n * so lets make some domain errors for those too. Grouping them as a sealed interface is useful since that way we can resolve *all* errors in a type safe manner.\n *\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.Ior\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.raise.Effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.fold\n * import arrow.core.raise.toEither\n * import arrow.core.raise.toIor\n * import arrow.core.raise.toOption\n * import arrow.core.raise.ensureNotNull\n * import arrow.core.raise.ensure\n * import io.kotest.matchers.collections.shouldNotBeEmpty\n * import io.kotest.matchers.shouldBe\n * import arrow.core.shouldBeInstanceOf\n * import java.io.File\n * import java.io.FileNotFoundException\n * -->\n * ```kotlin\n * @JvmInline\n * value class Content(val body: List<String>)\n *\n * sealed interface FileError\n * @JvmInline value class SecurityError(val msg: String?) : FileError\n * @JvmInline value class FileNotFound(val path: String) : FileError\n * object EmptyPath : FileError {\n *   override fun toString() = "EmptyPath"\n * }\n * ```\n *\n * We can finish our function, but we need to refactor the return type from `Unit` to `Content` and the error type from `EmptyPath` to `FileError`.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * fun readFile(path: String?): Effect<FileError, Content> = effect {\n *   ensureNotNull(path) { EmptyPath }\n *   ensure(path.isNotEmpty()) { EmptyPath }\n *   try {\n *     val lines = File(path).readLines()\n *     Content(lines)\n *   } catch (e: FileNotFoundException) {\n *     raise(FileNotFound(path))\n *   } catch (e: SecurityException) {\n *     raise(SecurityError(e.message))\n *   }\n * }\n * ```\n *\n * The `readFile` function defines a `suspend fun` that will return:\n *\n * - the `Content` of a given `path`\n * - a `FileError`\n * - An unexpected fatal error (`OutOfMemoryException`)\n *\n * Since these are the properties of our `Effect` function, we can turn it into a value.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * suspend fun main() {\n *    readFile("").toEither() shouldBe Either.Left(EmptyPath)\n *    readFile("gradle.properties").toIor() shouldBe Ior.Left(FileNotFound("gradle.properties"))\n *    readFile("README.MD").toOption { None } shouldBe None\n *\n *    readFile("build.gradle.kts").fold({ _: FileError -> null }, { it })\n *      .shouldBeInstanceOf<Content>()\n *       .body.shouldNotBeEmpty()\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-raise-02.kt -->\n *\n * The functions above are available out of the box, but it's easy to define your own extension functions in terms\n * of `fold`. Implementing the `toEither()` operator is as simple as:\n *\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n * import arrow.core.raise.Effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.fold\n * import arrow.core.identity\n * -->\n * ```kotlin\n * suspend fun <R, A> Effect<R, A>.toEither(): Either<R, A> =\n *   fold({ Either.Left(it) }) { Either.Right(it) }\n *\n * suspend fun <A> Effect<None, A>.toOption(): Option<A> =\n *   fold(::identity) { Some(it) }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-raise-03.kt -->\n *\n * Adding your own syntax to `Raise<R>` is not advised, yet, but will be easy once context parameters become available.\n *\n * ```\n * context(_: Raise<R>)\n * suspend fun <R, A> Either<R, A>.bind(): A =\n *   when (this) {\n *     is Either.Left -> raise(value)\n *     is Either.Right -> value\n *   }\n *\n * context(_: Raise<None>)\n * fun <A> Option<A>.bind(): A =\n *   fold({ raise(it) }, ::identity)\n * ```\n *\n * ## Handling errors\n *\n * An Effect<R, A> has 2 error channels: `Throwable` and `R`\n * There are two separate handlers to transform either of the error channels.\n *\n * - `recover` to handle, and transform any error of type `R`.\n * - `catch` to handle, and transform an error of type `Throwable`.\n *\n * ### recover\n *\n * `recover` handles the error of type `R`,\n * by providing a new value of type `A`, raising a different error of type `E`, or throwing an exception.\n *\n * Let's take a look at some examples:\n *\n * We define a `val failed` of type `Effect<String, Int>`, that represents a failed effect with value "failed".\n *\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.core.raise.Effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.recover\n * import arrow.core.raise.catch\n * -->\n * ```kotlin\n * val failed: Effect<String, Int> =\n *   effect { raise("failed") }\n * ```\n *\n * We can `recover` the failure, and resolve it by providing a default value of `-1` or the length of the `error: String`.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val default: Effect<Nothing, Int> =\n *   failed.recover { -1 }\n *\n * val resolved: Effect<Nothing, Int> =\n *   failed.recover { it.length }\n * ```\n *\n * As you can see the resulting `error` is now of type `Nothing`, since we did not raise any new errors.\n * So our `Effect` knows that no short-circuiting will occur during execution. Awesome!\n * But it can also infer to any other error type that you might want instead, because it's never going to occur.\n * So as you see below, we can even assign our `Effect<Nothing, A>` to `Effect<E, A>`, where `E` can be any type.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val default2: Effect<Double, Int> = default\n * val resolved2: Effect<Unit, Int> = resolved\n * ```\n *\n * `recover` also allows us to _change_ the error type when we resolve the error of type `R`.\n * Below we handle our error of `String` and turn it into `List<Char>` using `reversed().toList()`.\n * This is a powerful operation, since it allows us to transform our error types across boundaries or layers.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val newError: Effect<List<Char>, Int> =\n *   failed.recover { str ->\n *     raise(str.reversed().toList())\n *   }\n * ```\n *\n * Finally, since `recover` supports `suspend` we can safely call other `suspend` code and throw `Throwable` into the `suspend` system.\n * This is typically undesired, since you should prefer lifting `Throwable` into typed values of `R` to make them compile-time tracked.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val newException: Effect<Nothing, Int> =\n *   failed.recover { str -> throw RuntimeException(str) }\n * ```\n *\n * ### catch\n *\n * `catch` gives us the same powers as `recover`, but instead of resolving `R` we're recovering from any unexpected `Throwable`.\n * Unexpected, because the expectation is that all `Throwable` get turned into `R` unless it's a fatal/unexpected.\n * This operator is useful when you need to work/wrap foreign code, especially Java SDKs or any code that is heavily based on exceptions.\n *\n * Below we've defined a `foreign` value that represents wrapping a foreign API which might throw `RuntimeException`.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val foreign = effect<String, Int> {\n *   throw RuntimeException("BOOM!")\n * }\n * ```\n *\n * We can `catch` to run the effect recovering from any exception,\n * and recover it by providing a default value of `-1` or the length of the [Throwable.message].\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val default3: Effect<String, Int> =\n *   foreign.catch { -1 }\n *\n * val resolved3: Effect<String, Int> =\n *   foreign.catch { it.message?.length ?: -1 }\n * ```\n *\n * A big difference with `recover` is that `catch` **cannot** change the error type of `R` because it doesn't resolve it, so it stays unchanged.\n * You can however compose `recover`, and `catch` to resolve the error type **and** recover the exception.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val default4: Effect<Nothing, Int> =\n *   foreign\n *     .recover<String, Nothing, Int> { -1 }\n *     .catch { -2 }\n * ```\n *\n * `catch` however offers an overload that can _refine the exception_.\n * Let's say you're wrapping some database interactions that might throw `java.sql.SqlException`, or `org.postgresql.util.PSQLException`,\n * then you might only be interested in those exceptions and not `Throwable`. `catch` allows you to install multiple handlers for specific exceptions.\n * If the desired exception is not matched, then it stays in the `suspend` exception channel and will be thrown or recovered at a later point.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val default5: Effect<String, Int> =\n *   foreign\n *     .catch { _: RuntimeException -> -1 }\n *     .catch { _: java.sql.SQLException -> -2 }\n * ```\n *\n * Finally, since `catch` also supports `suspend` we can safely call other `suspend` code and throw `Throwable` into the `suspend` system.\n * This can be useful if refinement of exceptions is not sufficient, for example in the case of `org.postgresql.util.PSQLException` you might want to\n * check the `SQLState` to check for a `foreign key violation` and rethrow the exception if not matched.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * suspend fun java.sql.SQLException.isForeignKeyViolation(): Boolean = true\n *\n * val rethrown: Effect<String, Int> =\n *   failed.catch { ex: java.sql.SQLException ->\n *     if(ex.isForeignKeyViolation()) raise("foreign key violation")\n *     else throw ex\n *   }\n * ```\n *\n * <!--- KNIT example-raise-04.kt -->\n *\n * Note:\n *  Handling errors can also be done with `try/catch` but this is **not recommended**, it uses `CancellationException` which is used to cancel `Coroutine`s and is advised not to capture in Kotlin.\n *  The `CancellationException` from `Effect` is `RaiseCancellationException`, this a public type, thus can be distinguished from any other `CancellationException` if necessary.\n *\n * ## Structured Concurrency\n *\n * `Effect<R, A>` relies on `kotlin.cancellation.CancellationException` to `raise` error values of type `R` inside the `Continuation` since it effectively cancels/short-circuits it.\n * For this reason `raise` adheres to the same rules as [`Structured Concurrency`](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/coroutines-basics.html#structured-concurrency)\n *\n * Let's overview below how `raise` behaves with the different concurrency builders from Arrow Fx & KotlinX Coroutines.\n * In the examples below we're going to be using a utility to show how _sibling tasks_ get cancelled.\n * The utility function shown below called `awaitExitCase` will `never` finish suspending, and completes a `Deferred` with the `ExitCase`.\n * `ExitCase` is a sealed class that can be a value of `Failure(Throwable)`, `Cancelled(CancellationException)`, or `Completed`.\n * Since `awaitExitCase` suspends forever, it can only result in `Cancelled(CancellationException)`.\n *\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.core.raise.effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.fold\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.ExitCase\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.guaranteeCase\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.parZip\n * import io.kotest.assertions.AssertionErrorBuilder.Companion.fail\n * import io.kotest.matchers.shouldBe\n * import arrow.core.shouldBeTypeOf\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.CompletableDeferred\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.awaitCancellation\n * -->\n * ```kotlin\n * suspend fun <A> awaitExitCase(exit: CompletableDeferred<ExitCase>): A =\n *   guaranteeCase(::awaitCancellation) { exitCase -> exit.complete(exitCase) }\n *\n * ```\n *\n * ### Arrow Fx Coroutines\n * All operators in Arrow Fx Coroutines run in place, so they have no way of leaking `raise`.\n * It's therefore always safe to compose `effect` with any Arrow Fx combinator. Let's see some small examples below.\n *\n * #### parZip\n *\n * ```kotlin\n *  suspend fun main() {\n *    val error = "Error"\n *    val exit = CompletableDeferred<ExitCase>()\n *   effect<String, Int> {\n *     parZip({ awaitExitCase<Int>(exit) }, { raise(error) }) { a: Int, b: Int -> a + b }\n *   }.fold({ it shouldBe error }, { fail("Int can never be the result") })\n *   exit.await().shouldBeTypeOf<ExitCase>()\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-raise-05.kt -->\n *\n * #### parTraverse\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.core.raise.effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.fold\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.ExitCase\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.guaranteeCase\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.parMap\n * import io.kotest.assertions.AssertionErrorBuilder.Companion.fail\n * import io.kotest.matchers.shouldBe\n * import arrow.core.shouldBeTypeOf\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.CompletableDeferred\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.awaitCancellation\n *\n * suspend fun <A> awaitExitCase(exit: CompletableDeferred<ExitCase>): A =\n *  guaranteeCase(::awaitCancellation) { exitCase -> exit.complete(exitCase) }\n *\n * suspend fun <A> CompletableDeferred<A>.getOrNull(): A? =\n *  if (isCompleted) await() else null\n * -->\n * ```kotlin\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   val error = "Error"\n *   val exits = (0..3).map { CompletableDeferred<ExitCase>() }\n *   effect<String, List<Unit>> {\n *     (0..4).parMap { index ->\n *       if (index == 4) raise(error)\n *       else awaitExitCase(exits[index])\n *     }\n *   }.fold({ msg -> msg shouldBe error }, { fail("Int can never be the result") })\n *   // It's possible not all parallel task got launched, and in those cases awaitCancellation never ran\n *   exits.forEach { exit -> exit.getOrNull()?.shouldBeTypeOf<ExitCase.Cancelled>() }\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-raise-06.kt -->\n *\n * `parTraverse` will launch 5 tasks, for every element in `1..5`.\n * The last task to get scheduled will `raise` with "error", and it will cancel the other launched tasks before returning.\n *\n * #### raceN\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.core.raise.effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.fold\n * import arrow.core.merge\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.ExitCase\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.guaranteeCase\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.raceN\n * import io.kotest.assertions.AssertionErrorBuilder.Companion.fail\n * import io.kotest.matchers.shouldBe\n * import arrow.core.shouldBeTypeOf\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.CompletableDeferred\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.awaitCancellation\n *\n * suspend fun <A> awaitExitCase(exit: CompletableDeferred<ExitCase>): A =\n *   guaranteeCase(::awaitCancellation) { exitCase -> exit.complete(exitCase) }\n *\n * suspend fun <A> CompletableDeferred<A>.getOrNull(): A? =\n *   if (isCompleted) await() else null\n * -->\n * ```kotlin\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   val error = "Error"\n *   val exit = CompletableDeferred<ExitCase>()\n *   effect<String, Int> {\n *     raceN({ awaitExitCase<Int>(exit) }) { raise(error) }\n *       .merge() // Flatten Either<Int, Int> result from race into Int\n *   }.fold({ msg -> msg shouldBe error }, { fail("Int can never be the result") })\n *   // It's possible not all parallel task got launched, and in those cases awaitCancellation never ran\n *   exit.getOrNull()?.shouldBeTypeOf<ExitCase.Cancelled>()\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-raise-07.kt -->\n *\n * `raceN` races `n` suspend functions in parallel, and cancels all participating functions when a winner is found.\n * We can consider the function that `raise`s the winner of the race, except with a raised value instead of a successful one.\n * So when a function in the race `raise`s, and thus short-circuiting the race, it will cancel all the participating functions.\n *\n * #### bracketCase / Resource\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.core.raise.effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.fold\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.ExitCase\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.bracketCase\n * import io.kotest.assertions.AssertionErrorBuilder.Companion.fail\n * import io.kotest.matchers.shouldBe\n * import arrow.core.shouldBeTypeOf\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.CompletableDeferred\n * import kotlin	YES	0	*\n * A [Prism] is a loss less invertible optic that can look into a structure and optionally find its focus.\n * Mostly used for finding a focus that is only present under certain conditions i.e. list head Prism<List<Int>, Int>\n *\n * A (polymorphic) [PPrism] is useful when setting or modifying a value for a polymorphic sum type\n * i.e. PPrism<Option<String>, Option<Int>, String, Int>\n *\n * A [PPrism] gathers the two concepts of pattern matching and constructor and thus can be seen as a pair of functions:\n * - `getOrModify: A -> Either<A, B>` meaning it returns the focus of a [PPrism] OR the original value\n * - `reverseGet : B -> A` meaning we can construct the source type of a [PPrism] from a focus `B`\n *\n * @param S the source of a [PPrism]\n * @param T the modified source of a [PPrism]\n * @param A the focus of a [PPrism]\n * @param B the modified focus of a [PPrism]\n

cpp	YES	0	\n * About the ordering of integrity check, full poison check, and the specific *alloc functions\n *\n * 1. Integrity check:\n *        a. verifies the heap management information is not corrupt;\n *        b. this allows any other testing, that walks the heap, to run safely.\n *\n * 2. Place full poison check before or after a specific *alloc function:\n *        a. after  => when the *alloc function operates on an existing allocation;\n *        b. before => when the *alloc function creates a new, not modified, allocation.\n *\n *    In a free() or realloc() call, the focus is on their allocation. It is checked first and\n *    reported on first if an error exists. Full posion check is done after.\n *\n *    For malloc(), calloc(), and zalloc(), full posion check is done first because these\n *    functions do not modify an existing allocation.\n

It is not anticipated that a particular\n * named user would be authenticated by multiple methods.  This would\n * make the user vulnerable to attacks which negotiate the least secure\n * method from among a set (such as PAP rather than CHAP). c	YES	0	\n * Compressed packet format:\n *\n * The first octet contains the packet type (top 3 bits), TCP\n * 'push' bit, and flags that indicate which of the 4 TCP sequence\n * numbers have changed (bottom 5 bits).  The next octet is a\n * conversation number that associates a saved IP/TCP header with\n * the compressed packet.  The next two octets are the TCP checksum\n * from the original datagram.  The next 0 to 15 octets are\n * sequence number changes, one change per bit set in the header\n * (there may be no changes and there are two special cases where\n * the receiver implicitly knows what changed -- see below).\n *\n * There are 5 numbers which can change (they are always inserted\n * in the following order): TCP urgent pointer, window,\n * acknowlegement, sequence number and IP ID.  (The urgent pointer\n * is different from the others in that its value is sent, not the\n * change in value.)  Since typical use of SLIP links is biased\n * toward small packets (see comments on MTU/MSS below), changes\n * use a variable length coding with one octet for numbers in the\n * range 1 - 255 and 3 octets (0, MSB, LSB) for numbers in the\n * range 256 - 65535 or 0.  (If the change in sequence number or\n * ack is more than 65535, an uncompressed packet is sent.)\n 
c	YES	0	\n * Packet types (must not conflict with IP protocol version)\n *\n * The top nibble of the first octet is the packet type.  There are\n * three possible types: IP (not proto TCP or tcp with one of the\n * control flags set); uncompressed TCP (a normal IP/TCP packet but\n * with the 8-bit protocol field replaced by an 8-bit connection id --\n * this type of packet syncs the sender & receiver); and compressed\n * TCP (described above).\n *\n * LSB of 4-bit field is TCP "PUSH" bit (a worthless anachronism) and\n * is logically part of the 4-bit "changes" field that follows.  Top\n * three bits are actual packet type.  For backward compatibility\n * and in the interest of conserving bits, numbers are chosen so the\n * IP protocol version number (4) which normally appears in this nibble\n * means "IP packet".\n

c	YES	0	*\n * @file\n *\n * IPv6 address scopes, zones, and scoping policy.\n *\n * This header provides the means to implement support for IPv6 address scopes,\n * as per RFC 4007. An address scope can be either global or more constrained.\n * In lwIP, we say that an address "has a scope" or "is scoped" when its scope\n * is constrained, in which case the address is meaningful only in a specific\n * "zone." For unicast addresses, only link-local addresses have a scope; in\n * that case, the scope is the link. For multicast addresses, there are various\n * scopes defined by RFC 4007 and others. For any constrained scope, a system\n * must establish a (potentially one-to-many) mapping between zones and local\n * interfaces. For example, a link-local address is valid on only one link (its\n * zone). That link may be attached to one or more local interfaces. The\n * decisions on which scopes are constrained and the mapping between zones and\n * interfaces is together what we refer to as the "scoping policy" - more on\n * this in a bit.\n *\n * In lwIP, each IPv6 address has an associated zone index. This zone index may\n * be set to "no zone" (IP6_NO_ZONE, 0) or an actual zone. We say that an\n * address "has a zone" or "is zoned" when its zone index is *not* set to "no\n * zone." In lwIP, in principle, each address should be "properly zoned," which\n * means that if the address has a zone if and only if has a scope. As such, it\n * is a rule that an unscoped (e.g., global) address must never have a zone.\n * Even though one could argue that there is always one zone even for global\n * scopes, this rule exists for implementation simplicity. Violation of the\n * rule will trigger assertions or otherwise result in undesired behavior.\n *\n * Backward compatibility prevents us from requiring that applications always\n * provide properly zoned addresses. We do enforce the rule that the in the\n * lwIP link layer (everything below netif->output_ip6() and in particular ND6)\n * *all* addresses are properly zoned. Thus, on the output paths down the\n * stack, various places deal with the case of addresses that lack a zone.\n * Some of them are best-effort for efficiency (e.g. the PCB bind and connect\n * API calls' attempts to add missing zones); ultimately the IPv6 output\n * handler (@ref ip6_output_if_src) will set a zone if necessary.\n *\n * Aside from dealing with scoped addresses lacking a zone, a proper IPv6\n * implementation must also ensure that a packet with a scoped source and/or\n * destination address does not leave its zone. This is currently implemented\n * in the input and forward functions. However, for output, these checks are\n * deliberately omitted in order to keep the implementation lightweight. The\n * routing algorithm in @ref ip6_route will take decisions such that it will\n * not cause zone violations unless the application sets bad addresses, though.\n *\n * In terms of scoping policy, lwIP implements the default policy from RFC 4007\n * using macros in this file. This policy considers link-local unicast\n * addresses and (only) interface-local and link-local multicast addresses as\n * having a scope. For all these addresses, the zone is equal to the interface.\n * As shown below in this file, it is possible to implement a custom policy.\n

c	YES	0	* Enable round-trip delay compensation.\n * Compensate for the round-trip delay by calculating the clock offset from\n * the originate, receive, transmit and destination timestamps, as per RFC.\n *\n * The calculation requires compiler support for 64-bit integers. Also, either\n * SNTP_SET_SYSTEM_TIME_US or SNTP_SET_SYSTEM_TIME_NTP has to be implemented\n * for setting the system clock with sub-second precision. Likewise, either\n * SNTP_GET_SYSTEM_TIME or SNTP_GET_SYSTEM_TIME_NTP needs to be implemented\n * with sub-second precision.\n *\n * Although not strictly required, it makes sense to combine this option with\n * SNTP_CHECK_RESPONSE >= 2 for sanity-checking of the received timestamps.\n * Also, in order for the round-trip calculation to work, the difference\n * between the local clock and the NTP server clock must not be larger than\n * about 34 years. If that limit is exceeded, the implementation will fall back\n * to setting the clock without compensation. In order to ensure that the local\n * clock is always within the permitted range for compensation, even at first\n * try, it may be necessary to store at least the current year in non-volatile\n * memory.\n

c	YES	0	* \\file bearssl_block.h\n *\n * # Block Ciphers and Symmetric Ciphers\n *\n * This file documents the API for block ciphers and other symmetric\n * ciphers.\n *\n *\n * ## Procedural API\n *\n * For a block cipher implementation, up to three separate sets of\n * functions are provided, for CBC encryption, CBC decryption, and CTR\n * encryption/decryption. Each set has its own context structure,\n * initialised with the encryption key.\n *\n * For CBC encryption and decryption, the data to encrypt or decrypt is\n * referenced as a sequence of blocks. The implementations assume that\n * there is no partial block; no padding is applied or removed. The\n * caller is responsible for handling any kind of padding.\n *\n * Function for CTR encryption are defined only for block ciphers with\n * blocks of 16 bytes or more (i.e. AES, but not DES/3DES).\n *\n * Each implemented block cipher is identified by an "internal name"\n * from which are derived the names of structures and functions that\n * implement the cipher. For the block cipher of internal name "`xxx`",\n * the following are defined:\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_BLOCK_SIZE`\n *\n *     A macro that evaluates to the block size (in bytes) of the\n *     cipher. For all implemented block ciphers, this value is a\n *     power of two.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_cbcenc_keys`\n *\n *     Context structure that contains the subkeys resulting from the key\n *     expansion. These subkeys are appropriate for CBC encryption. The\n *     structure first field is called `vtable` and points to the\n *     appropriate OOP structure.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_cbcenc_init(br_xxx_cbcenc_keys *ctx, const void *key, size_t len)`\n *\n *     Perform key expansion: subkeys for CBC encryption are computed and\n *     written in the provided context structure. The key length MUST be\n *     adequate for the implemented block cipher. This function also sets\n *     the `vtable` field.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_cbcenc_run(const br_xxx_cbcenc_keys *ctx, void *iv, void *data, size_t len)`\n *\n *     Perform CBC encryption of `len` bytes, in place. The encrypted data\n *     replaces the cleartext. `len` MUST be a multiple of the block length\n *     (if it is not, the function may loop forever or overflow a buffer).\n *     The IV is provided with the `iv` pointer; it is also updated with\n *     a copy of the last encrypted block.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_cbcdec_keys`\n *\n *     Context structure that contains the subkeys resulting from the key\n *     expansion. These subkeys are appropriate for CBC decryption. The\n *     structure first field is called `vtable` and points to the\n *     appropriate OOP structure.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_cbcdec_init(br_xxx_cbcenc_keys *ctx, const void *key, size_t len)`\n *\n *     Perform key expansion: subkeys for CBC decryption are computed and\n *     written in the provided context structure. The key length MUST be\n *     adequate for the implemented block cipher. This function also sets\n *     the `vtable` field.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_cbcdec_run(const br_xxx_cbcdec_keys *ctx, void *iv, void *data, size_t num_blocks)`\n *\n *     Perform CBC decryption of `len` bytes, in place. The decrypted data\n *     replaces the ciphertext. `len` MUST be a multiple of the block length\n *     (if it is not, the function may loop forever or overflow a buffer).\n *     The IV is provided with the `iv` pointer; it is also updated with\n *     a copy of the last _encrypted_ block.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_ctr_keys`\n *\n *     Context structure that contains the subkeys resulting from the key\n *     expansion. These subkeys are appropriate for CTR encryption and\n *     decryption. The structure first field is called `vtable` and\n *     points to the appropriate OOP structure.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_ctr_init(br_xxx_ctr_keys *ctx, const void *key, size_t len)`\n *\n *     Perform key expansion: subkeys for CTR encryption and decryption\n *     are computed and written in the provided context structure. The\n *     key length MUST be adequate for the implemented block cipher. This\n *     function also sets the `vtable` field.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_ctr_run(const br_xxx_ctr_keys *ctx, const void *iv, uint32_t cc, void *data, size_t len)` (returns `uint32_t`)\n *\n *     Perform CTR encryption/decryption of some data. Processing is done\n *     "in place" (the output data replaces the input data). This function\n *     implements the "standard incrementing function" from NIST SP800-38A,\n *     annex B: the IV length shall be 4 bytes less than the block size\n *     (i.e. 12 bytes for AES) and the counter is the 32-bit value starting\n *     with `cc`. The data length (`len`) is not necessarily a multiple of\n *     the block size. The new counter value is returned, which supports\n *     chunked processing, provided that each chunk length (except possibly\n *     the last one) is a multiple of the block size.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_ctrcbc_keys`\n *\n *     Context structure that contains the subkeys resulting from the\n *     key expansion. These subkeys are appropriate for doing combined\n *     CTR encryption/decryption and CBC-MAC, as used in the CCM and EAX\n *     authenticated encryption modes. The structure first field is\n *     called `vtable` and points to the appropriate OOP structure.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_ctrcbc_init(br_xxx_ctr_keys *ctx, const void *key, size_t len)`\n *\n *     Perform key expansion: subkeys for combined CTR\n *     encryption/decryption and CBC-MAC are computed and written in the\n *     provided context structure. The key length MUST be adequate for\n *     the implemented block cipher. This function also sets the\n *     `vtable` field.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_ctrcbc_encrypt(const br_xxx_ctrcbc_keys *ctx, void *ctr, void *cbcmac, void *data, size_t len)`\n *\n *     Perform CTR encryption of some data, and CBC-MAC. Processing is\n *     done "in place" (the output data replaces the input data). This\n *     function applies CTR encryption on the data, using a full\n *     block-size counter (i.e. for 128-bit blocks, the counter is\n *     incremented as a 128-bit value). The 'ctr' array contains the\n *     initial value for the counter (used in the first block) and it is\n *     updated with the new value after data processing. The 'cbcmac'\n *     value shall point to a block-sized value which is used as IV for\n *     CBC-MAC, computed over the encrypted data (output of CTR\n *     encryption); the resulting CBC-MAC is written over 'cbcmac' on\n *     output.\n *\n *     The data length MUST be a multiple of the block size.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_ctrcbc_decrypt(const br_xxx_ctrcbc_keys *ctx, void *ctr, void *cbcmac, void *data, size_t len)`\n *\n *     Perform CTR decryption of some data, and CBC-MAC. Processing is\n *     done "in place" (the output data replaces the input data). This\n *     function applies CTR decryption on the data, using a full\n *     block-size counter (i.e. for 128-bit blocks, the counter is\n *     incremented as a 128-bit value). The 'ctr' array contains the\n *     initial value for the counter (used in the first block) and it is\n *     updated with the new value after data processing. The 'cbcmac'\n *     value shall point to a block-sized value which is used as IV for\n *     CBC-MAC, computed over the encrypted data (input of CTR\n *     encryption); the resulting CBC-MAC is written over 'cbcmac' on\n *     output.\n *\n *     The data length MUST be a multiple of the block size.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_ctrcbc_ctr(const br_xxx_ctrcbc_keys *ctx, void *ctr, void *data, size_t len)`\n *\n *     Perform CTR encryption or decryption of the provided data. The\n *     data is processed "in place" (the output data replaces the input\n *     data). A full block-sized counter is applied (i.e. for 128-bit\n *     blocks, the counter is incremented as a 128-bit value). The 'ctr'\n *     array contains the initial value for the counter (used in the\n *     first block), and it is updated with the new value after data\n *     processing.\n *\n *     The data length MUST be a multiple of the block size.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_ctrcbc_mac(const br_xxx_ctrcbc_keys *ctx, void *cbcmac, const void *data, size_t len)`\n *\n *     Compute CBC-MAC over the provided data. The IV for CBC-MAC is\n *     provided as 'cbcmac'; the output is written over the same array.\n *     The data itself is untouched. The data length MUST be a multiple\n *     of the block size.\n *\n *\n * It shall be noted that the key expansion functions return `void`. If\n * the provided key length is not allowed, then there will be no error\n * reporting; implementations need not validate the key length, thus an\n * invalid key length may result in undefined behaviour (e.g. buffer\n * overflow).\n *\n * Subkey structures contain no interior pointer, and no external\n * resources are allocated upon key expansion. They can thus be\n * discarded without any explicit deallocation.\n *\n *\n * ## Object-Oriented API\n *\n * Each context structure begins with a field (called `vtable`) that\n * points to an instance of a structure that references the relevant\n * functions through pointers. Each such structure contains the\n * following:\n *\n *   - `context_size`\n *\n *     The size (in bytes) of the context structure for subkeys.\n *\n *   - `block_size`\n *\n *     The cipher block size (in bytes).\n *\n *   - `log_block_size`\n *\n *     The base-2 logarithm of cipher block size (e.g. 4 for blocks\n *     of 16 bytes).\n *\n *   - `init`\n *\n *     Pointer to the key expansion function.\n *\n *   - `run`\n *\n *     Pointer to the encryption/decryption function.\n *\n * For combined CTR/CBC-MAC encryption, the `vtable` has a slightly\n * different structure:\n *\n *   - `context_size`\n *\n *     The size (in bytes) of the context structure for subkeys.\n *\n *   - `block_size`\n *\n *     The cipher block size (in bytes).\n *\n *   - `log_block_size`\n *\n *     The base-2 logarithm of cipher block size (e.g. 4 for blocks\n *     of 16 bytes).\n *\n *   - `init`\n *\n *     Pointer to the key expansion function.\n *\n *   - `encrypt`\n *\n *     Pointer to the CTR encryption + CBC-MAC function.\n *\n *   - `decrypt`\n *\n *     Pointer to the CTR decryption + CBC-MAC function.\n *\n *   - `ctr`\n *\n *     Pointer to the CTR encryption/decryption function.\n *\n *   - `mac`\n *\n *     Pointer to the CBC-MAC function.\n *\n * For block cipher "`xxx`", static, constant instances of these\n * structures are defined, under the names:\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_cbcenc_vtable`\n *   - `br_xxx_cbcdec_vtable`\n *   - `br_xxx_ctr_vtable`\n *   - `br_xxx_ctrcbc_vtable`\n *\n *\n * ## Implemented Block Ciphers\n * \n * Provided implementations are:\n *\n * | Name      | Function | Block Size (bytes) | Key lengths (bytes) |\n * | :-------- | :------- | :----------------: | :-----------------: |\n * | aes_big   | AES      |        16          | 16, 24 and 32       |\n * | aes_small | AES      |        16          | 16, 24 and 32       |\n * | aes_ct    | AES      |        16          | 16, 24 and 32       |\n * | aes_ct64  | AES      |        16          | 16, 24 and 32       |\n * | aes_x86ni | AES      |        16          | 16, 24 and 32       |\n * | aes_pwr8  | AES      |        16          | 16, 24 and 32       |\n * | des_ct    | DES/3DES |         8          | 8, 16 and 24        |\n * | des_tab   | DES/3DES |         8          | 8, 16 and 24        |\n *\n * **Note:** DES/3DES nominally uses keys of 64, 128 and 192 bits (i.e. 8,\n * 16 and 24 bytes), but some of the bits are ignored by the algorithm, so\n * the _effective_ key lengths, from a security point of view, are 56,\n * 112 and 168 bits, respectively.\n *\n * `aes_big` is a "classical" AES implementation, using tables. It\n * is fast but not constant-time, since it makes data-dependent array\n * accesses.\n *\n * `aes_small` is an AES implementation optimized for code size. It\n * is substantially slower than `aes_big`; it is not constant-time\n * either.\n *\n * `aes_ct` is a constant-time implementation of AES; its code is about\n * as big as that of `aes_big`, while its performance is comparable to\n * that of `aes_small`. However, it is constant-time. This\n * implementation should thus be considered to be the "default" AES in\n * BearSSL, to be used unless the operational context guarantees that a\n * non-constant-time implementation is safe, or an architecture-specific\n * constant-time implementation can be used (e.g. using dedicated\n * hardware opcodes).\n *\n * `aes_ct64` is another constant-time implementation of AES. It is\n * similar to `aes_ct` but uses 64-bit values. On 32-bit machines,\n * `aes_ct64` is not faster than `aes_ct`, often a bit slower, and has\n * a larger footprint; however, on 64-bit architectures, `aes_ct64`\n * is typically twice faster than `aes_ct` for modes that allow parallel\n * operations (i.e. CTR, and CBC decryption, but not CBC encryption).\n *\n * `aes_x86ni` exists only on x86 architectures (32-bit and 64-bit). It\n * uses the AES-NI opcodes when available.\n *\n * `aes_pwr8` exists only on PowerPC / POWER architectures (32-bit and\n * 64-bit, both little-endian and big-endian). It uses the AES opcodes\n * present in POWER8 and later.\n *\n * `des_tab` is a classic, table-based implementation of DES/3DES. It\n * is not constant-time.\n *\n * `des_ct` is an constant-time implementation of DES/3DES. It is\n * substantially slower than `des_tab`.\n *\n * ## ChaCha20 and Poly1305\n *\n * ChaCha20 is a stream cipher. Poly1305 is a MAC algorithm. They\n * are described in [RFC 7539](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7539).\n *\n * Two function pointer types are defined:\n *\n *   - `br_chacha20_run` describes a function that implements ChaCha20\n *     only.\n *\n *   - `br_poly1305_run` describes an implementation of Poly1305,\n *     in the AEAD combination with ChaCha20 specified in RFC 7539\n *     (the ChaCha20 implementation is provided as a function pointer).\n *\n * `chacha20_ct` is a straightforward implementation of ChaCha20 in\n * plain C; it is constant-time, small, and reasonably fast.\n *\n * `chacha20_sse2` leverages SSE2 opcodes (on x86 architectures that\n * support these opcodes). It is faster than `chacha20_ct`.\n *\n * `poly1305_ctmul` is an implementation of the ChaCha20+Poly1305 AEAD\n * construction, where the Poly1305 part is performed with mixed 32-bit\n * multiplications (operands are 32-bit, result is 64-bit).\n *\n * `poly1305_ctmul32` implements ChaCha20+Poly1305 using pure 32-bit\n * multiplications (32-bit operands, 32-bit result). It is slower than\n * `poly1305_ctmul`, except on some specific architectures such as\n * the ARM Cortex M0+.\n *\n * `poly1305_ctmulq` implements ChaCha20+Poly1305 with mixed 64-bit\n * multiplications (operands are 64-bit, result is 128-bit) on 64-bit\n * platforms that support such operations.\n *\n * `poly1305_i15` implements ChaCha20+Poly1305 with the generic "i15"\n * big integer implementation. It is meant mostly for testing purposes,\n * although it can help with saving a few hundred bytes of code footprint\n * on systems where code size is scarce.\n

c	YES	0	* \\file bearssl_hash.h\n *\n * # Hash Functions\n *\n * This file documents the API for hash functions.\n *\n *\n * ## Procedural API\n *\n * For each implemented hash function, of name "`xxx`", the following\n * elements are defined:\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_vtable`\n *\n *     An externally defined instance of `br_hash_class`.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_SIZE`\n *\n *     A macro that evaluates to the output size (in bytes) of the\n *     hash function.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_ID`\n *\n *     A macro that evaluates to a symbolic identifier for the hash\n *     function. Such identifiers are used with HMAC and signature\n *     algorithm implementations.\n *\n *     NOTE: for the "standard" hash functions defined in [the TLS\n *     standard](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5246#section-7.4.1.4.1),\n *     the symbolic identifiers match the constants used in TLS, i.e.\n *     1 to 6 for MD5, SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512,\n *     respectively.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_context`\n *\n *     Context for an ongoing computation. It is allocated by the\n *     caller, and a pointer to it is passed to all functions. A\n *     context contains no interior pointer, so it can be moved around\n *     and cloned (with a simple `memcpy()` or equivalent) in order to\n *     capture the function state at some point. Computations that use\n *     distinct context structures are independent of each other. The\n *     first field of `br_xxx_context` is always a pointer to the\n *     `br_xxx_vtable` structure; `br_xxx_init()` sets that pointer.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_init(br_xxx_context *ctx)`\n *\n *     Initialise the provided context. Previous contents of the structure\n *     are ignored. This calls resets the context to the start of a new\n *     hash computation; it also sets the first field of the context\n *     structure (called `vtable`) to a pointer to the statically\n *     allocated constant `br_xxx_vtable` structure.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_update(br_xxx_context *ctx, const void *data, size_t len)`\n *\n *     Add some more bytes to the hash computation represented by the\n *     provided context.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_out(const br_xxx_context *ctx, void *out)`\n *\n *     Complete the hash computation and write the result in the provided\n *     buffer. The output buffer MUST be large enough to accommodate the\n *     result. The context is NOT modified by this operation, so this\n *     function can be used to get a "partial hash" while still keeping\n *     the possibility of adding more bytes to the input.\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_state(const br_xxx_context *ctx, void *out)`\n *\n *     Get a copy of the "current state" for the computation so far. For\n *     MD functions (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2 family), this is the running state\n *     resulting from the processing of the last complete input block.\n *     Returned value is the current input length (in bytes).\n *\n *   - `br_xxx_set_state(br_xxx_context *ctx, const void *stb, uint64_t count)`\n *\n *     Set the internal state to the provided values. The 'stb' and\n *     'count' values shall match that which was obtained from\n *     `br_xxx_state()`. This restores the hash state only if the state\n *     values were at an appropriate block boundary. This does NOT set\n *     the `vtable` pointer in the context.\n *\n * Context structures can be discarded without any explicit deallocation.\n * Hash function implementations are purely software and don't reserve\n * any resources outside of the context structure itself.\n *\n *\n * ## Object-Oriented API\n *\n * For each hash function that follows the procedural API described\n * above, an object-oriented API is also provided. In that API, function\n * pointers from the vtable (`br_xxx_vtable`) are used. The vtable\n * incarnates object-oriented programming. An introduction on the OOP\n * concept used here can be read on the BearSSL Web site:<br />\n * &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;[https://www.bearssl.org/oop.html](https://www.bearssl.org/oop.html)\n *\n * The vtable offers functions called `init()`, `update()`, `out()`,\n * `set()` and `set_state()`, which are in fact the functions from\n * the procedural API. That vtable also contains two informative fields:\n *\n *   - `context_size`\n *\n *     The size of the context structure (`br_xxx_context`), in bytes.\n *     This can be used by generic implementations to perform dynamic\n *     context allocation.\n *\n *   - `desc`\n *\n *     A "descriptor" field that encodes some information on the hash\n *     function: symbolic identifier, output size, state size,\n *     internal block size, details on the padding.\n *\n * Users of this object-oriented API (in particular generic HMAC\n * implementations) may make the following assumptions:\n *\n *   - Hash output size is no more than 64 bytes.\n *   - Hash internal state size is no more than 64 bytes.\n *   - Internal block size is a power of two, no less than 16 and no more\n *     than 256.\n *\n *\n * ## Implemented Hash Functions\n *\n * Implemented hash functions are:\n *\n * | Function  | Name    | Output length | State length |\n * | :-------- | :------ | :-----------: | :----------: |\n * | MD5       | md5     |     16        |     16       |\n * | SHA-1     | sha1    |     20        |     20       |\n * | SHA-224   | sha224  |     28        |     32       |\n * | SHA-256   | sha256  |     32        |     32       |\n * | SHA-384   | sha384  |     48        |     64       |\n * | SHA-512   | sha512  |     64        |     64       |\n * | MD5+SHA-1 | md5sha1 |     36        |     36       |\n *\n * (MD5+SHA-1 is the concatenation of MD5 and SHA-1 computed over the\n * same input; in the implementation, the internal data buffer is\n * shared, thus making it more memory-efficient than separate MD5 and\n * SHA-1. It can be useful in implementing SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0 and TLS\n * 1.1.)\n *\n *\n * ## Multi-Hasher\n *\n * An aggregate hasher is provided, that can compute several standard\n * hash functions in parallel. It uses `br_multihash_context` and a\n * procedural API. It is configured with the implementations (the vtables)\n * that it should use; it will then compute all these hash functions in\n * parallel, on the same input. It is meant to be used in cases when the\n * hash of an object will be used, but the exact hash function is not\n * known yet (typically, streamed processing on X.509 certificates).\n *\n * Only the standard hash functions (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384\n * and SHA-512) are supported by the multi-hasher.\n *\n *\n * ## GHASH\n *\n * GHASH is not a generic hash function; it is a _universal_ hash function,\n * which, as the name does not say, means that it CANNOT be used in most\n * places where a hash function is needed. GHASH is used within the GCM\n * encryption mode, to provide the checked integrity functionality.\n *\n * A GHASH implementation is basically a function that uses the type defined\n * in this file under the name `br_ghash`:\n *\n *     typedef void (*br_ghash)(void *y, const void *h, const void *data, size_t len);\n *\n * The `y` pointer refers to a 16-byte value which is used as input, and\n * receives the output of the GHASH invocation. `h` is a 16-byte secret\n * value (that serves as key). `data` and `len` define the input data.\n *\n * Three GHASH implementations are provided, all constant-time, based on\n * the use of integer multiplications with appropriate masking to cancel\n * carry propagation.\n

c	YES	0	* \\file bearssl_ec.h\n *\n * # Elliptic Curves\n *\n * This file documents the EC implementations provided with BearSSL, and\n * ECDSA.\n *\n * ## Elliptic Curve API\n *\n * Only "named curves" are supported. Each EC implementation supports\n * one or several named curves, identified by symbolic identifiers.\n * These identifiers are small integers, that correspond to the values\n * registered by the\n * [IANA](http://www.iana.org/assignments/tls-parameters/tls-parameters.xhtml#tls-parameters-8).\n *\n * Since all currently defined elliptic curve identifiers are in the 0..31\n * range, it is convenient to encode support of some curves in a 32-bit\n * word, such that bit x corresponds to curve of identifier x.\n *\n * An EC implementation is incarnated by a `br_ec_impl` instance, that\n * offers the following fields:\n *\n *   - `supported_curves`\n *\n *      A 32-bit word that documents the identifiers of the curves supported\n *      by this implementation.\n *\n *   - `generator()`\n *\n *      Callback method that returns a pointer to the conventional generator\n *      point for that curve.\n *\n *   - `order()`\n *\n *      Callback method that returns a pointer to the subgroup order for\n *      that curve. That value uses unsigned big-endian encoding.\n *\n *   - `xoff()`\n *\n *      Callback method that returns the offset and length of the X\n *      coordinate in an encoded point.\n *\n *   - `mul()`\n *\n *      Multiply a curve point with an integer.\n *\n *   - `mulgen()`\n *\n *      Multiply the curve generator with an integer. This may be faster\n *      than the generic `mul()`.\n *\n *   - `muladd()`\n *\n *      Multiply two curve points by two integers, and return the sum of\n *      the two products.\n *\n * All curve points are represented in uncompressed format. The `mul()`\n * and `muladd()` methods take care to validate that the provided points\n * are really part of the relevant curve subgroup.\n *\n * For all point multiplication functions, the following holds:\n *\n *   - Functions validate that the provided points are valid members\n *     of the relevant curve subgroup. An error is reported if that is\n *     not the case.\n *\n *   - Processing is constant-time, even if the point operands are not\n *     valid. This holds for both the source and resulting points, and\n *     the multipliers (integers). Only the byte length of the provided\n *     multiplier arrays (not their actual value length in bits) may\n *     leak through timing-based side channels.\n *\n *   - The multipliers (integers) MUST be lower than the subgroup order.\n *     If this property is not met, then the result is indeterminate,\n *     but an error value is not necessarily returned.\n * \n *\n * ## ECDSA\n *\n * ECDSA signatures have two standard formats, called "raw" and "asn1".\n * Internally, such a signature is a pair of modular integers `(r,s)`.\n * The "raw" format is the concatenation of the unsigned big-endian\n * encodings of these two integers, possibly left-padded with zeros so\n * that they have the same encoded length. The "asn1" format is the\n * DER encoding of an ASN.1 structure that contains the two integer\n * values:\n *\n *     ECDSASignature ::= SEQUENCE {\n *         r   INTEGER,\n *         s   INTEGER\n *     }\n *\n * In general, in all of X.509 and SSL/TLS, the "asn1" format is used.\n * BearSSL offers ECDSA implementations for both formats; conversion\n * functions between the two formats are also provided. Conversion of a\n * "raw" format signature into "asn1" may enlarge a signature by no more\n * than 9 bytes for all supported curves; conversely, conversion of an\n * "asn1" signature to "raw" may expand the signature but the "raw"\n * length will never be more than twice the length of the "asn1" length\n * (and usually it will be shorter).\n *\n * Note that for a given signature, the "raw" format is not fully\n * deterministic, in that it does not enforce a minimal common length.\n
