cpp	YES	0	 millis() 'magic multiplier' approximation
cpp	YES	0	 This function corrects the cumulative (296us / usec overflow) drift
cpp	YES	0	 seen in the original 'millis()' function.
cpp	YES	0	 Input:
cpp	YES	0	    'm' - 32-bit usec counter,           0 <= m <= 0xFFFFFFFF
cpp	YES	0	    'c' - 32-bit usec overflow counter   0 <= c <  0x00400000
cpp	YES	0	 Output:
cpp	YES	0	    Returns milliseconds in modulo 0x1,0000,0000 (0 to 0xFFFFFFFF)
cpp	YES	0	 Notes:
cpp	YES	0	 1) This routine approximates the 64-bit integer division,
cpp	YES	0	    quotient =  ( 2^32 c + m ) / 1000,
cpp	YES	0	    through the use of 'magic' multipliers. A slow division is replaced by
cpp	YES	0	    a faster multiply using a scaled multiplicative inverse of the divisor:
cpp	YES	0	    quotient =~ ( 2^32 c + m ) * k,  where k = Ceiling[ 2^n / 1000 ]
cpp	YES	0	    The precision difference between multiplier and divisor sets the
cpp	YES	0	    upper-bound of the dividend which can be successfully divided.
cpp	YES	0	    For this application, n = 64, and the divisor (1000) has 10-bits of 
cpp	YES	0	    precision. This sets the dividend upper-bound to (64 - 10) = 54 bits,
cpp	YES	0	    and that of 'c' to (54 - 32) = 22 bits. This corresponds to a value
cpp	YES	0	 2) A distributed multiply with offset-summing is used find k( 2^32 c + m ):
cpp	YES	0	      prd = (2^32 kh + kl) * ( 2^32 c + m )
cpp	YES	0	          = 2^64 kh c + 2^32 kl c + 2^32 kh m + kl m
cpp	YES	0	               (d)         (c)         (b)       (a)
cpp	YES	0	    Graphically, the offset-sums align in little endian like this:
cpp	YES	0	                  LS -> MS
cpp	YES	0	            32       64       96      128
cpp	YES	0	    | a[-1]  |  a[0]  |  a[1]  |  a[2]  |
cpp	YES	0	    |       m kl      |    0   |    0   |  a[-1] not needed
cpp	YES	0	    |        |       m kh      |        |
cpp	YES	0	    |        |       c kl      |        |  a[1] holds the result
cpp	YES	0	    |        |        |       c kh      |  a[2] can be discarded
cpp	YES	0	    As only the high-word of 'm kl' and low-word of 'c kh' contribute to the
cpp	YES	0	    overall result, only (2) 32-bit words are needed for the accumulator.
cpp	YES	0	 3) As C++ does not intrinsically test for addition overflows, one must
cpp	YES	0	    code specifically to detect them. This approximation skips these
cpp	YES	0	    overflow checks for speed, hence the sum,
cpp	YES	0	    highword( m kl ) + m kh + c kl  <  (2^64-1),  MUST NOT OVERFLOW.
cpp	YES	0	    To meet this criteria, not only do we have to pick 'k' to achieve our
cpp	YES	0	    desired precision, we also have to split 'k' appropriately to avoid
cpp	YES	0	    any addition overflows.
cpp	YES	0	    'k' should be also chosen to align the various products on byte
cpp	YES	0	    boundaries to avoid any 64-bit shifts before additions, as they incur
cpp	YES	0	    major time penalties. The 'k' chosen for this specific division by 1000
cpp	YES	0	    was picked primarily to avoid shifts as well as for precision.
cpp	YES	0	    For the reasons list above, this routine is NOT a general one.
cpp	YES	0	    Changing divisors could break the overflow requirement and force
cpp	YES	0	    picking a 'k' split which requires shifts before additions.
cpp	YES	0	              ** Test THOROUGHLY after making changes **
cpp	YES	0	 4) Results of time benchmarks run on an ESP8266 Huzzah feather are:
cpp	YES	0	         usec   x Orig   Comment
cpp	YES	0	 Orig:   3.18   1.00     Original code
cpp	YES	0	 Corr:  13.21   4.15     64-bit reference code
cpp	YES	0	 Test:   4.60   1.45     64-bit magic multiply, 4x32
cpp	YES	0	 The magic multiplier routine runs ~3x faster than the reference. Execution
cpp	YES	0	 times can vary considerably with the numbers being multiplied, so one
cpp	YES	0	 should derate this factor to around 2x, worst case.
cpp	YES	0	   Reference function: corrected millis(), 64-bit arithmetic,
cpp	YES	0	                       truncated to 32-bits by return
cpp	NO	0	   {
cpp	NO	0	     // Get usec system time, usec overflow conter
cpp	NO	0	     ......
cpp	YES	0	   } //millis_corr
cpp	YES	0	 5) See this link for a good discussion on magic multipliers:
cpp	YES	0	    http://ridiculousfish.com/blog/posts/labor-of-division-episode-i.html
cpp	YES	0	 LS part
cpp	YES	0	 MS part, magic multiplier
cpp	YES	0	 Accumulator, 64-bit, little endian
cpp	YES	0	 ..........., 32-bit  segments
cpp	YES	0	 Zero high-acc
cpp	YES	0	 Get usec system time, usec overflow counter
cpp	YES	0	 (a) Init. low-acc with high-word of 1st product. The right-shift
cpp	YES	0	     falls on a byte boundary, hence is relatively quick.
cpp	YES	0	 (b) Offset sum, low-acc
cpp	YES	0	 (c) Offset sum, low-acc
cpp	YES	0	 (d) Truncated sum, high-acc
cpp	YES	0	 Extract result, high-acc

cpp	YES	0	\n core_esp8266_vm - Implements logic to enable external SRAM/PSRAM to be used\n                   as if it were on-chip memory by code.\n\n Copyright (c) 2020 Earle F. Philhower, III   All rights reserved.\n\n This library is free software; you can redistribute it and/or\n modify it under the terms of the GNU Lesser General Public\n License as published by the Free Software Foundation; either\n version 2.1 of the License, or (at your option) any later version.\n\n This library is distributed in the hope that it will be useful,\n but WITHOUT ANY WARRANTY; without even the implied warranty of\n MERCHANTABILITY or FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE.  See the GNU\n Lesser General Public License for more details.\n\n You should have received a copy of the GNU Lesser General Public\n License along with this library; if not, write to the Free Software\n Foundation, Inc., 51 Franklin St, Fifth Floor, Boston, MA  02110-1301  USA\n\n\n The original exception handler idea was taken from @pvvx's public domain\n misaligned-flash-read exception handler, available here:\n https://github.com/pvvx/esp8266web/blob/master/app/sdklib/system/app_main.c\n\n\n Theory of Operation:\n\n The Xtensa core generates a hardware exception (unrelated to C++ exceptions)\n when an address that's defined as invalid for load or store.  The XTOS ROM\n routines capture the machine state and call a standard C exception handler\n routine (or the default one which resets the system).\n\n We hook into this exception callback and decode the EXCVADDR (the address\n being accessed) and use the exception PC to read out the faulting\n instruction.  We decode that instruction and simulate it's behavior\n (i.e. either loading or storing some data to a register/external memory)\n and then return to the calling application.\n\n We use the hardware SPI interface to talk to an external SRAM/PSRAM, and\n implement a simple cache to minimize the amount of times we actually need\n to go out over the (slow) SPI bus.  The SPI is set up in a DIO mode which\n uses no more pins than normal SPI, but provides for ~2X faster transfers.\n\n NOTE: This works fine for processor accesses, but cannot be used by any\n of the peripherals' DMA.  For that, we'd need a real MMU.\n\n Hardware Configuration (make sure you have 3.3V compatible SRAMs):\n * SPI interfaced byte-addressible SRAM/PSRAM:  24LC1024 or smaller\n      CS   -> GPIO15\n      SCK  -> GPIO14\n      MOSI -> GPIO13\n      MISO -> GPIO12\n   (note these are GPIO numbers, not the Arduion Dxx ones.  Refer to your\n    ESP8266 board schematic for the mapping of GPIO to pin.)\n * Higher density PSRAM (ESP-PSRAM64H/etc.) works as well, but may be too\n   large to effectively use with UMM.  Only 256K is available vial malloc,\n   but addresses above 256K do work and can be used for fixed buffers.\n\n

cpp	YES	0	\n * "Cache_Read_Enable" as in Instruction Read Cache enable, ICACHE.\n *\n * The Boot ROM "Cache_Read_Enable" API enables virtual execution of code in\n * flash memory via an instruction cache, ICACHE. The cache size can be set to\n * 16K or 32K, and the NONOS SDK 2.x will always set ICACHE to 32K during\n * initialization.\n *\n * When you select a 16K vs. a 32K ICACHE size, you get 48K contiguous IRAM to\n * work with. The NONOS SDK 2.x does not have an option to select 16K/32K. This\n * is where this Boot ROM wrapper for Cache_Read_Enable comes in.\n * Note, there is support for 16K/32K cache size in NONOS SDK 3.0; however, I\n * do not see an option to have it has part of your general IRAM. That SDK adds\n * it to the heap.\n *\n * With this wrapper function, we override the SDK's ICACHE size.\n * A build-time define MMU_ICACHE_SIZE selects 16K or 32K ICACHE size.\n *\n * mmu_status is used to help understand calling behavior. At some point, it\n * should be trimmed down to the essentials.\n *\n * During NONOS SDK init, it will call to enable. Then call later, to process a\n * spi_flash_get_id request, it will disable/enable around the Boot ROM SPI calls.\n *\n *\n *\n *                   Arguments for Cache_Read_Enable\n *\n * The first two arguments appear to specify which 1MB block of the flash to\n * access with the ICACHE.\n *\n *   The first argument, map, is partly understood. It has three values 0, 1,\n *   and 2+. The value 0 selects the even 1MB block, and 1 selects the odd 1MB\n *   block, in other words, bit20 of the flash address. No guesses for a value\n *   of 2 or greater.\n *\n *   The second argument, p, bit 21 of the flash address. Or, it may be bits 23,\n *   22, 21 of the flash address. A three-bit field is cleared in the register\n *   for this argument; however, I have not seen any examples of it being used\n *   that way.\n *\n * The third argument, v, holds our center of attention. A value of 0 selects\n * 16K, and a value of 1 selects a 32K ICACHE. This is the only parameter we\n * need to modify on Cache_Read_Enable calls.\n *\n *\n *\n *                   Clues and Information sources\n *\n * "Cache_Read_Enable" is underdocumented. Main sources of information were from\n * rboot, zboot, https://richard.burtons.org/2015/06/12/esp8266-cache_read_enable/,\n * and other places. And some additional experimentation.\n *\n * Searching through the NONOS SDK shows nothing on this API; however, some\n * clues on what the NONOS SDK might be doing with ICACHE related calls can be\n * found in the RTOS SDK.\n * eg. ESP8266_RTOS_SDK/blob/master/components/spi_flash/src/spi_flash_raw.c\n * also calls to it in the bootloader.\n *\n

cpp	YES	0	\n  The thinking behind the ordering of Integrity Check, Full Poison Check, and\n  the specific *alloc function.\n\n  1. Integrity Check - verifies the heap management information is not corrupt.\n     This allows any other testing, that walks the heap, to run safely.\n\n  2. Place Full Poison Check before or after a specific *alloc function?\n     a. After, when the *alloc function operates on an existing allocation.\n     b. Before, when the *alloc function creates a new, not modified, allocation.\n\n     In a free() or realloc() call, the focus is on their allocation. It is\n     checked 1st and reported on 1ST if an error exists. Full Poison Check is\n     done after.\n\n     For malloc(), calloc(), and zalloc() Full Poison Check is done 1st since\n     these functions do not modify an existing allocation.\n

c	YES	0	*\n    Regarding constant-time (CT) HMAC:\n\n    Basically, constant-time algorithms makes it harder for attackers to learn things about your system based on the execution time of code.\n    Good intro here: https://www.bearssl.org/constanttime.html\n\n    It should be noted that every HMAC is already partially constant-time. Quoting the link above:\n    "Hash functions implemented by BearSSL (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512) consist in bitwise logical operations and additions on 32-bit or 64-bit words,\n    naturally yielding constant-time operations. HMAC is naturally as constant-time as the underlying hash function. The size of the MACed data, and the size of the key,\n    may leak, though; only the contents are protected."\n\n    For messages much smaller than getCtMaxDataLength(), constant-time processing takes substantially longer time to complete than a normal HMAC,\n    determined by the size of (getCtMaxDataLength() - getCtMinDataLength()).\n    Constant-time processing also sets limits on the data length.\n\n    Making the fixed data length limits variable will generally defeat the purpose of using constant-time.\n    Using data that exceeds the fixed data length limits will create the wrong HMAC.\n

It is based on HMAC. The provided implementation uses SHA-256 as the underlying hash function.\n\n        The constructor initializes the HKDF implementation with the input data to use for HKDF processing. (calls HKDF::init())\n\n        @param keyMaterial An array containing the key material to use when deriving subkeys. Salt is non-secret and can be empty.\n                   Its role is normally to bind the input to a conventional identifier that qualify it within the used protocol or application.\n        @param saltLength The length of the salt array, in bytes.\n

c	YES	0	 #################### Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) ####################
c	YES	0	*\n    From https://www.bearssl.org/apidoc/bearssl__aead_8h.html\n\n    An AEAD algorithm processes messages and provides confidentiality (encryption) and checked integrity (MAC). It uses the following parameters:\n\n     - A symmetric key. Exact size depends on the AEAD algorithm.\n     - A nonce (IV). Size depends on the AEAD algorithm; for most algorithms, it is crucial for security that any given nonce value is never used twice for the same key and distinct messages.\n     - Data to encrypt and protect.\n     - Additional authenticated data, which is covered by the MAC but otherwise left untouched (i.e. not encrypted).\n\n    The AEAD algorithm encrypts the data, and produces an authentication tag.\n    It is assumed that the encrypted data, the tag, the additional authenticated data and the nonce are sent to the receiver;\n    the additional data and the nonce may be implicit (e.g. using elements of the underlying transport protocol, such as record sequence numbers).\n    The receiver will recompute the tag value and compare it with the one received;\n    if they match, then the data is correct, and can be decrypted and used;\n    otherwise, at least one of the elements was altered in transit, normally leading to wholesale rejection of the complete message.\n

c	YES	0	*\n        Encrypt the data array using the ChaCha20 stream cipher and use Poly1305 for message authentication.\n        The function generates in place an equal-length ChaCha20 encrypted version of the data array.\n        More information about this encryption standard can be found here: https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7539 , https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8439\n        Uses the BearSSL cryptographic library.\n\n        Encryption of small messages (up to a few hundred data bytes) takes around 0.5-1 ms with the default nonceGenerator, half of this without keySalt.\n\n        The output values of ChaCha20Poly1305::encrypt should be passed as input values to ChaCha20Poly1305::decrypt.\n\n        Note that a 12 byte nonce is generated via getNonceGenerator() every time ChaCha20Poly1305::encrypt is called.\n        If the same key and nonce combination is used more than once for distinct messages, the encryption will be broken, so keep the following in mind:\n\n        By default the nonce is generated via the hardware random number generator of the ESP8266.\n        The entropy of this source may not be sufficient to avoid nonce collisions, so to further reduce the risk of encryption failure\n        it is recommended that a keySalt is always provided when using the default nonceGenerator. Using a keySalt will create a\n        pseudorandom subkey from the original key via HKDF, and use that for the encryption/decryption.\n        The same key + keySalt will always generate the same subkey.\n\n        An alternative to using a keySalt is to change the nonceGenerator so that it does not rely on random numbers.\n        One way to do this would be to use a counter that guarantees the same key + nonce combination is never used.\n        This may not be easily achievable in all scenarios, however.\n\n        @param data An array containing the data to encrypt. The encrypted data is generated in place, so when the function returns the data array will contain the encrypted data.\n        @param dataLength The length of the data array in bytes.\n        @param key The secret encryption key to use. Must be 32 bytes (ENCRYPTION_KEY_LENGTH) long.\n        @param keySalt The salt to use when generating a subkey from key. Note that the same salt must be used during decryption as during encryption. Set to nullptr to prevent subkey generation.\n        @param keySaltLength The length of keySalt in bytes.\n        @param resultingNonce The array that will store the nonce generated during encryption. Must be able to contain at least 12 bytes. The nonce is not secret and must be passed to the decryption function.\n        @param resultingTag The array that will store the message authentication tag generated during encryption. Must be able to contain at least 16 bytes. The tag is not secret and must be passed to the decryption function.\n        @param aad Additional authenticated data. This data will be covered by the Poly1305 MAC, but not encrypted.\n                  You can include the unencrypted parts of your message as AAD to ensure that the encrypted content cannot\n                  be re-sent with replaced unencrypted data by an attacker.\n                  Defaults to nullptr.\n        @param aadLength The length of the aad array in bytes. Defaults to 0.\n

c	YES	0	 The purpose of scheduled functions is to trigger, from SYS stack (like in
c	YES	0	 an interrupt or a system event), registration of user code to be executed
c	YES	0	 in user stack (called CONT stack) without the common restrictions from
c	YES	0	 system context.  Details are below.
c	YES	0	 The purpose of recurrent scheduled function is to independently execute
c	YES	0	 user code in CONT stack on a regular basis.
c	YES	0	 It has been introduced with ethernet service in mind, it can also be used
c	YES	0	 It allows these services to be run even from a user loop not going back
c	YES	0	 to `loop()`.
c	YES	0	 Ticker + scheduled function offer the same service but recurrent
c	YES	0	 scheduled function happen more often: every yield() (vs every loop()),
c	YES	0	 and time resolution is microsecond (vs millisecond). Details are below.
c	YES	0	 compute_scheduled_recurrent_grain() is used by delay() to give a chance to
c	YES	0	 all recurrent functions to run per their timing requirement.
c	YES	0	 scheduled functions called once:
c	YES	0	 * internal queue is FIFO.
c	YES	0	 * Add the given lambda to a fifo list of lambdas, which is run when
c	YES	0	   `loop` function returns.
c	YES	0	 * Use lambdas to pass arguments to a function, or call a class/static
c	YES	0	   member function.
c	YES	0	 * Please ensure variables or instances used from inside lambda will exist
c	YES	0	   when lambda is later called.
c	YES	0	 * There is no mechanism for cancelling scheduled functions.
c	YES	0	 * `yield` can be called from inside lambdas.
c	YES	0	 * Returns false if the number of scheduled functions exceeds
c	YES	0	   SCHEDULED_FN_MAX_COUNT (or memory shortage).
c	YES	0	 * Run the lambda only once next time.
c	YES	0	 * A scheduled function can schedule a function.
c	YES	0	 Run all scheduled functions.
c	YES	0	 Use this function if your are not using `loop`,
c	YES	0	 or `loop` does not return on a regular basis.
c	YES	0	 recurrent scheduled function:
c	YES	0	 * Internal queue is a FIFO.
c	YES	0	 * Run the lambda periodically about every <repeat_us> microseconds until
c	YES	0	   it returns false.
c	YES	0	 * Note that it may be more than <repeat_us> microseconds between calls if
c	YES	0	   `yield` is not called frequently, and therefore should not be used for
c	YES	0	   timing critical operations.
c	YES	0	 * There is no mechanism for externally cancelling recurrent scheduled
c	YES	0	   functions.  However a user function returning false will cancel itself.
c	YES	0	 * Long running operations or yield() or delay() are not allowed in the
c	YES	0	   recurrent function.
c	YES	0	 * If alarm is used, anytime during scheduling when it returns true,
c	YES	0	   any remaining delay from repeat_us is disregarded, and fn is executed.
c	YES	0	 Test recurrence and run recurrent scheduled functions.
c	YES	0	 (internally called at every `yield()` and `loop()`)
c	YES	0	 ESP_SCHEDULE_H

cpp	YES	0	\n * Adaptation of _xtos_set_exception_handler for Arduino ESP8266 core\n *\n * This replacement for the Boot ROM `_xtos_set_exception_handler` is used to\n * install our replacement `_xtos_c_wrapper_handler`. This change protects the\n * value of `excvaddr` from corruption.\n *\n *\n *                             Details\n *\n * The issue, the Boot ROM "C" wrapper for exception handlers,\n * `_xtos_c_wrapper_handler`, turns interrupts back on. This leaves `excvaddr`\n * exposed to possible overwrite before it is read. For example, if an interrupt\n * is taken during the exception handler processing and the ISR handler\n * generates a new exception, the original value of `excvaddr` is lost.  To\n * address this issue we have a replacement `_xtos_c_wrapper_handler` in file\n * `exc-c-wrapper-handler.S`.\n *\n * An overview, of an exception at entry: New interrupts are blocked by EXCM\n * being set. Once cleared, interrupts above the current INTLEVEL and exceptions\n * (w/o creating a DoubleException) can occur.\n *\n * Using our replacement for `_xtos_c_wrapper_handler`, INTLEVEL is raised to 15\n * with EXCM cleared.\n *\n * The original Boot ROM `_xtos_c_wrapper_handler` at entry would set INTLEVEL\n * to 3 with EXCM cleared, save registers, then do a `rsil 0` (interrupts fully\n * enabled!) just before calling the registered "C" Exception handler. Our\n * replacement keeps INTLEVEL at 15. This is needed to support the Arduino model\n * of interrupts disabled while an ISR runs.\n *\n * And we also need it for umm_malloc to work safely with an IRAM heap from an\n * ISR call. While malloc() will supply DRAM for all allocation from an ISR, we\n * want free() to safely operate from an ISR to avoid a leak potential.\n *\n * If an exception handler needs interrupts enabled, it would be done after it\n * has consumed the value of `excvaddr`. Whether such action is safe is left to\n * the exception handler writer to determine. However, with our current\n * architecture, I am not convinced it can be done safely.\n *\n

cpp	YES	0	*\n        The ESP32 Technical Reference Manual v4.1 chapter 24 has the following to say about random number generation (no information found for ESP8266):\n\n        "When used correctly, every 32-bit value the system reads from the RNG_DATA_REG register of the random number generator is a true random number.\n        These true random numbers are generated based on the noise in the Wi-Fi/BT RF system.\n        When Wi-Fi and BT are disabled, the random number generator will give out pseudo-random numbers.\n\n        When Wi-Fi or BT is enabled, the random number generator is fed two bits of entropy every APB clock cycle (normally 80 MHz).\n        Thus, for the maximum amount of entropy, it is advisable to read the random register at a maximum rate of 5 MHz.\n        A data sample of 2 GB, read from the random number generator with Wi-Fi enabled and the random register read at 5 MHz,\n        has been tested using the Dieharder Random Number Testsuite (version 3.31.1).\n        The sample passed all tests."\n\n        Since ESP32 is the sequal to ESP8266 it is unlikely that the ESP8266 is able to generate random numbers more quickly than 5 MHz when run at a 80 MHz frequency.\n        A maximum random number frequency of 0.5 MHz is used here to leave some margin for possibly inferior components in the ESP8266.\n        It should be noted that the ESP8266 has no Bluetooth functionality, so turning the WiFi off is likely to cause RANDOM_REG32 to use pseudo-random numbers.\n\n        It is possible that yield() must be called on the ESP8266 to properly feed the hardware random number generator new bits, since there is only one processor core available.\n        However, no feeding requirements are mentioned in the ESP32 documentation, and using yield() could possibly cause extended delays during nonce generation.\n        Thus only delayMicroseconds() is used below.\n

c	YES	0	\n Most of the comments here are gleamed from the xtensa files found at the site\n listed below and are mostly unverified:\n https://github.com/qca/open-ath9k-htc-firmware/tree/master/sboot/magpie_1_1/sboot/athos/src/xtos\n  * exc-c-wrapper-handler.S\n  * exc-sethandler.c\n
c	NO	0	\n  The Boot ROM sets up a table of dispatch handlers at 0x3FFFC000. This table\n  has an entry for each of the EXCCAUSE values, 0 through 63. The exception\n  handler at the `User Exception Vector` uses EXCCAUSE with the base address\n  0x3FFFC000 to build a jump address to the respective cause handler. Of the\n  cause handle functions, `_xtos_c_wrapper_handler` and `_xtos_unhandled_exception`\n  are of interest.\n\n  Exception handler entries that do not have a specific handler are set to\n  `_xtos_unhandled_exception`. This handler will execute a `break 1, 1`\n  (0x4000DC4Bu) before doing a `rfe` (return from exception).  Since the PC has\n  not changed, the event that caused the 1st exception will likely keep\n  repeating until the HWDT kicks in.\n\n  These exception handling functions are in assembly, and do not conform to the\n  typical "C" function conventions. cpp	YES	0	 This is the entry point of the application.\n * It gets called on the default stack, which grows down from the top\n * of DRAM area.\n * .bss has not been zeroed out yet, but .data and .rodata are in place.\n * Cache is not enabled, so only ROM and IRAM functions can be called.\n * Peripherals (except for SPI0 and UART0) are not initialized.\n * This function does not return.\n 
cpp	YES	0	\n   A bit of explanation for this entry point:\n\n   SYS is the SDK task/context used by the upperlying system to run its\n   administrative tasks (at least WLAN and lwip's receive callbacks and\n   Ticker).  NONOS-SDK is designed to run user's non-threaded code in\n   another specific task/context with its own stack in BSS.\n\n   Some clever fellows found that the SYS stack was a large and quite unused\n   piece of ram that we could use for the user's stack instead of using user's\n   main memory, thus saving around 4KB on ram/heap.\n\n   A problem arose later, which is that this stack can heavily be used by\n   the SDK for some features.  One of these features is WPS.  We still don't\n   know if other features are using this, or if this memory is going to be\n   used in future SDK releases.\n\n   WPS being flawed by its poor security, or not being used by lots of\n   users, it has been decided that we are still going to use that memory for\n   user's stack and disable the use of WPS.\n\n   app_entry() jumps to app_entry_custom() defined as "weakref" calling\n   itself a weak customizable function, allowing to use another one when\n   this is required (see core_esp8266_app_entry_noextra4k.cpp, used by WPS).\n\n   (note: setting app_entry() itself as "weak" is not sufficient and always\n    ends up with the other "noextra4k" one linked, maybe because it has a\n    default ENTRY(app_entry) value in linker scripts).\n\n   References:\n   https://github.com/esp8266/Arduino/pull/4553\n   https://github.com/esp8266/Arduino/pull/4622\n   https://github.com/esp8266/Arduino/issues/4779\n   https://github.com/esp8266/Arduino/pull/4889\n\n

cpp	YES	0	\n  Some general architecture for GDB integration with the UART to enable\n  serial debugging.\n\n  UART1 is transmit only and can never be used by GDB.\n\n  When gdbstub_has_uart_isr_control() (only true in the case GDB is enabled),\n  UART0 needs to be under the control of the GDB stub for enable/disable/irq\n  (but speed, parity, etc. still alllowable).  Basically, GDB needs to make\n  sure that UART0 is never really disabled.\n\n  GDB sets up UART0 with a fifo and a 2-character timeout during init.  This\n  is required to ensure that GDBStub can check every character coming in, even\n  if it is not read by the user app or if the commands don't hit the FIFO\n  interrupt level.  It checks every character that comes in, and if GDB isn't\n  active just passes them to the user RAM FIFO unless it's a Ctrl-C (0x03).\n\n  GDBStub doesn't care about the struct uart_*, and allocating it or freeing\n  it has no effect (so you can do Serial.end() and free the uart...but as\n  mentioned above even if you Serial.end, the actual UART0 HW will still be\n  kept running to enable GDB to do commands.\n

Philhower, III.  All rights reserved.\n\n  The core idea is to have a programmable waveform generator with a unique\n  high and low period (defined in microseconds or CPU clock cycles).  TIMER1 is\n  set to 1-shot mode and is always loaded with the time until the next edge\n  of any live waveforms.\n\n  Up to one waveform generator per pin supported.\n\n  Each waveform generator is synchronized to the ESP clock cycle counter, not the\n  timer. cpp	YES	0	\n *  Replacement for the ROM aes_unwrap() function. It uses the heap instead of\n *  the static DRAM address at 0x3FFFEA80, which may step on the SYS stack in\n *  special circumstances such as HWDT Stack Dump.\n *\n *  When not using WPS, the address space 0x3FFFE000 up to 0x40000000 is mostly\n *  available for the stacks. The one known exception is the ROM AES APIs. When\n *  `aes_decrypt_init` is called, it uses memory at 0x3FFFEA80 up to 0x3FFFEB30\n *  for a buffer. At the finish, `aes_decrypt_deinit` zeros out the buffer.\n *\n *  The NONOS SDK appears to have replacements for most of the ROM's AES APIs.\n *  However, the SDK still calls on the ROM's aes_unwrap function, which uses\n *  the ROM's AES APIs to operate. These calls can overwrite some of the stack\n *  space. To resolve the problem, this module replaces `aes_unwrap`.\n *\n *  Final note, so far, I have not seen a problem when using the extra 4K heap\n *  option without the "debug HWDT". It is when combined with the HWDT Stack\n *  Dump that a problem shows. This combination adds a Boot ROM stack, which\n *  pushes up the SYS and CONT stacks into the AES Buffer space. Then the\n *  problem shows.\n *\n *  While debugging with painted stack space, during WiFi Connect, Reconnect,\n *  and about every hour, a block of memory 0x3FFFEA80 - 0x3FFFEB30 (176 bytes)\n *  was zeroed by the Boot ROM function aes_decrypt_init. All other painted\n *  memory in the area was untouched after starting WiFi.\n 
cpp	YES	0	 Using the ROM version of aes_unwrap should be fine for the no extra 4K case
cpp	YES	0	 which is usually used in conjunction with WPS.
cpp	YES	0	 This is required for DEBUG_ESP_HWDT.
cpp	YES	0	 The need is unconfirmed for the extra 4K heap case.

c	YES	0	 opened frequently, reducing number of readings from the spi flash for
c	YES	0	 finding those files.
c	YES	0	 This will grow each fd by 6 bytes. If your files are opened in patterns
c	YES	0	 with a degree of temporal locality, the system is optimized.
c	YES	0	 Examples can be letting spiffs serve web content, where one file is the css.
c	YES	0	 The css is accessed for each html file that is opened, meaning it is
c	YES	0	 accessed almost every second time a file is opened. Another example could be
c	YES	0	 a log file that is often opened, written, and closed.
c	YES	0	 The size of the cache is number of given file descriptors, as it piggybacks
c	YES	0	 on the fd update mechanism. The cache lives in the closed file descriptors.
c	YES	0	 When closed, the fd know the whereabouts of the file. Instead of forgetting
c	YES	0	 this, the temporal cache will keep handling updates to that file even if the
c	YES	0	 fd is closed. If the file is opened again, the location of the file is found
c	YES	0	 directly. If all available descriptors become opened, all cache memory is
c	YES	0	 lost.
c	YES	0	 Temporal file cache hit score. Each time a file is opened, all cached files
c	YES	0	 will lose one point. If the opened file is found in cache, that entry will
c	YES	0	 gain SPIFFS_TEMPORAL_CACHE_HIT_SCORE points. One can experiment with this
c	YES	0	 value for the specific access patterns of the application. However, it must
c	YES	0	 be between 1 (no gain for hitting a cached entry often) and 255.
c	YES	0	 Enable to be able to map object indices to memory.
c	YES	0	 This allows for faster and more deterministic reading if cases of reading
c	YES	0	 large files and when changing file offset by seeking around a lot.
c	YES	0	 When mapping a file's index, the file system will be scanned for index pages
c	YES	0	 and the info will be put in memory provided by user. When reading, the
c	YES	0	 memory map can be looked up instead of searching for index pages on the
c	YES	0	 medium. This way, user can trade memory against performance.
c	YES	0	 Whole, parts of, or future parts not being written yet can be mapped. The
c	YES	0	 memory array will be owned by spiffs and updated accordingly during garbage

c	YES	0	 By default SPIFFS in some cases relies on the property of NOR flash that bits
c	YES	0	 cannot be set from 0 to 1 by writing and that controllers will ignore such
c	YES	0	 bit changes. This results in fewer reads as SPIFFS can in some cases perform
c	YES	0	 blind writes, with all bits set to 1 and only those it needs reset set to 0.
c	YES	0	 Most of the chips and controllers allow this behavior, so the default is to
c	YES	0	 use this technique. If your controller is one of the rare ones that don't,
c	YES	0	 turn this option on and SPIFFS will perform a read-modify-write instead.

c	YES	0	\n * spiffs_nucleus.h\n *\n *  Created on: Jun 15, 2013\n *      Author: petera\n 
c	YES	0	 SPIFFS layout\n *\n * spiffs is designed for following spi flash characteristics:\n *   - only big areas of data (blocks) can be erased\n *   - erasing resets all bits in a block to ones\n *   - writing pulls ones to zeroes\n *   - zeroes cannot be pulled to ones, without erase\n *   - wear leveling\n *\n * spiffs is also meant to be run on embedded, memory constraint devices.\n *\n * Entire area is divided in blocks. Entire area is also divided in pages.\n * Each block contains same number of pages. A page cannot be erased, but a\n * block can be erased.\n *\n * Entire area must be block_size * x\n * page_size must be block_size / (2^y) where y > 2\n *\n * ex: area = 1024*1024 bytes, block size = 65536 bytes, page size = 256 bytes\n *\n * BLOCK 0  PAGE 0       object lookup 1\n *          PAGE 1       object lookup 2\n *          ...\n *          PAGE n-1     object lookup n\n *          PAGE n       object data 1\n *          PAGE n+1     object data 2\n *          ...\n *          PAGE n+m-1   object data m\n *\n * BLOCK 1  PAGE n+m     object lookup 1\n *          PAGE n+m+1   object lookup 2\n *          ...\n *          PAGE 2n+m-1  object lookup n\n *          PAGE 2n+m    object data 1\n *          PAGE 2n+m    object data 2\n *          ...\n *          PAGE 2n+2m-1 object data m\n * ...\n *\n * n is number of object lookup pages, which is number of pages needed to index all pages\n * in a block by object id\n *   : block_size / page_size * sizeof(obj_id) / page_size\n * m is number data pages, which is number of pages in block minus number of lookup pages\n *   : block_size / page_size - block_size / page_size * sizeof(obj_id) / page_size\n * thus, n+m is total number of pages in a block\n *   : block_size / page_size\n *\n * ex: n = 65536/256*2/256 = 2, m = 65536/256 - 2 = 254 => n+m = 65536/256 = 256\n *\n * Object lookup pages contain object id entries. Each entry represent the corresponding\n * data page.\n * Assuming a 16 bit object id, an object id being 0xffff represents a free page.\n * An object id being 0x0000 represents a deleted page.\n *\n * ex: page 0 : lookup : 0008 0001 0aaa ffff ffff ffff ffff ffff ..\n *     page 1 : lookup : ffff ffff ffff ffff ffff ffff ffff ffff ..\n *     page 2 : data   : data for object id 0008\n *     page 3 : data   : data for object id 0001\n *     page 4 : data   : data for object id 0aaa\n *     ...\n *\n *\n * Object data pages can be either object index pages or object content.\n * All object data pages contains a data page header, containing object id and span index.\n * The span index denotes the object page ordering amongst data pages with same object id.\n * This applies to both object index pages (when index spans more than one page of entries),\n * and object data pages.\n * An object index page contains page entries pointing to object content page. The entry index\n * in a object index page correlates to the span index in the actual object data page.\n * The first object index page (span index 0) is called object index header page, and also\n * contains object flags (directory/file), size, object name etc.\n *\n * ex:\n *  BLOCK 1\n *    PAGE 256: objectl lookup page 1\n *      [*123] [ 123] [ 123] [ 123]\n *      [ 123] [*123] [ 123] [ 123]\n *      [free] [free] [free] [free] ...\n *    PAGE 257: objectl lookup page 2\n *      [free] [free] [free] [free] ...\n *    PAGE 258: object index page (header)\n *      obj.id:0123 span.ix:0000 flags:INDEX\n *      size:1600 name:ex.txt type:file\n *      [259] [260] [261] [262]\n *    PAGE 259: object data page\n *      obj.id:0123 span.ix:0000 flags:DATA\n *    PAGE 260: object data page\n *      obj.id:0123 span.ix:0001 flags:DATA\n *    PAGE 261: object data page\n *      obj.id:0123 span.ix:0002 flags:DATA\n *    PAGE 262: object data page\n *      obj.id:0123 span.ix:0003 flags:DATA\n *    PAGE 263: object index page\n *      obj.id:0123 span.ix:0001 flags:INDEX\n *      [264] [265] [fre] [fre]\n *      [fre] [fre] [fre] [fre]\n *    PAGE 264: object data page\n *      obj.id:0123 span.ix:0004 flags:DATA\n *    PAGE 265: object data page\n *      obj.id:0123 span.ix:0005 flags:DATA\n *\n

cpp	YES	0	\n * TCB0 is set to tick every 2 clock cycles. TCB0's interrupt handler is called every 8192 ticks.\n * Therefore, in relation to the CPU frequency, the number of microseconds for each interrupt are:\n *      1 MHz :  16384 uS\n *      2 MHz :   8192 uS\n *      4 MHz :   4096 uS\n *      8 MHz :   2048 uS\n *     16 MHz :   1024 uS\n *     20 MHz :    819 uS\n *\n * The whole number of milliseconds per TCB0 interrupt can be then derived:\n *      1 MHz :  16 mS\n *      2 MHz :   8 mS\n *      4 MHz :   4 mS\n *      8 MHz :   2 mS\n *     16 MHz :   1 mS\n *     20 MHz :   0 mS\n *\n * The fractional number of milliseconds (thus, microseconds) per TCB0 interrupt are then:\n *      1 MHz : 384 uS\n *      2 MHz : 192 uS\n *      4 MHz :  96 uS\n *      8 MHz :  48 uS\n *     16 MHz :  24 uS\n *     20 MHz : 819 uS\n *\n * To reduce memory usage (with a slight lost of precision for some CPU frequency), those values can\n * be divided by 8 and thus they become:\n *      1 MHz :  48 steps\n *      2 MHz :  24 steps\n *      4 MHz :  12 steps\n *      8 MHz :   6 steps\n *     16 MHz :   3 steps\n *     20 MHz : 102 steps\n

cpp	YES	0	\n * Timer0 is set to tick every 64 clock cycles. Timer0's overflow handler is called every 256 ticks.\n * Therefore, in relation to the CPU frequency, the number of microseconds for each overflow are:\n *    128 kHz : 128000 uS\n *      1 MHz :  16384 uS\n *      2 MHz :   8192 uS\n *      4 MHz :   4096 uS\n *      8 MHz :   2048 uS\n *     12 MHz :   1365 uS\n *     16 MHz :   1024 uS\n *     20 MHz :    819 uS\n *\n * The whole number of milliseconds per Timer0 overflow can be then derived:\n *    128 kHz : 128 mS\n *      1 MHz :  16 mS\n *      2 MHz :   8 mS\n *      4 MHz :   4 mS\n *      8 MHz :   2 mS\n *     12 MHz :   1 mS\n *     16 MHz :   1 mS\n *     20 MHz :   0 mS\n *\n * The fractional number of milliseconds (thus, microseconds) per Timer0 overflow are then:\n *    128 kHz :   0 uS\n *      1 MHz : 384 uS\n *      2 MHz : 192 uS\n *      4 MHz :  96 uS\n *      8 MHz :  48 uS\n *     12 MHz : 365 uS\n *     16 MHz :  24 uS\n *     20 MHz : 819 uS\n *\n * To reduce memory usage (with a slight lost of precision for some CPU frequency), those values can\n * be divided by 8 and thus they become:\n *    128 kHz :   0 steps\n *      1 MHz :  48 steps\n *      2 MHz :  24 steps\n *      4 MHz :  12 steps\n *      8 MHz :   6 steps\n *     12 MHz :  46 steps\n *     16 MHz :   3 steps\n *     20 MHz : 102 steps\n

cpp	YES	0	\n     * AVR ADC reference voltage   = 5.0 V\n     * AVR ADC input voltage range = 0.0 V to 5.0 V\n     * AVR ADC resolution          = 10 bit (0 to 1023)\n     *\n     * FHT input value range       = -127 to +128\n     *\n     * Input signal\n     *     Waveform     voltage : Vs\n     *     Bias         voltage : Vb\n     *     Biased input voltage : Vi = Vs + Vb\n     *\n     * ADC reading\n     *     Value read by ADC              : ADC =  Vi * 1023 / 5.0\n     *     ADC read offset         factor : OF  = -Vb * 1023 / 5.0\n     *     ADC read scale          factor : SF  = 255 / c	YES	0	\n * Using this implementation, NodeMCU in SPI-slave mode is register-based, half-duplex, and working in\n * a bulk of 4 or 32 bytes.\n *\n * Therefore for a master (any master) to send and receive data to a NodeMCU in SPI-slave mode, the master\n * must follow this procedure (for a bulk of four bytes):\n *\n *     # Send data\n *           + Assert the SS pin to low;\n *           + Send 0x01          via: transfer(dummy, 0x01 );\n *           + Send one byte data via: transfer(dummy, data1);\n *           + Send one byte data via: transfer(dummy, data2);\n *           + Send one byte data via: transfer(dummy, data3);\n *           + Send one byte data via: transfer(dummy, data4);\n *           + Deassert the SS pin to high.\n *\n *     # Receive data\n *           + Assert the SS pin to low;\n *           + Send 0x04          via: transfer(dummy, 0x04);\n *           + Read one byte data via: transfer(data1, 0x00);\n *           + Read one byte data via: transfer(data2, 0x00);\n *           + Read one byte data via: transfer(data3, 0x00);\n *           + Read one byte data via: transfer(data4, 0x00);\n *           + Deassert the SS pin to high.\n *\n *     WARNING : # If the NodeMCU is booting at a moment when the SPI-master deasserted the SS pin,\n *                 the NodeMCU will fail to boot.\n *               # The official Arduino SPISlave example, workaround this issue by pulsing the SS pin\n *                 before and after the transfer sequence (instead of asserting and deasserting it).\n *               # Another workaround is to use tri-state buffers on all the GPIOs. The eCxx NodeMCU\n *                 development board is using this method.\n *\n *     NOTE    : # You can also use a call to transfer(uint8_t*, 5) to send data.\n *               # You can also use a call to write() followed by transfer(uint8_t*, 4) to receive data.\n *               # To use the 32 bytes variant use the command [ 0x02, 0x00 ] for sending data and the\n *                 command [ 0x03, 0x00 ] for receiving data.\n *\n * The flow for a NodeMCU in SPI-slave mode is as follow:\n *\n *     # Receive data:\n *           + If there is any pending data to be read then canRead() will return true and\n *             the next steps can be executed;\n *           + Read four bytes data via: readFromMaster(uint8_t (&)[4]).\n *\n *     # Send data:\n *           + Sending data can only be done if canRead() return 'false';\n *           + Send four bytes data via: writeToMaster(const uint8_t (&)[4]).\n *\n *     NOTE : To use the 32 bytes variant use the functions readFromMaster(uint8_t (&)[32])\n *            and writeToMaster(const uint8_t (&)[32]).\n 
c	YES	0	\n         * WARNING : SPI-master mode only!\n         * \n         * NOTE : # In the case of a master device with multiple slaves, multiple SS pins will be required.\n         *          Therefore, transactions must be done manually for each slave using the following steps:\n         *              1. Disable interrupts (if the timing is critical).\n         *              2. Call ntmBegin() to set the SPI parameters.\n         *              3. Select the SS pin for the slave device to be addressed using digitalWrite().\n         *              4. Call write() and/or transfer() as many times as needed.\n         *              5. Re-enable interrupts in case it was disabled.\n         *        # An 'eCxx::AtomicGuard' class instance can be used to conveniently disable and re-enable\n         *          interrupts within a function.\n         *        # Do not call ntmSelectSlave() and ntmDeselectSlave() because they will always use the\n         *          default SS pin.\n

java	YES	0	*\n * This is google-java-format, a new Java formatter that follows the Google Java Style Guide quite\n * precisely---to the letter and to the spirit.\n *\n * <p>This formatter uses the javac parser to generate an AST. Because the AST loses information\n * about the non-tokens in the input (including newlines, comments, etc.), and even some tokens\n * (e.g., optional commas or semicolons), this formatter lexes the input again and follows along in\n * the resulting list of tokens. Its lexer splits all multi-character operators (like "&gt;&gt;")\n * into multiple single-character operators. Each non-token is assigned to a token---non-tokens\n * following a token on the same line go with that token; those following go with the next token---\n * and there is a final EOF token to hold final comments.\n *\n * <p>The formatter walks the AST to generate a Greg Nelson/Derek Oppen-style list of formatting\n * {@link Op}s [1--2] that then generates a structured {@link Doc}. Each AST node type has a visitor\n * to emit a sequence of {@link Op}s for the node.\n *\n * <p>Some data-structure operations are easier in the list of {@link Op}s, while others become\n * easier in the {@link Doc}. The {@link Op}s are walked to attach the comments. As the {@link Op}s\n * are generated, missing input tokens are inserted and incorrect output tokens are dropped,\n * ensuring that the output matches the input even in the face of formatter errors. Finally, the\n * formatter walks the {@link Doc} to format it in the given width.\n *\n * <p>This formatter also produces data structures of which tokens and comments appear where on the\n * input, and on the output, to help output a partial reformatting of a slightly edited input.\n *\n * <p>Instances of the formatter are immutable and thread-safe.\n *\n * <p>[1] Nelson, Greg, and John DeTreville. Personal communication.\n *\n * <p>[2] Oppen, Derek C. "Prettyprinting". ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems,\n * Volume 2 Issue 4, Oct. 1980, pp. 465–483.\n

cpp	YES	0	! A "memory resource adaptor" adapts a "thing that can allocate memory" to the
cpp	YES	0	! std::pmr::memory_resource interface. It's used in exec::function when the function's
cpp	YES	0	! type parameters do not require that its eventual receiver have an environment that's

cpp	YES	0	 the resulting address is byte-aligned, and we need to adjust right by

cpp	YES	0	 we might need.

cpp	YES	0	! returned to the caller.

cpp	YES	0	! caller waiting on its result and no enclosing async scope — for

cpp	YES	0	! work that should be *tracked* by a scope (so the scope can be joined

cpp	YES	0	! @c stdexec::sync_wait.

cpp	YES	0	!       of the C++26 working draft. The standardized way to spawn

cpp	YES	0	!       which requires an async scope to take ownership of the
cpp	YES	0	!       operation.

cpp	YES	0	 This file defines function<ReturnType(Arguments...)>, which is a type-erased sender

cpp	YES	0	*\n * This is an implementation of the BWOS queue as described in\n * BWoS: Formally Verified Block-based Work Stealing for Parallel Processing (Wang et al. 2023)\n *\n * BLOCK COUNTER ENCODING:\n * ----------------------\n * Block counters (last_block_, start_block_, and internal counters) are 64-bit values with:\n *   - Bits [63:32]: Round number (32-bit unsigned, wraps on overflow)\n *   - Bits [31:0]:  Block index within the circular block array (masked by mask_)\n *\n * The round number increments each time the index wraps around from mask_ to 0.\n * This encoding allows:\n *   - Direct comparison of counters to determine relative order\n *   - ABA problem prevention through round tracking\n *   - Efficient atomic operations on a single 64-bit value\n *\n * TWO-LEVEL ROUND SYSTEM:\n * ----------------------\n * 1. Queue-level rounds: Tracked in last_block_/start_block_ upper 32 bits\n *    - Increments when the owner wraps around the circular block array\n *    - Passed to blocks during reclaim() to initialize block-level rounds\n *\n * 2. Block-level rounds: Stored in head_/steal_tail_ upper 32 bits\n *    - Prevents ABA problems when blocks are reused\n *    - Synchronized through takeover()/grant() atomic swaps\n *    - Verified by is_writable() before block reuse\n *\n * THREAD SAFETY:\n * -------------\n * - Owner thread: Exclusively calls push_back() and pop_back()\n * - Thief threads: Multiple threads can concurrently call steal_front()\n * - last_block_: Modified only by owner (relaxed ordering)\n * - start_block_: Modified only by owner when reclaiming blocks\n * - Block synchronization via head_/steal_tail_ swaps and acquire/release ordering\n

cpp	YES	0	 shared components of split and ensure_started
cpp	YES	0	 The split and ensure_started algorithms are very similar in implementation.
cpp	YES	0	 The salient differences are:
cpp	YES	0	 split: the input async operation is always connected. It is only
cpp	YES	0	   started when one of the split senders is connected and started.
cpp	YES	0	   split senders are copyable, so there are multiple operation states
cpp	YES	0	   to be notified on completion. These are stored in an intrusive
cpp	YES	0	   linked list.
cpp	YES	0	 ensure_started: the input async operation is always started, so
cpp	YES	0	   the internal receiver will always be completed. The ensure_started
cpp	YES	0	   sender is move-only and single-shot, so there will only ever be one
cpp	YES	0	   operation state to be notified on completion.
cpp	YES	0	 The shared state should add-ref itself when the input async
cpp	YES	0	 operation is started and release itself when its completion
cpp	YES	0	 is notified.
cpp	YES	0	 The receiver does not hold a reference to the shared state.
cpp	YES	0	 should never be called
cpp	YES	0	 The operation state of ensure_started, and each operation state of split, has one of these,
cpp	YES	0	 created when the sender is connected. There are 0 or more of them for each underlying async
cpp	YES	0	 operation. It is what ensure_started- and split-sender's `connect` fn returns. It holds a
cpp	YES	0	 ref count to the shared state.
cpp	YES	0	 Scenario: there are no more split senders, this is the only operation state, the
cpp	YES	0	 underlying operation has not yet been started, and the receiver's stop token is already
cpp	YES	0	 in the "stop requested" state. Then registering the stop callback will call
cpp	YES	0	 __local_state::operator() on *this synchronously. It may also be called asynchronously
cpp	YES	0	 at any point after the callback is registered. Beware. We are guaranteed, however, that
cpp	YES	0	 __local_state::operator() will not complete the operation or decrement the shared state's
cpp	YES	0	 ref count until after *this has been added to the waiters list.
cpp	YES	0	 We haven't put __state in the waiters list yet and we are holding a ref count to
cpp	YES	0	 __sh_state_, so nothing can happen to the __sh_state_ here.
cpp	YES	0	 Start the shared op. As an optimization, skip it if the receiver's stop token has already
cpp	YES	0	 been signaled.
cpp	YES	0	 successfully added the waiter
cpp	YES	0	 Otherwise, failed to add the waiter because of a stop-request.
cpp	YES	0	 Complete synchronously with set_stopped().
cpp	YES	0	 Stop request callback:
cpp	YES	0	 We reach here when a split/ensure_started sender has received a stop request from the
cpp	YES	0	 receiver to which it is connected.
cpp	YES	0	 Remove this operation from the waiters list. Removal can fail if:
cpp	YES	0	   1. It was already removed by another thread, or
cpp	YES	0	   2. It hasn't been added yet (see `start` below), or
cpp	YES	0	   3. The underlying operation has already completed.
cpp	YES	0	 In each case, the right thing to do is nothing. If (1) then we raced with another
cpp	YES	0	 thread and lost. In that case, the other thread will take care of it. If (2) then
cpp	YES	0	 `start` will take care of it. If (3) then this stop request is safe to ignore.
cpp	YES	0	 The following code and the __notify function cannot both execute. This is because the
cpp	YES	0	 __notify function is called from the shared state's __notify_waiters function, which
cpp	YES	0	 first sets __waiters_ to the completed state. As a result, the attempt to remove `this`
cpp	YES	0	 from the waiters list above will fail and this stop request is ignored.
cpp	YES	0	 This is called from __shared_state::__notify_waiters when the input async operation

cpp	YES	0	 __notify cannot race with __local_state::operator(). See comment in

cpp	YES	0	! @brief A sender factory that produces a sender which completes
cpp	YES	0	!        synchronously with the given values on the value channel.
cpp	YES	0	! @c just is the simplest sender factory: it captures zero or more values
cpp	YES	0	! and produces a sender that, when connected and started, immediately
cpp	YES	0	! delivers those values via @c set_value to the connected receiver — all
cpp	YES	0	! within the receiver's @c start() call, without any context transition.
cpp	YES	0	! It is the canonical way to inject literal values into a sender pipeline.
cpp	YES	0	! auto s0 = stdexec::just();              // value-completes with no datums
cpp	YES	0	! auto s1 = stdexec::just(42);            // value-completes with one int
cpp	YES	0	! auto s2 = stdexec::just(1, 2, 3);       // value-completes with three ints
cpp	YES	0	! auto s3 = stdexec::just(std::string{"x"}, 7);  // mixed types are fine
cpp	YES	0	! See [exec.just] in the C++26 working draft for the normative specification.
cpp	YES	0	! **Completion signatures.**
cpp	YES	0	! Given @c just(ts...) with argument-pack types @c Ts..., the resulting
cpp	YES	0	! sender has the single completion signature:
cpp	YES	0	! set_value_t(std::decay_t<Ts>...)
cpp	YES	0	! Each argument is decay-copied into the resulting sender. The error and
cpp	YES	0	! stopped channels are empty — @c just never completes with @c set_error
cpp	YES	0	! or @c set_stopped.
cpp	YES	0	! **Exception behavior.**
cpp	YES	0	! The factory call itself is @c noexcept when every decay-copy is
cpp	YES	0	! @c noexcept. The produced sender's @c start() is @c noexcept by
cpp	YES	0	! construction.
cpp	YES	0	! @c just does not consult the receiver's stop token; it always
cpp	YES	0	! synchronously completes with @c set_value.

cpp	YES	0	! overload, retained for backwards compatibility.

cpp	YES	0	! @brief A pipeable sender adaptor that handles a predecessor sender's
cpp	YES	0	!        stopped completion by invoking a nullary callable.
cpp	YES	0	! @c upon_stopped maps the stopped channel of a sender into a value
cpp	YES	0	! completion by invoking a callable with *no arguments* and forwarding its
cpp	YES	0	! return value downstream. The value and error channels are forwarded
cpp	YES	0	! unchanged. This is the canonical way to *recover from* cancellation:
cpp	YES	0	! turn a stopped completion into a substitute value and continue.
cpp	YES	0	! Both call syntaxes are supported (the second is the *pipeable* form):
cpp	YES	0	! auto s1 = stdexec::upon_stopped(sndr, f);   // direct invocation
cpp	YES	0	! auto s2 = sndr | stdexec::upon_stopped(f);  // pipe syntax
cpp	YES	0	! The two forms are expression-equivalent. See [exec.then] in the
cpp	YES	0	! C++26 working draft for the normative specification (@c upon_stopped is
cpp	YES	0	! specified alongside @c then and @c upon_error).
cpp	YES	0	! Given a predecessor sender @c sndr with completion signatures
cpp	YES	0	! set_value_t(Vs...)               // forwarded unchanged
cpp	YES	0	! set_error_t(Es)...               // forwarded unchanged
cpp	YES	0	! set_stopped_t()                  // (must be present)
cpp	YES	0	! the sender produced by <tt>upon_stopped(sndr, f)</tt> has completion signatures
cpp	YES	0	! set_value_t(Vs...)               // forwarded unchanged from sndr
cpp	YES	0	! set_value_t(R)                   // R = decltype(std::invoke(f))
cpp	YES	0	!                                  // (or set_value_t() when R is void)
cpp	YES	0	! set_error_t(Es)...               // forwarded unchanged from sndr
cpp	YES	0	! set_error_t(std::exception_ptr)  // added when invoking f may throw
cpp	YES	0	!                                  // (no set_stopped_t in the output)
cpp	YES	0	! @c f must be invocable with *no* arguments — this requirement is enforced
cpp	YES	0	! by the @c requires clause on the operator overloads. The original
cpp	YES	0	! @c set_stopped_t completion is *consumed*: the resulting sender will
cpp	YES	0	! never complete via @c set_stopped (unless @c f itself returns a sender
cpp	YES	0	! that does, which @c upon_stopped does not — see @c let_stopped for that).
cpp	YES	0	! If invoking @c f throws, the exception is delivered through
cpp	YES	0	! @c set_error_t(std::exception_ptr) on the resulting sender. When @c f is
cpp	YES	0	! @c noexcept, no @c std::exception_ptr error completion is added.
cpp	YES	0	! @c upon_stopped does not interact with the receiver's stop token. It
cpp	YES	0	! reacts to the predecessor's @c set_stopped by invoking @c f; it does
cpp	YES	0	! not itself initiate cancellation.
cpp	YES	0	!   auto sndr = just_stopped()
cpp	NO	0	!             | upon_stopped([] { return 42; });

cpp	YES	0	 [exec.spawn.future] paragraph 3

cpp	YES	0	 NOT TO SPEC: see https://github.com/cplusplus/sender-receiver/issues/356
cpp	YES	0	 NOTE: _Rcvr is unconstrained because the thing we pass doesn't satisfy receiver
cpp	YES	0	 Write this before synchronizing with the producer, below.
cpp	YES	0	 We need store-release on success to ensure that the future completion of the
cpp	YES	0	 producer can see the callback we wrote into __callback_, and we need load-acquire
cpp	YES	0	 on failure in case we're about to observe that the producer has already finished
cpp	YES	0	 so we can see the result it produced. The success order must be stronger than the
cpp	YES	0	 failure order so success has to be acquire-release.
cpp	YES	0	 Since our CAS succeeded, we can conclude that we observed a null __registered_receiver_
cpp	YES	0	 and successfully updated it to point to the receiver. That means the consumer has
cpp	YES	0	 successfully registered a receiver and it's up to the producer to complete it when the
cpp	YES	0	 result is ready; alternatively, a stop request may arrive leading __try_cancel to try
cpp	YES	0	 to complete us eagerly with set_stopped. In either case, __try_cancel and __complete
cpp	YES	0	 will negotiate how to complete the future and we have nothing left to do.
cpp	YES	0	 NOTE: we didn't update __registered_receiver_
cpp	YES	0	 __try_cancel ran before both __complete and __consume; now we need to negotiate with
cpp	YES	0	 __complete to decide whether it finished in time to consume its output.
cpp	YES	0	 We need acquire-release semantics here. If we succeed in abandoning the operation then
cpp	YES	0	 the producer will be responsible for invoking __destroy, which means it needs to see
cpp	YES	0	 the write to __callback_, which requires a store-release. IF we fail to abandon the
cpp	YES	0	 operation then that means the producer finished in time for us to consume its result,
cpp	YES	0	 which means we need a load-acquire to consume it properly.
cpp	YES	0	 Either the producer completed before we CAS'd, or it snuck in and completed between
cpp	YES	0	 our CAS and our exchange; in either case, we ought to consume its result.
cpp	YES	0	 Our exchange observed the same (this + 1) that the CAS did, which means that the producer
cpp	YES	0	 didn't finish in time; also, by setting __registered_receiver_ to (this), we've marked the
cpp	YES	0	 operation as "ready for destruction" by the producer so the current object may already be
cpp	YES	0	 destroyed. We must complete with set_stopped.
cpp	YES	0	 We're about to mark the consuming side as complete, at which point the producing side is
cpp	YES	0	 free to destroy this object so we can't "optimize" by deferring this stop request
cpp	YES	0	 We need store-release semantics if we happen to be completing the consumer side before
cpp	YES	0	 the producer side has finished because we need to publish the writes committed in the
cpp	YES	0	 above call to request_stop for the destructor not to commit a data race. We need
cpp	YES	0	 load-acquire semantics if we happen to be second to consume the writes done by the
cpp	YES	0	 producer so the destructor can destroy that data without committing a data race. In
cpp	YES	0	 combination, we need acquire-release semantics here.
cpp	YES	0	 The producer hadn't finished by the time we marked the consumer as done so we've handed
cpp	YES	0	 over clean-up responsibility and have nothing else to do.
cpp	YES	0	 The producer side completed before we did so we're responsible for clean-up.
cpp	YES	0	 Type-erased receiver. Several possible values:
cpp	YES	0	   1. `nullptr` means "unset"
cpp	YES	0	   2. `this` means either the producer or consumer is done with the operation and the
cpp	YES	0	      other (whichever hasn't completed yet) is responsible for clean-up
cpp	YES	0	   3. `this` + 1 means that the future has received a stop request and __try_cancel has
cpp	YES	0	      marked the operation so that __complete and __consume can negotiate how to complete
cpp	YES	0	   4. any other value means __consume has "registered" its receiver to be completed
cpp	YES	0	      by __complete when it is invoked
cpp	YES	0	 Type-erased completion callback.
cpp	YES	0	 The void* will receive the address of the receiver, which will need to have its
cpp	YES	0	 type unerased. The __spawn_future_state* will receive either `this`, indicating the
cpp	YES	0	 callback ought to complete the receive with the value of __result_, which can be
cpp	YES	0	 retrieved through the self-pointer, or nullptr, indicating that the receiver should
cpp	YES	0	 be completed with set_stopped because the future received and processed a stop request
cpp	YES	0	 before the producer could finish.
cpp	YES	0	 NOTE: __rcvr's type is unconstrained because the thing we pass doesn't satisfy receiver
cpp	YES	0	 Consider: it'd be nice to eagerly destruct __op_ here; to do that, we'd need to store
cpp	YES	0	           it in an anonymous union, use a scope-guard in the constructor to ensure it
cpp	YES	0	           gets destructed in the event that try_associate() throws, and manually destroy
cpp	YES	0	           it here *before* updating __registered_receiver_. I'm not sure it would be to
cpp	YES	0	           spec to do that, though.
cpp	YES	0	 We need acquire-release semantics here to ensure correct synchronization whether we
cpp	YES	0	 arrived before or after the consumer. In the case we finish first, we need to store-release
cpp	YES	0	 so the consumer can see what we've written; in the case we finish second, we need to
cpp	YES	0	 load-acquire so we can see what the consumer has written.
cpp	YES	0	 The producer side has completed first and we've updated __registered_receiver_ with
cpp	YES	0	 (__self) to mark things as such; the consumer side is responsible for all further
cpp	YES	0	 actions.
cpp	YES	0	 There are two possible histories here; the consumer side either
cpp	YES	0	  1. abandoned the operation without ever starting, or
cpp	YES	0	  2. was started but received a stop request and successfully cancelled before we
cpp	YES	0	     could produce our value.
cpp	YES	0	 In either case, the producer is "too late" and there's nothing to do but clean up.
cpp	YES	0	 The consumer side has been started and a stop request was received before __consume
cpp	YES	0	 could be invoked; the producer has also completed before __consume could be invoked
cpp	YES	0	 and we've left (__self) in place of (__self + 1) so, when __consume gets around to
cpp	YES	0	 observing __registered_receiver_, it'll see that the producer has finished and complete
cpp	YES	0	 the receiver with the value we produced. This state is similar to the producer having
cpp	YES	0	 finished first; by overwriting __registered_receiver_ with (__self), we've erased the
cpp	YES	0	 fact that the stop request happened to come in before we did.
cpp	YES	0	 The producer finished after the consumer register a receiver for us to complete. There
cpp	YES	0	 may be an incoming or outstanding stop request that causes __try_start to race with us
cpp	YES	0	 but, if so, we don't need to worry about it--invoking __callback_ like __self will
cpp	YES	0	 eagerly destroy the stop callback, which will either prevent __try_cancel from being
cpp	YES	0	 invoked, or will block until it returns. In either case, our call to __callback_ has
cpp	YES	0	 "won" and __try_cancel will no-op.
cpp	YES	0	 Having completed the receiver, we are responsible for cleaning up the allocated state.
cpp	YES	0	 Consider: there's a sense in which we only need to invoke request_stop if we've arrived
cpp	YES	0	           here before the producer has invoked __complete so I wonder whether it's possible
cpp	YES	0	           to avoid invoking request_stop when it's unnecessary. It might be.
cpp	YES	0	           We *must* invoke request_stop before returning from the function if our CAS
cpp	YES	0	           succeeds (because we arrived before either __complete or __consume), or if the
cpp	YES	0	           CAS fails and reports that the consumer finished first and the later exchange
cpp	YES	0	           observes that the producer still hasn't finished.
cpp	YES	0	           The most obvious risk to deferring a call to request_stop is that the stop source
cpp	YES	0	           might be destroyed before our invocation. There's also a risk that we get our
cpp	YES	0	           memory ordering wrong; I've learned through analyzing TSAN failures that
cpp	YES	0	           request_stop constitutes a store-release that must be load-acquired before the
cpp	YES	0	           destructor runs so we need to be careful about synchronizing with the final
cpp	YES	0	           owner of this object.
cpp	YES	0	           It might be safe to invoke request_stop before the early return when the CAS
cpp	YES	0	           succeeds and between a failed CAS and the later exchange. In the first case
cpp	YES	0	           (after a successful CAS), the final owner of the object will be the slower of
cpp	YES	0	           the producer or consumer, which will complete the receiver before destroying the
cpp	YES	0	           operation. Completing the receiver will entail destroying the stop callback that
cpp	YES	0	           has invoked us, which will synchronize with us. In the second case (after a
cpp	YES	0	           failed CAS and before the subsequent exchange), we know that the consumer has
cpp	YES	0	           already finished and it's the producer that will destroy the operation. We'll
cpp	YES	0	           synchronize with the producer either by invoking a store-release before
cpp	YES	0	           completing the receiver, or the producer will complete the receiver and destroy
cpp	YES	0	           the stop callback.
cpp	YES	0	           Upon further reflection, the above analysis is flawed: invoking request_stop
cpp	YES	0	           after a successful CAS would lead to data races when the consumer successfully
cpp	YES	0	           abandons the operation (i.e. it observes the (__self + 1) value and successfully
cpp	YES	0	           replaces it with (__self) before completing the receiver with set_stopped). In
cpp	YES	0	           that scenario, the consumer thread would be responsible for destroying the stop
cpp	YES	0	           callback, not the producer thread, and there would be no other store-release
cpp	YES	0	           to publish the writes from request_stop to the producer thread before it runs
cpp	YES	0	           the operation's destructor.
cpp	YES	0	           Perhaps we can salvage the effort by deferring the request_stop to __complete.
cpp	YES	0	           When our CAS succeeds, we know that we've run before either of the producer or
cpp	YES	0	           consumer, which means a call to __consume is still in the future. If that call
cpp	YES	0	           observes (__self + 1) then we know that both __try_cancel and __consume have run
cpp	YES	0	           before __complete, and the consumer is going to try to abandon the producer's
cpp	YES	0	           work. It would be sensible for the consumer to issue the stop request before it
cpp	YES	0	           performs the exchange(__self, acq_rel) that is its attempt to so signal and the
cpp	YES	0	           store-release entailed by that exchange would synchronize with the producer as
cpp	YES	0	           required.
cpp	YES	0	 It feels wasteful to do this when we might not need to but, once we update
cpp	YES	0	 __registered_receiver_ to (__self + 1), there's a chance the current object
cpp	YES	0	 will be destroyed so it's not safe to defer this.
cpp	YES	0	 This operation constitutes a write that must be published to whichever thread invokes
cpp	YES	0	 __destroy.
cpp	YES	0	 If neither __complete nor __consume has been invoked then mark us as having stop requested.
cpp	YES	0	 This only succeeds if stop is requested very early in the process so it's quite unlikely.
cpp	YES	0	 We need to store-release on success so that whichever of the consumer or producer
cpp	YES	0	 ends up invoking __destroy sees the write we performed in request_stop(); we need
cpp	YES	0	 load-acquire on failure so we can safely read the value of __callback_ that may have
cpp	YES	0	 been written by the consumer.
cpp	YES	0	 We succeeded, meaning that __registered_receiver_ was nullptr on entry, which signals
cpp	YES	0	 that __try_cancel ran before either of __consume or __complete. Leaving (__self + 1)
cpp	YES	0	 as the sentinel will allow the two forthcoming functions to negotiate how to
cpp	YES	0	 complete the overall operation.
cpp	YES	0	 __complete has already finished and left a value behind; we should let __consume
cpp	YES	0	 consume it.
cpp	YES	0	 We would normally need to perform a store-release here to ensure the consumer sees
cpp	YES	0	 the write we performed by invoking request_stop, but we're running inside a stop
cpp	YES	0	 callback that the consumer will destroy before destroying this object and destroying
cpp	YES	0	 a stop callback is a synchronizing operation so we're good.
cpp	YES	0	 __consume has registered a receiver and __sentinel is its address; the producer may invoke
cpp	YES	0	 __complete at any moment, which would ordinarily risk destroying the current object out
cpp	YES	0	 from under us but, because we're running in a stop callback, the completion path will
cpp	YES	0	 block until we're done before doing that so we're still safe.
cpp	YES	0	 Do two things:
cpp	YES	0	  1. store a copy of __callback_ on the stack so we can use it after the operation is
cpp	YES	0	     destroyed, and
cpp	YES	0	  2. try to mark the operation as abandoned so that the producer can take clean-up
cpp	YES	0	     responsibility.
cpp	YES	0	 We have already synchronized with the consumer by performing a load-acquire above (and
cpp	YES	0	 we know it was the *consumer* we synchronized with because __sentinel contains the address
cpp	YES	0	 of the receiver it registered), but we haven't yet synchronized with the producer.
cpp	YES	0	 There are two possible futures here:
cpp	YES	0	  1. we mark the operation as abandoned before the producer finishes, or
cpp	YES	0	  2. the producer finishes before we can abandon the operation.
cpp	YES	0	 In the first case, we can synchronize with the producer by performing a store-release on
cpp	YES	0	 __registered_receiver_; when the producer completes, it will load-acquire that value and
cpp	YES	0	 clean up.
cpp	YES	0	 In the second case, the producer will complete the registered receiver, which will have
cpp	YES	0	 the side effect of destroying the stop callback that we're running inside, which is a
cpp	YES	0	 synchronization point with us.
cpp	YES	0	 So, we store-release here in case we're in case 1.
cpp	YES	0	 __registered_receiver_ still contained the value we observed during the CAS, which means
cpp	YES	0	 the producer still hadn't updated it to contain (__self). This means we succeeded in
cpp	YES	0	 marking the operation as abandoned and the producer will destroy it when it completes
cpp	YES	0	 (which could happen at any moment); we need to complete the consumer with set_stopped. We
cpp	YES	0	 invoke __cb (the copy of __callback_ that we put on the stack) with a null self-pointer
cpp	YES	0	 to signal that it ought to invoke set_stopped(std::move(*__rcvr)) without touching the
cpp	YES	0	 operation.
cpp	YES	0	 The producer beat us to the punch; it's busy trying to complete and is about to
cpp	YES	0	 destroy the operation. Bail out.
cpp	YES	0	 __data_of<_Sender> is a unique_ptr specialization
cpp	YES	0	 __callback_ is left unconstructed until __run() is called; if the constructor invocation
cpp	YES	0	 throws then __callback_ is never constructed or destructed at all, otherwise, its destructor
cpp	YES	0	 is invoked when the receiver contract is completed in __complete, below.

cpp	YES	0	! @brief A sender factory that obtains a sender from a scheduler.
cpp	YES	0	! @c schedule is the bridge between a *scheduler* (a lightweight handle
cpp	YES	0	! to an execution context) and the *sender* world: it produces a sender
cpp	YES	0	! that, when connected and started, eventually completes with @c set_value
cpp	YES	0	! to the connected receiver *from the context of the scheduler*. It is
cpp	YES	0	! the canonical way to begin a sender pipeline that needs to run on a
cpp	YES	0	! specific execution context (a thread pool, a GPU stream, an event loop,
cpp	NO	0	! …).
cpp	NO	0	! auto sched = stdexec::get_parallel_scheduler();
cpp	NO	0	! auto sndr  = stdexec::schedule(sched);
cpp	YES	0	! The sender returned by @c schedule(sched) is informally called a
cpp	YES	0	! "schedule-sender" or "schedule sender". The expression
cpp	YES	0	! <tt>schedule(sch)</tt> is *expression-equivalent* to
cpp	YES	0	! <tt>sch.schedule()</tt>, which is the customization point that
cpp	YES	0	! scheduler authors implement.
cpp	YES	0	! @c schedule also drives the @c stdexec::scheduler concept: a type @c S
cpp	YES	0	! satisfies @c scheduler if (and roughly only if) @c schedule(s) is a
cpp	YES	0	! valid expression returning a sender, and @c S is equality-comparable
cpp	YES	0	! and nothrow-move-constructible.
cpp	YES	0	! See [exec.schedule] in the C++26 working draft for the normative
cpp	YES	0	! The exact signatures are determined by the scheduler's implementation,
cpp	YES	0	! but every conforming schedule-sender includes:
cpp	YES	0	! set_value_t()                   // delivered on the scheduler's context
cpp	YES	0	! set_stopped_t()                 // typical: stop-token observed during scheduling
cpp	YES	0	! set_error_t(...)                // implementation-defined; some schedulers can fail
cpp	YES	0	! @c set_value carries no datums. The point of @c schedule is the
cpp	YES	0	! *context transition*, not the value — downstream adaptors (@c then,
cpp	YES	0	! @c let_value, etc.) chained onto the schedule-sender therefore run on
cpp	YES	0	! the scheduler's context.
cpp	YES	0	! A schedule-sender that has not yet started executing on the scheduler's
cpp	YES	0	! context typically observes the receiver's stop token and may complete
cpp	YES	0	! with @c set_stopped instead. Once it has begun running on the
cpp	YES	0	! scheduler's context, the value completion is delivered.
cpp	YES	0	!     schedule(sched)                                // hop onto sched
cpp	YES	0	!     | then([] { return 42; });                     // ... and compute on it
cpp	YES	0	!   (void)v;

cpp	YES	0	 [exec.sched]
cpp	YES	0	! @brief A lightweight handle to an *execution context* — the
cpp	YES	0	!        abstraction over things that can run sender pipelines.
cpp	YES	0	! A *scheduler* is a small, value-like handle to a (potentially heavy
cpp	YES	0	! and immovable) *execution resource*: a thread pool, a GPU stream, an
cpp	YES	0	! event loop, an inline run-loop, etc. The only operation a scheduler
cpp	YES	0	! must support is @c stdexec::schedule, which obtains a sender that, when
cpp	YES	0	! connected and started, eventually value-completes on that resource.

cpp	YES	0	! @brief A sender consumer that synchronously blocks the calling thread
cpp	YES	0	!        until a sender completes and returns its result.
cpp	YES	0	! @c sync_wait is the bridge from the asynchronous sender world back into
cpp	YES	0	! synchronous code. You give it a sender; it connects the sender to a
cpp	YES	0	! built-in receiver, starts the resulting operation, then drives an
cpp	YES	0	! internal @c run_loop on the calling thread until the operation
cpp	YES	0	! completes. The result is returned as a <tt>std::optional</tt> of a
cpp	YES	0	! tuple of the value-completion datums.
cpp	YES	0	! This is the most common way to "run" a sender in a top-level program or
cpp	YES	0	! a test — it's what you reach for in a @c main() or when synchronously
cpp	YES	0	! waiting on a single sub-pipeline. For fire-and-forget execution, prefer
cpp	YES	0	! @c exec::start_detached or @c stdexec::spawn.
cpp	NO	0	! auto [v] = stdexec::sync_wait(stdexec::just(42)).value();
cpp	YES	0	! // v == 42
cpp	YES	0	! See [exec.sync.wait] in the C++26 working draft for the normative
cpp	YES	0	! Given an input sender @c sndr that, in some environment, completes with
cpp	YES	0	! exactly one of:
cpp	YES	0	! | Sender completion             | What @c sync_wait does                                          |
cpp	NO	0	! | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
cpp	YES	0	! | @c set_value_t(Vs...)         | Returns @c std::optional<std::tuple<Vs...>> engaged.            |
cpp	YES	0	! | @c set_error_t(std::exception_ptr) | Rethrows the exception via @c std::rethrow_exception.     |
cpp	YES	0	! | @c set_error_t(std::error_code)    | Throws @c std::system_error(error_code).                  |
cpp	YES	0	! | @c set_error_t(E)             | Throws @c E directly.                                           |
cpp	YES	0	! | @c set_stopped_t()            | Returns an empty (disengaged) @c std::optional.                 |

cpp	YES	0	! @c sync_wait *mandates* that its argument sender have exactly one
cpp	YES	0	! @c set_value_t completion signature. A sender that can succeed in more
cpp	YES	0	! than one way (e.g. <tt>just(1) | when_all(just(std::string{"x"}))</tt>
cpp	YES	0	! yielding two distinct tuples) requires @c sync_wait_with_variant
cpp	YES	0	! instead. The static assertion in @c sync_wait will point this out at
cpp	YES	0	! compile time, with a hint to use the variant form.
cpp	YES	0	! **Delegation scheduler.**
cpp	YES	0	! The internal @c run_loop is exposed via @c get_delegation_scheduler on
cpp	YES	0	! the receiver's environment, so senders that need to enqueue work back
cpp	YES	0	! onto the waiting thread (e.g. continuations after an I/O wait) can do
cpp	YES	0	! so safely. This is what enables algorithms like @c continues_on to
cpp	YES	0	! return execution to the calling thread of @c sync_wait.

cpp	YES	0	! - On any thread that participates in an event loop or executor — you

cpp	YES	0	!   (main, tests, leaf utilities), not pipeline composition.
