cpp	YES	0	! @brief Customization point object for the *value* completion signal of
cpp	YES	0	!        the sender/receiver protocol.
cpp	YES	0	! `set_value(rcvr, vs...)` is the call an operation state makes on its
cpp	YES	0	! receiver to deliver a successful asynchronous result. It is one of
cpp	YES	0	! three terminal completion signals (alongside @ref set_error_t and

cpp	YES	0	! @brief The fundamental concept of the receiver model: a callback-shaped
cpp	YES	0	!        object that consumes the result of an asynchronous operation.
cpp	YES	0	! A *receiver* is the destination half of a sender/receiver pair. It is
cpp	YES	0	! the object on which a started operation eventually invokes one of
cpp	YES	0	! @c set_value, @c set_error, or @c set_stopped to deliver its
cpp	YES	0	! completion. Receivers are typically synthesized by sender consumers
cpp	YES	0	! and adaptors — most user code never writes a receiver by hand; it
cpp	YES	0	! writes senders and composes them.
cpp	YES	0	! Concretely, a type @c R satisfies @c receiver if:
cpp	YES	0	! 1. @c R is opted into the concept via a @c receiver_concept type
cpp	YES	0	!    alias deriving from @c stdexec::receiver_tag.
cpp	YES	0	! 2. @c R provides an environment via @c stdexec::get_env (so child
cpp	YES	0	!    operations can query for the stop token, allocator, scheduler,
cpp	YES	0	!    etc.).
cpp	YES	0	! 3. @c R's decayed type is @em nothrow move-constructible — receivers
cpp	YES	0	!    are moved into operation states by sender adaptors, and that move
cpp	YES	0	!    must not throw.
cpp	YES	0	! 4. @c R's decayed type is constructible from an @c R.
cpp	YES	0	! Note that this concept alone does *not* require @c R to accept any
cpp	YES	0	! particular completion signals — for that, see @c receiver_of, which
cpp	YES	0	! takes a @c completion_signatures pack and validates that the receiver
cpp	YES	0	! has matching @c set_value / @c set_error / @c set_stopped members.
cpp	YES	0	! See [exec.recv.concepts] in the C++26 working draft.
cpp	YES	0	! @see stdexec::receiver_of   — receiver plus specific completion signatures
cpp	YES	0	! @see stdexec::receiver_tag  — the tag type that opts a class into this concept
cpp	YES	0	! @brief A @c receiver that accepts a specific set of completion
cpp	YES	0	!        signatures.
cpp	YES	0	! `receiver_of<R, Sigs>` says: "R is a receiver, and for every
cpp	YES	0	! @c set_xxx_t(Args...) signature in @c Sigs (a
cpp	YES	0	! @c stdexec::completion_signatures pack), R has a matching member that
cpp	YES	0	! is callable with @c Args... ". This is the constraint that ensures a

cpp	YES	0	 If __is_root_env<_Env> is true, then this sender has no parent, so there is no need

cpp	YES	0	! @brief A sender adaptor that runs work on a different scheduler and then
cpp	YES	0	!        transfers execution *back* to the original scheduler.
cpp	YES	0	! @c on is the "go there, do work, come back" scheduling adaptor. It has
cpp	YES	0	! two distinct shapes:
cpp	YES	0	! 1. **Whole-sender form:** <tt>on(sched, sndr)</tt> — runs the entirety
cpp	YES	0	!    of @c sndr on @c sched's execution resource. When @c sndr completes,
cpp	YES	0	!    execution transfers back to the scheduler that started the operation
cpp	YES	0	!    (the "start scheduler"), and the completion is delivered there.
cpp	YES	0	!    This is the principal difference between @c on and
cpp	YES	0	!    @ref starts_on_t — @c starts_on stays on @c sched; @c on returns home.
cpp	YES	0	! 2. **Closure-insertion form:** <tt>on(sndr, sched, closure)</tt> — runs
cpp	YES	0	!    @c sndr on its *current* scheduler, then transfers to @c sched,
cpp	YES	0	!    applies @c closure (a sender-adaptor closure) to the result, runs
cpp	YES	0	!    *that* on @c sched, and finally transfers back to the original
cpp	YES	0	!    completion scheduler. Useful for inserting a CPU-bound transform
cpp	YES	0	!    into an otherwise I/O-bound pipeline (or vice versa) without
cpp	YES	0	!    permanently changing context.
cpp	YES	0	!    This form also has a pipe shorthand:
cpp	YES	0	!    <tt>sndr | on(sched, closure)</tt>.
cpp	YES	0	! // Form 1: run sndr on sched, return to start scheduler.
cpp	NO	0	! auto s1 = stdexec::on(sched, sndr);
cpp	YES	0	! // Form 2: run sndr in place, hop to sched for closure, hop back.
cpp	NO	0	! auto s2 = stdexec::on(sndr, sched, stdexec::then([](int x){ return x*2; }));
cpp	NO	0	! auto s3 = sndr | stdexec::on(sched, stdexec::then([](int x){ return x*2; }));
cpp	YES	0	! See [exec.on] in the C++26 working draft for the normative specification.
cpp	YES	0	! **The round trip.**
cpp	YES	0	! What distinguishes @c on from @c starts_on and @c continues_on is the
cpp	YES	0	! restoration of the original scheduler:
cpp	YES	0	! | Adaptor                | Where work runs | Where completion is delivered  |
cpp	NO	0	! | ---------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------ |
cpp	YES	0	! | @c starts_on(sch,s)    | on @c sch       | on @c sch                      |
cpp	YES	0	! | @c continues_on(s,sch) | on @c s's sched | on @c sch                      |
cpp	YES	0	! | @c on(sch,s)           | on @c sch       | on the *start scheduler*       |
cpp	YES	0	! | @c on(s,sch,closure)   | mixed (see above) | on the *start scheduler*     |
cpp	YES	0	! The "start scheduler" is read from the receiver's environment via
cpp	YES	0	! @c get_start_scheduler (form 1) or @c get_completion_scheduler<set_value_t>
cpp	YES	0	! of @c sndr's environment (form 2).
cpp	YES	0	! Form 1 (<tt>on(sched, sndr)</tt>): essentially @c sndr's completion
cpp	YES	0	! signatures, with possible additional @c set_error_t completions from
cpp	YES	0	! the two scheduling hops.
cpp	YES	0	! Form 2 (<tt>on(sndr, sched, closure)</tt>): the completion signatures
cpp	YES	0	! of <tt>closure(continues_on(sndr, sched))</tt> after the final transfer
cpp	YES	0	! back, again with possible additional @c set_error_t completions from
cpp	YES	0	! the scheduling hops.
cpp	YES	0	! If scheduling onto @c sched (or back) fails, an error completion is
cpp	YES	0	! delivered on an unspecified execution agent.
cpp	YES	0	! Cancellation flows through the scheduling hops normally; a stop
cpp	YES	0	! request observed between hops typically results in @c set_stopped.
cpp	YES	0	!   auto gpu = get_parallel_scheduler();   // pretend: GPU
cpp	YES	0	!   // Compute on the GPU, but stay on the start scheduler afterwards:
cpp	YES	0	!     just(21)

cpp	YES	0	!   (void)v;  // == 42; sync_wait sees the result on its starting context
cpp	YES	0	! @see stdexec::starts_on      — begin on a scheduler and *stay* there

cpp	YES	0	 [exec.spawn]
cpp	YES	0	! @brief A sender consumer that eagerly starts a sender and ties its
cpp	YES	0	!        lifetime to an *async scope*.
cpp	YES	0	! @c spawn is the standard "fire-and-forget into a scope" consumer.
cpp	YES	0	! You give it a sender, a @c scope_token (a handle to an async scope),
cpp	YES	0	! and optionally an environment, and @c spawn:
cpp	YES	0	! 1. allocates an operation state on the heap (using an allocator
cpp	YES	0	!    queried from the environment or the sender's own environment),
cpp	YES	0	! 2. tries to associate the resulting operation with the scope via
cpp	YES	0	!    <tt>token.try_associate()</tt>,
cpp	YES	0	! 3. if the association succeeds, eagerly @c start s the operation,
cpp	YES	0	!    and on completion deallocates the state and releases the scope
cpp	YES	0	!    association.
cpp	YES	0	! If association fails (typically because the scope has already begun
cpp	YES	0	! shutting down), @c spawn destroys the state and returns without
cpp	YES	0	! starting the operation. The result of the sender, if any, is
cpp	YES	0	! discarded — @c spawn returns @c void.
cpp	YES	0	! See [exec.spawn] in the C++26 working draft for the normative
cpp	YES	0	! stdexec::spawn(stdexec::just(42) | stdexec::then([](int x) {
cpp	NO	0	! }), scope.get_token());
cpp	YES	0	! // Later, before destroying scope:
cpp	YES	0	! **Completion requirements.**
cpp	YES	0	! The argument sender must not be able to complete with @c set_error
cpp	YES	0	! — @c spawn cannot deliver an error to a non-existent caller. The
cpp	YES	0	! @c requires clause enforces this with a
cpp	YES	0	! <tt>__never_sends<set_error_t, ...></tt> check; the diagnostic
cpp	YES	0	! overload says "spawn expects a sender that cannot fail" if the check
cpp	YES	0	! fires.
cpp	YES	0	! Successful and stopped completions are both accepted; their results
cpp	YES	0	! are discarded.
cpp	YES	0	! **Scope semantics.**
cpp	YES	0	! The scope is the *owner of lifetime* for the spawned operation.
cpp	YES	0	! Calling code is expected to eventually @c join() the scope (or
cpp	YES	0	! otherwise wait for all spawned work to drain) before destroying it
cpp	YES	0	! — typically once at program shutdown, or once per logical unit of
cpp	YES	0	! related background work.
cpp	YES	0	! @c spawn is the canonical fire-and-forget consumer for any work
cpp	YES	0	! that has a clear "owning context" (a request, a session, a worker).
cpp	YES	0	! For top-level work with no owning scope, use @c exec::start_detached
cpp	YES	0	! (an stdexec extension). For fire-and-forget work whose completion
cpp	YES	0	! you want to *observe* (without blocking), use
cpp	YES	0	! @see stdexec::spawn_future   — like @c spawn, but returns a sender that completes
cpp	YES	0	!                                when the spawned work completes
cpp	YES	0	! @brief Spawn @c __sndr into the scope identified by @c __tkn, using
cpp	YES	0	!        a default (empty) environment.
cpp	YES	0	! Equivalent to <tt>spawn(__sndr, __tkn, env<>{})</tt>.
cpp	YES	0	 Hidden from Doxygen: this diagnostic-only overload shares its signature

cpp	YES	0	 constraint), which the Sphinx C++ domain cannot disambiguate.
cpp	YES	0	! @brief Diagnostic overload — selected when the sender's completion

cpp	YES	0	 NB: The variant type implemented here default-constructs into the valueless  
cpp	YES	0	 state. This is different from std::variant which default-constructs into the 
cpp	YES	0	 first alternative. This is done to simplify the implementation and to avoid  
cpp	YES	0	 the need for a default constructor for each alternative type.                
cpp	YES	0	 Construct into the valueless state:
cpp	YES	0	 The following emplace functions must take great care to avoid use-after-free bugs.
cpp	YES	0	 If the object being constructed calls `start` on a newly created operation state
cpp	YES	0	 (as does the object returned from `submit`), and if `start` completes inline, it
cpp	YES	0	 could cause the destruction of the outer operation state that owns *this. The
cpp	YES	0	 function below uses the following pattern to avoid this:
cpp	YES	0	 1. Store the new index in __index_.
cpp	YES	0	 2. Create a scope guard that will reset __index_ to __variant_npos if the
cpp	YES	0	    constructor throws.
cpp	YES	0	 3. Construct the new object in the storage, which may cause the invalidation of
cpp	YES	0	    *this. The emplace function must not access any members of *this after this point.
cpp	YES	0	 4. Dismiss the scope guard, which will leave __index_ set to the new index.
cpp	YES	0	 5. Return a reference to the new object -- which may be invalid! Calling code
cpp	YES	0	    must be aware of the danger.

cpp	YES	0	! any: a library for ad hoc polymorphism with value semantics
cpp	YES	0	! @par Terminology:
cpp	YES	0	! - "root":
cpp	YES	0	!   A type satisfying the @c root concept that is used as the nucleus of a "model".
cpp	YES	0	!   There are 5 root types:
cpp	YES	0	!   - @c __iroot:                 the abstract root
cpp	YES	0	!   - @c __value_root:            holds a concrete value
cpp	YES	0	!   - @c __reference_root:        holds a concrete reference
cpp	YES	0	!   - @c __value_proxy_root:      holds a type-erased value model
cpp	YES	0	!   - @c __reference_proxy_root:  holds a type-erased reference model
cpp	YES	0	!   Aside from @c __iroot, all root types inherit from @c __iabstract<Interface>, where
cpp	YES	0	!   @c Interface is the interface that the root type implements.
cpp	YES	0	!   The @c root concept is defined as:
cpp	YES	0	!   @code
cpp	YES	0	!   template <class Root>
cpp	YES	0	!   concept root = requires (Root& root)
cpp	NO	0	!     __any::__value(root);
cpp	NO	0	!     { __any::reset(root); } -> std::same_as<void>;
cpp	NO	0	!     { __any::type(root) } -> std::same_as<const __type_index &>;
cpp	NO	0	!     { __any::data(root) } -> std::same_as<void *>;
cpp	NO	0	!     { __any::empty(root) } -> std::same_as<bool>;
cpp	NO	0	!   };
cpp	YES	0	!   @endcode
cpp	YES	0	! - "model":
cpp	YES	0	!   A polymorphic wrapper around a root that is constructed by recursively applying a
cpp	YES	0	!   given interface and its base interfaces to the root type. For example, given an
cpp	YES	0	!   interface @c Derived that __extends @c Base, the value proxy model is a type derived
cpp	YES	0	!   from @c Derived<Base<__value_proxy_root<Derived>>>. Model types implement their given
cpp	YES	0	!   interfaces in terms of the root type. There are 5 model types:
cpp	YES	0	!   - @c __iabstract:             akin to an abstract base class for the
cpp	YES	0	!                                 interface
cpp	YES	0	!   - @c __value_model:           implements the interface for a concrete value
cpp	YES	0	!   - @c __reference_model:       implements the interface for a concrete
cpp	YES	0	!                                 reference
cpp	YES	0	!   - @c __value_proxy_model:     implements the interface over a type-erased
cpp	YES	0	!                                 value model
cpp	YES	0	!   - @c __reference_proxy_model: implements the interface over a type-erased
cpp	YES	0	!                                 reference model
cpp	YES	0	! - "proxy":
cpp	YES	0	!   A level of indirection that stores either a type-erased model in a small buffer or a
cpp	YES	0	!   pointer to an object stored elsewhere. The @c __value_proxy_root and @c
cpp	YES	0	!   __reference_proxy_root types model the @c root concept and contain an array of bytes
cpp	YES	0	!   in which they stores either a polymorphic model in-situ or a (tagged) pointer to a
cpp	YES	0	!   heap-allocated model. The @c __value_proxy_model and @c __reference_proxy_model types
cpp	YES	0	!   implement the given interface in terms of the root type.
cpp	YES	0	! @par Notes:
cpp	YES	0	! - @c Interface<Base> inherits directly from @c any::interface<Interface,Base>, which
cpp	YES	0	!   inherits directly from @c Base.
cpp	YES	0	! - Given an interface template @c Derived that __extends @c Base, the type
cpp	YES	0	!   @c __iabstract<Derived> is derived from @c __iabstract<Base>.
cpp	YES	0	! - In the case of multiple interface extension, the inheritance is forced to be linear.
cpp	YES	0	!   As a result, for an interface @c C that __extends @c A and @c B (in that order),
cpp	YES	0	!   @c __iabstract<C> will have a linear inheritance hierarchy; it will be an alias for
cpp	YES	0	!   @c C<B<A<__iroot>>>. The result is that @c __iabstract<C> inherits from @c __iabstract<A>
cpp	YES	0	!   but not from @c __iabstract<B>.
cpp	YES	0	! - The "`__proxy_root`" types both implement an @c emplace function that accepts a
cpp	YES	0	!   concrete value or reference, wraps it in the appropriate "`__model`" type, and stores
cpp	YES	0	!   it either in-situ or on the heap depending on its size and whether it is nothrow
cpp	YES	0	!   moveable.
cpp	YES	0	! - The @c __root types (excluding @c __iroot) all inherit from @c __iabstract<Interface>.
cpp	YES	0	!   The @c __model types implement the interface in terms of the root type.
cpp	YES	0	! - @c any<Derived> inherits from @c __value_proxy_model<Derived>, which in turn inherits
cpp	YES	0	!   from @c Derived<Base<__value_proxy_root<Derived>>>, which in turn inherits from
cpp	YES	0	!   @c Derived<Base<__iroot>> (aka @c __iabstract<Derived> ).
cpp	YES	0	! - @c __any_ptr<Derived> is implemented in terms of a mutable private
cpp	YES	0	!   @c __reference_proxy_model<Derived> data member, which in turn inherits from
cpp	YES	0	!   @c Derived<Base<__reference_proxy_root<Derived>>>.

cpp	YES	0	 connect_t
cpp	YES	0	! @brief Customization point object that *connects* a sender to a
cpp	YES	0	!        receiver, producing an operation state.
cpp	YES	0	! @c connect is the central seam of the sender model. Calling
cpp	YES	0	! @c stdexec::connect(sndr, rcvr) does *not* run the sender; it
cpp	YES	0	! produces an *operation state* — an opaque, immovable, startable
cpp	YES	0	! object that, when subsequently passed to @c stdexec::start, will
cpp	YES	0	! eventually deliver exactly one completion signal (@c set_value,
cpp	YES	0	! @c set_error, or @c set_stopped) to the receiver.
cpp	YES	0	! Every sender adaptor and consumer ultimately reaches for @c connect.
cpp	YES	0	! Most user code does not call it directly — @c sync_wait, @c spawn,
cpp	YES	0	! and the various adaptors do — but it is the operation a sender
cpp	YES	0	! author *must* support, either by exposing a `.connect(receiver)`
cpp	YES	0	! member, by being a coroutine awaitable (so the fallback awaitable
cpp	YES	0	! adapter applies), or — historically — via @c tag_invoke (now
cpp	YES	0	! deprecated).

cpp	NO	0	 ===============
cpp	YES	0	 Understanding why a particular sender doesn't connect to a particular
cpp	YES	0	 receiver is nigh impossible in the current design due to limitations in
cpp	YES	0	 how the compiler reports overload resolution failure in the presence of
cpp	YES	0	 constraints. `__debug_sender` is a utility to assist with the process. It
cpp	YES	0	 gives you the deep template instantiation backtrace that you need to
cpp	YES	0	 understand where in a chain of senders the problem is occurring.
cpp	YES	0	 ```c++
cpp	NO	0	   void __debug_sender(_Sender&& __sndr, _Env = {});
cpp	YES	0	 **Usage:**
cpp	YES	0	 To find out where in a chain of senders a sender is failing to connect
cpp	YES	0	 to a receiver, pass it to `__debug_sender`, optionally with an
cpp	YES	0	 environment argument; e.g. `__debug_sender(sndr [, env])`
cpp	YES	0	 To find out why a sender will not connect to a receiver of a particular
cpp	YES	0	 signature, specify the set of completion signatures as an explicit template
cpp	YES	0	 argument that names an instantiation of `completion_signatures`; e.g.:
cpp	YES	0	 `__debug_sender<completion_signatures<set_value_t(int)>>(sndr [, env])`.
cpp	YES	0	 **How it works:**
cpp	YES	0	 The `__debug_sender` function `connect`'s the sender to a
cpp	YES	0	 `__debug_receiver`, whose environment is augmented with a special
cpp	YES	0	 `__is_debug_env_t` query. An additional fall-back overload is added to
cpp	YES	0	 the `connect` CPO that recognizes receivers whose environments respond to
cpp	YES	0	 that query and lets them through. Then in a non-immediate context, it
cpp	YES	0	 looks for a `tag_invoke(connect_t...)` overload for the input sender and
cpp	YES	0	 receiver. This will recurse until it hits the `tag_invoke` call that is
cpp	YES	0	 causing the failure.
cpp	YES	0	 At least with clang, this gives me a nice backtrace, at the bottom of
cpp	YES	0	 which is the faulty `tag_invoke` overload with a mention of the
cpp	YES	0	 constraint that failed.

cpp	YES	0	! @brief Customization point object that begins the execution of an
cpp	YES	0	!        operation state.
cpp	YES	0	! @c start is the trigger that turns a connected sender into a running
cpp	YES	0	! asynchronous operation. The operation state returned by
cpp	YES	0	! @c stdexec::connect does nothing until it is passed to @c start; from
cpp	YES	0	! that moment on, it is running and will eventually deliver exactly one
cpp	YES	0	! completion signal to the receiver it was connected with.
cpp	YES	0	! See [exec.opstate.start] in the C++26 working draft.
cpp	YES	0	! **Lifetime contract.**
cpp	YES	0	! The operation state passed to @c start must:
cpp	YES	0	! 1. Be an *lvalue* — @c start(op) with @c op an rvalue is ill-formed.
cpp	YES	0	!    The reason: the caller is responsible for keeping the operation
cpp	YES	0	!    state alive until completion, which only makes sense for objects
cpp	YES	0	!    with stable identity.
cpp	YES	0	! 2. Remain alive until the receiver has been completed. The operation
cpp	YES	0	!    state itself typically holds child operation states (for sender
cpp	YES	0	!    adaptors) and references to the receiver's storage — destroying
cpp	YES	0	!    it early would invalidate those.
cpp	YES	0	! Once @c start returns, the operation is running but may or may not
cpp	YES	0	! have already completed (an inline-completing operation may have
cpp	YES	0	! completed synchronously before @c start returned; an async operation
cpp	YES	0	! may complete arbitrarily later).
cpp	YES	0	! An operation state opts in by exposing a @c noexcept,
cpp	YES	0	! @c void-returning `.start()` member:
cpp	YES	0	!   // Immovable — once constructed, must stay put:
cpp	NO	0	!   my_opstate(my_opstate&&) = delete;
cpp	YES	0	!   void start() noexcept {
cpp	YES	0	!     // Begin async work; eventually call set_value/set_error/set_stopped
cpp	YES	0	!     // on the receiver stored in this op-state.
cpp	YES	0	! `start()` *must* be @c noexcept — there's nowhere for it to throw to,
cpp	YES	0	! since the caller is typically the runtime, not user code that can
cpp	YES	0	! handle exceptions. It must also return @c void. The dispatch site
cpp	YES	0	! enforces both with static asserts.

cpp	YES	0	! @brief The customization point object for starting an operation state.
cpp	YES	0	! @c start is an instance of @ref start_t. See @ref start_t for the
cpp	YES	0	! full description, the lifetime contract, and customization examples.
cpp	YES	0	! @brief An in-progress, *immovable*, *startable* representation of an
cpp	YES	0	!        asynchronous operation — the result of connecting a sender to
cpp	YES	0	!        a receiver.
cpp	YES	0	! An *operation state* is what you get from @c stdexec::connect: it is the
cpp	YES	0	! concrete, type-erased-by-construction record of one specific sender
cpp	YES	0	! being driven into one specific receiver. Calling @c stdexec::start on
cpp	YES	0	! it begins the work; the operation runs until it eventually invokes
cpp	YES	0	! one of @c set_value / @c set_error / @c set_stopped on the receiver
cpp	YES	0	! it was constructed with.
cpp	YES	0	! Three properties define the concept @c operation_state:
cpp	YES	0	! 1. The type is destructible — operations clean up cleanly when their
cpp	YES	0	!    storage goes away (typically after they have completed).
cpp	YES	0	! 2. The type is an object type (not a reference, not a function) —
cpp	YES	0	!    operation states are *stored*, not passed by handle.

cpp	YES	0	 The following code is used to normalize completion signatures. "Normalization" means that
cpp	YES	0	 that rvalue-references are stripped from the types in the completion signatures. For example,

cpp	YES	0	 Storage for the (count, state) pair referenced in the spec; we store
cpp	YES	0	 the spec'd "state" in the lower three bits and the spec'd "count" in
cpp	YES	0	 all the rest of the bits; the states named in the spec map like so:
cpp	YES	0	   unused             = all bits zero
cpp	YES	0	   open               = any count |                  __join_needed
cpp	YES	0	   closed             = any count |                  __join_needed | __closed
cpp	YES	0	   open-and-joining   = any count | __join_running | __join_needed
cpp	YES	0	   closed-and-joining = any count | __join_running | __join_needed | __closed
cpp	YES	0	   unused-and-closed  = zero      |                                  __closed
cpp	YES	0	   joined             = zero      |                                  __closed
cpp	YES	0	 INVARIANT: __bits_ = (count << 3) | (state & 7)
cpp	YES	0	 An intrusive singly-linked list of join-sender operation states;
cpp	YES	0	 elements of the list have been "registered" to be completed when the
cpp	YES	0	 last outstanding associated operation completes. The value can be
cpp	YES	0	 the possibly-null pointer to the head of the list (where nullptr
cpp	YES	0	 means the list is empty) or `this`, which is the sentinel value that
cpp	YES	0	 indicates that the last associated operation has been disassociated
cpp	YES	0	 and any previously-registered join operations have been (or are about
cpp	YES	0	 to be) completed.
cpp	YES	0	 returns true in the unused and unused-and-closed states; since the bit
cpp	YES	0	 pattern for joined matches the unused-and-closed bit pattern, returns
cpp	YES	0	 returns true in the unused, open, and open-and-joining states
cpp	YES	0	 returns true in the closed, closed-and-joining, unused-and-closed, and
cpp	YES	0	 joined states
cpp	YES	0	 returns true in the joined state, which shares a representation with the
cpp	YES	0	 unused-and-closed state; for the scope to be fully joined, the number of
cpp	YES	0	 outstanding associated operations must be zero, so we check for exact
cpp	YES	0	 equality with __closed rather than using it as a bit mask
cpp	YES	0	 returns true in the open-and-joining and closed-and-joining states
cpp	YES	0	 returns false in the unused, unused-and-closed, and joined states;
cpp	YES	0	 returns true if the destructor is safe to run
cpp	YES	0	 acceptable terminal states are __bits == 0 and __bits == __closed; we
cpp	YES	0	 can check for both at once by expecting __bits with the __closed bit
cpp	YES	0	 cleared to be equal to zero
cpp	YES	0	 extracts from __bits what the spec calls count, which is the number of
cpp	YES	0	 outstanding operations associated with this scope
cpp	YES	0	 extracts from __bits what the spec calls state, which determines where
cpp	YES	0	 composes ___new_count and __new_state into the packed representation we store
cpp	YES	0	 in __bits
cpp	YES	0	 no high bits set
cpp	YES	0	 we need acquire semantics in case the join operation being started is about to
cpp	YES	0	 observe that the last decrement has already happened; in that case, we need to
cpp	YES	0	 establish that all of the now-completed associated operations happen-before the
cpp	YES	0	 completion of this join operation
cpp	YES	0	 __registered_join_ops_ == this when the list has been cleared

cpp	YES	0	! @brief A variadic sender factory that runs multiple senders concurrently
cpp	YES	0	!        and completes when all of them have completed, concatenating
cpp	YES	0	!        their value datums.
cpp	YES	0	! @c when_all is the canonical *parallel composition* primitive in the
cpp	YES	0	! sender model. You give it zero or more senders; it returns a single
cpp	YES	0	! sender that, when connected and started, starts *all* of the input
cpp	YES	0	! senders concurrently. When every input has completed, @c when_all's
cpp	YES	0	! sender completes with a value tuple that is the concatenation of every
cpp	YES	0	! input's value datums.
cpp	YES	0	! If any one input can fail or be stopped, @c when_all uses an internal
cpp	YES	0	! @c inplace_stop_source. An unhappy completion requests stop on the
cpp	YES	0	! other inputs before the combined operation completes.
cpp	YES	0	! auto s = stdexec::when_all(
cpp	YES	0	!   stdexec::just(1),
cpp	YES	0	!   stdexec::just(2.5),
cpp	NO	0	!   stdexec::just(std::string{"x"}));
cpp	NO	0	! auto [i, d, str] = stdexec::sync_wait(std::move(s)).value();
cpp	YES	0	! // i == 1, d == 2.5, str == "x"
cpp	YES	0	! See [exec.when.all] in the C++26 working draft for the normative
cpp	YES	0	! @c when_all requires that each input sender have exactly one
cpp	YES	0	! @c set_value_t completion signature — otherwise the *output* value
cpp	YES	0	! signature would be a combinatorial explosion of all possible
cpp	YES	0	! concatenations. The constraint is enforced at connect time with a
cpp	YES	0	! diagnostic pointing at @ref when_all_with_variant_t, which lifts the
cpp	YES	0	! restriction (at the cost of producing a variant per input).
cpp	YES	0	! Given inputs @c sndr_i with completion signatures
cpp	YES	0	! // For each i in 1..n:
cpp	YES	0	! set_value_t(Vi...)        // exactly one such signature per input
cpp	YES	0	! set_error_t(Eij)...       // zero or more per input
cpp	YES	0	! set_stopped_t()           // optional per input
cpp	YES	0	! the resulting sender has completion signatures:
cpp	YES	0	! set_value_t(V1..., V2..., ..., Vn...)   // concatenation of every input
cpp	YES	0	! set_error_t(Eij)...                     // union across all inputs
cpp	YES	0	! set_error_t(std::exception_ptr)         // added if any decay-copy may throw
cpp	YES	0	! set_stopped_t()                         // added if any input has it
cpp	YES	0	! The value datums of each input are decay-copied into the resulting
cpp	YES	0	! sender's state while it waits for the slowest input to finish; the
cpp	YES	0	! final tuple is built from those decay-copies. If any decay-copy
cpp	YES	0	! throws, the operation transitions to the error path.
cpp	YES	0	! **Concurrency.**
cpp	YES	0	! "Concurrently" here means *the inputs are not sequenced relative to
cpp	YES	0	! each other* — @c when_all starts every child operation in a fold
cpp	YES	0	! expression before returning from @c start. Whether they actually
cpp	YES	0	! execute in parallel depends on the schedulers they're attached to:
cpp	YES	0	! independent @c starts_on / @c continues_on branches across different
cpp	YES	0	! schedulers truly run in parallel; multiple @c just-rooted branches
cpp	YES	0	! all complete synchronously inside @c when_all's @c start.
cpp	YES	0	! **Error and stop semantics.**
cpp	YES	0	! At most *one* completion is delivered to the downstream receiver. If
cpp	YES	0	! several children produce errors or stopped completions, the first
cpp	YES	0	! one observed wins; subsequent failures are dropped. Concretely:
cpp	YES	0	! - First child to call @c set_error wins; its error becomes the result.
cpp	YES	0	! - First child to call @c set_stopped wins (if no error has been seen).
cpp	YES	0	! - On either, the internal stop source is signalled so the remaining
cpp	YES	0	!   children can wind down promptly.
cpp	YES	0	! @c when_all chains the receiver's stop token to its internal
cpp	YES	0	! stop-source, so an outer stop request propagates to every child.

c	YES	0	\nThe duration of the 1/4 (quarter note) is specified in the constructor.\n\nNote mapping is from C4 to B7:\n    C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C D E F G A B c d e f g a b c' d' e' f' g' a' b'\n\nRest is specified using 'r'.\n\nSharp and flat are indicated by '+' and '-'.\n\nPitch Slides (Portamento):\n    > to slide pitch up   (smoothly move up   one semitone over duration)\n    < to slide pitch down (smoothly move down one semitone over duration)\n\nThe length of the note (duration) is specified using an integer or fraction:\n     1   for 1/1  (whole     note)\n     2   for 1/2  (half      note)\n     4   for 1/4  (quarter   note)\n     8   for 1/8  (eighth    note)\n    16   for 1/16 (sixteenth note)\n     2/3 for two   notes in the time of three quarter notes (each = 3/2 of a quarter)\n     3/1 for three notes in the time of one   quarter note  (each = 1/3 of a quarter)\n     3/2 for three notes in the time of two   quarter notes (each = 2/3 of a quarter)\n     5/4 for five  notes in the time of four  quarter notes (each = 4/5 of a quarter)\n     7/4 for seven notes in the time of four  quarter notes (each = 4/7 of a quarter)\n\nThe play() method accepts four separate score strings:\n    bool play(const char *scoreInFlash[4], size_t length[4]);\n  - scoreInFlash[0..2] are the three independent note tracks.\n  - scoreInFlash[3]    is the percussion track.\n  - Any element may be nullptr to leave that track silent.\n  - Track lengths need not be equal; shorter tracks simply stop earlier.\n\nNotes between tracks are played by their defined durations, like a real score.\nEach track advances independently with its own phase accumulator and timing.\nUse rests ('r') to align events between tracks when synchronisation is needed.\n\nModifiers (must be written after the duration):\n    . to shorten  note duration by 50%\n    _ to lengthen note duration by 50%\n    ! to increase note volume   by 40%\n    & to tie (connects pitch and envelope to the next note)\n\nThe tempo can be changed using the notation (track 0 only; ignored in tracks 1 and 2):\n    i to decrease tempo by 20%\n    I to increase tempo by 20%\n    | to reset    tempo\n\nThe volume can be changed per track using the notation:\n    v to decrease volume by 20%\n    V to increase volume by 20%\n    = to reset    volume\n
c	YES	0	\n=== Percussion Notation Extension ===\nSymbols (used in the percussion track, scoreInFlash[3]):\n    k  Kick drum   -> ~100 Hz    , dur = 1/2 x 1/4, fast   decay -- waveform: Sine\n    t  Tom/Bongo   -> ~300 Hz    , dur = 2/3 x 1/4, medium decay -- waveform: Triangle\n    w  Woodblock   -> ~250-400 Hz, dur = 1/2 x 1/4, short  burst -- waveform: Saw Down\n    s  Snare       -> ~200 Hz    , dur = 1/2 x 1/4, short  burst -- waveform: Square\n    y  Cymbal      -> ~2-4 kHz   , dur =   2 x 1/4, long   decay  - waveform: Saw Up\n\nPercussion symbols are envelope-driven and ignore score duration notation.\nUse 'r' (rest) in the percussion track to advance its time cursor and synchronise percussion hits with events in the note tracks.\nOnly volume modifiers (v, V, =) are recognised in the percussion track; all other modifiers are ignored.\nPercussion waveforms are fixed per instrument and cannot be changed.\n

cpp	YES	0	    K1 by 1 bit.

cpp	YES	0	 handed across an FFI boundary by repe::plugin_call. Neither carries a null terminator, and both
cpp	YES	0	 are reachable by anyone who can send a message. Every buffer here is heap allocated at exactly
cpp	YES	0	 the size of its contents so ASAN reports a read one byte past the end.
cpp	YES	0	 Most random bytes fail header validation, which would leave the registry itself barely exercised,
cpp	YES	0	 so the input is also replayed wrapped in a well formed header. That splits the work: the raw pass
cpp	YES	0	 fuzzes the header parser, the wrapped pass fuzzes the query dispatch and body reader behind it.
cpp	YES	0	 Reflection needs external linkage, so these cannot live in an anonymous namespace.
cpp	YES	0	 Wide enough that the dispatch has somewhere to go and the reader has more than one shape to
cpp	YES	0	 resolve against. Three surfaces matter here and each is represented:
cpp	YES	0	   - plain members, where the read target is a fixed type
cpp	YES	0	   - std::function members, which is how a call with typed parameters is registered, and so
cpp	YES	0	     the only way to reach the reader that parses arguments
cpp	YES	0	   - a variant, whose resolution re-parses speculatively -- the path where a reader is most
cpp	YES	0	     likely to walk off the end of a buffer it does not own
cpp	YES	0	 The fuzzer supplies these arguments, so every one of them arrives at its own extremes.
cpp	YES	0	 Signed overflow in the body of a target is undefined behavior in the target, not a finding
cpp	YES	0	 about the registry, and UBSan stops the run on it either way -- so the arithmetic here goes
cpp	YES	0	 through unsigned, where wrapping is defined and the result is still a function of the input.
cpp	YES	0	 Member functions listed in a glz::meta reach different endpoint registrations than the
cpp	YES	0	 std::function members above -- register_member_function_endpoint and its with_params variant.
cpp	YES	0	 The with_params one parks its argument in a `static thread_local`, which is the kind of state
cpp	YES	0	 that survives between inputs and turns a crash into one that will not reproduce, so it is
cpp	YES	0	 worth having under the fuzzer rather than only under the unit tests.
cpp	YES	0	 Wraps rather than overflows, for the reason given on `doubled` above. `counter` accumulates

cpp	YES	0	 Exactly sized, so there is no slack after the message for an over-read to land in harmlessly.

cpp	YES	0	 immediately, so a regression shows up as a hung test rather than a failed assertion.
cpp	YES	0	 The wrapper reader holds a level while it scans for the "unexpected" key, and every path has
cpp	YES	0	 to give it back -- the two that rewind and re-read the object through a counting reader
cpp	YES	0	 included. Leaking it capped a run of wrappers at 256.
cpp	YES	0	 Reads share one context rather than filling a std::vector<std::expected<...>>, which is the
cpp	YES	0	 same test but instantiates vector's iterator comparison against std::expected; libc++ on the
cpp	YES	0	 P2996 clang recurses into its own operator== constraint there and fails to compile.
cpp	YES	0	 Holding the level on the error paths is what still catches a truncated wrapper when the
cpp	YES	0	 buffer is not null terminated.
cpp	YES	0	 A partial read stops on a success path, so it has to close its level like any other exit;
cpp	YES	0	 otherwise the count creeps up across reads that share a context.
cpp	YES	0	 The JSON analogue of the BEVE cascade: two array alternatives, so every level tries both,
cpp	YES	0	 with a malformed leaf at the bottom that every level retries. 339 bytes took 40 seconds
cpp	YES	0	 before the speculation budget capped the total re-parsed bytes; the cost no longer grows
cpp	YES	0	 with depth.
cpp	YES	0	 malformed leaf
cpp	YES	0	 Each element tries alt_a first and fails inside its object, which leaves that level counted
cpp	YES	0	 until the alternative is rewound. Without the rewind this errors once 256 elements have been
cpp	YES	0	 attempted, even though the document is two levels deep.

cpp	YES	0	 recursion guard never fires -- at its 84-level limit the key would be 2^84 bytes.

cpp	YES	0	 levels is a 33 MB key and 26 is 134 MB -- both large enough to prove the point, small
cpp	YES	0	 enough that a regression here fails this assert instead of taking the machine with it.

cpp	YES	0	*\n       * @brief Register wrapping middleware that executes around route handlers\n       *\n       * Wrapping middleware can execute code before AND after the handler by wrapping\n       * the next() function. This enables natural timing measurements, response\n       * transformation, and comprehensive error handling.\n       *\n       * Use cases:\n       * - Request/response timing and metrics\n       * - Logging with full context (including response status and timing)\n       * - Response transformation (compression, encryption, header injection)\n       * - Error handling around handlers (try-catch wrapping)\n       * - Any cross-cutting concerns that need both before and after logic\n       *\n       * CRITICAL SAFETY REQUIREMENT:\n       * ============================\n       * The next() handler MUST be called synchronously within the middleware function.\n       * The next_handler type is intentionally non-copyable and non-movable to prevent\n       * accidental storage and asynchronous invocation.\n       *\n       * Storing next() or calling it asynchronously will result in:\n       * - Compile-time errors (if you try to copy/move it)\n       * - Undefined behavior due to dangling references (if you work around the safety)\n       *\n       * The request, response, and handler objects are only valid during the synchronous\n       * execution of the middleware chain.\n       *\n       * CORRECT Usage:\n       * ```cpp\n       * server.wrap([](const request& req, response& res, auto next) {\n       *     auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();\n       *     next(); // ✓ Synchronous call - correct\n       *     auto duration = std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - start;\n       *     std::cout << "Request took " << duration.count() << "ns\\n";\n       * });\n       * ```\n       *\n       * INCORRECT Usage (will not compile):\n       * ```cpp\n       * server.wrap([](const request& req, response& res, auto next) {\n       *     // ✗ COMPILE ERROR: next_handler is non-copyable\n       *     std::thread([next]() {\n       *         std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::seconds(1));\n       *         next(); // Would cause dangling references\n       *     }).detach();\n       * });\n       * ```\n       *\n       * For asynchronous operations, complete them BEFORE or AFTER calling next():\n       * ```cpp\n       * server.wrap([](const request& req, response& res, auto next) {\n       *     // Async work BEFORE handler\n       *     auto data = fetch_from_cache_async().get();\n       *\n       *     next(); // Synchronous handler execution\n       *\n       *     // Async work AFTER handler (fire and forget logging)\n       *     std::async(std::launch::async, [status = res.status_code]() {\n       *         log_to_remote_server(status);\n       *     });\n       * });\n       * ```\n       *\n       * Execution order with multiple middleware:\n       * ```cpp\n       * server.wrap([](auto&, auto&, auto next) {\n       *     std::cout << "A before\\n";\n       *     next();\n       *     std::cout << "A after\\n";\n       * });\n       * server.wrap([](auto&, auto&, auto next) {\n       *     std::cout << "B before\\n";\n       *     next();\n       *     std::cout << "B after\\n";\n       * });\n       * // Output: A before -> B before -> handler -> B after -> A after\n       * ```\n       *\n       * @tparam F Callable type (must satisfy wrapping_middleware_callable concept)\n       * @param middleware The wrapping middleware function\n       * @return Reference to this server for method chaining\n

cpp	YES	0	 How many times over the input an alias may replay before the read gives up. Deliberately
cpp	YES	0	 looser than the speculative-parse factor: re-parsing the same bytes to resolve a variant is
cpp	YES	0	 waste to be capped, while replaying an anchor is the feature working as intended, and a
cpp	YES	0	 generated config that references a large anchor from thousands of entries is ordinary. What
cpp	YES	0	 floor below rather than by this factor.
cpp	YES	0	 ...plus a floor, since the factor alone is meaningless for the small inputs where the
cpp	YES	0	 exponential shape lives: a 306 byte document expands 60000x, so any multiple of its own
cpp	YES	0	 size stops it. The floor is what every ordinary document actually reads against, and it is
cpp	YES	0	 set where the exponential case costs a bounded ~40 MB and a tenth of a second instead of
cpp	YES	0	 gigabytes and minutes -- while staying far above what a hand-written document replays.
cpp	YES	0	 How many times over the input a read may materialize complex-key text, and the floor it
cpp	YES	0	 reads against. A mapping key that is not a scalar is stored by its JSON form, and JSON
cpp	YES	0	 escaping is multiplicative under nesting: every level that carries the previous one as its
cpp	YES	0	 key doubles that level's backslashes, so each `? ` in `? ? ? ...` doubles the key while
cpp	YES	0	 adding two bytes to the input. 52 bytes of input reach a 134 MB key, 72 bytes reach more
cpp	YES	0	 memory than a machine has, and nothing about the shape looks unusual on the way down --
cpp	YES	0	 nesting is linear in the input, so the recursion guard is no help: by its 84-level limit the
cpp	YES	0	 key would be 2^84 bytes.
cpp	YES	0	 Bounding materialized bytes is what the memory and the time both track. The constants match
cpp	YES	0	 the alias budget for the same reason it chose them: a complex key's JSON form is comparable
cpp	YES	0	 to the YAML that produced it, so any multiple of the document stops growth that does not
cpp	YES	0	 track the document at all, and the floor is what ordinary documents actually read against.

cpp	YES	0	 BSON - https://bsonspec.org/spec.html
cpp	YES	0	 A BSON document is the top-level container and is encoded as:
cpp	YES	0	     int32 length | e_list | 0x00
cpp	YES	0	 The int32 length includes itself and the terminating null byte. All
cpp	YES	0	 multi-byte integers and floats on the wire are little-endian.
cpp	YES	0	 Each element in e_list is:
cpp	YES	0	     byte type | cstring key | value...
cpp	YES	0	 where cstring is a UTF-8 byte sequence terminated by 0x00.
cpp	YES	0	 BSON arrays are encoded as documents whose keys are the decimal string
cpp	YES	0	 representations of their indices ("0", "1", "2", ...), in order.
cpp	YES	0	 Element type codes. These identify the wire format of a document value.
cpp	YES	0	 IEEE 754 binary64
cpp	YES	0	 int32 length (bytes+1) | UTF-8 | 0x00
cpp	YES	0	 embedded BSON document
cpp	YES	0	 document with integer-string keys

cpp	YES	0	 DEPRECATED (read-only support)
cpp	YES	0	 12 bytes
cpp	YES	0	 0x00 = false, 0x01 = true
cpp	YES	0	 int64 ms since Unix epoch, UTC
cpp	YES	0	 no value bytes
cpp	YES	0	 cstring pattern | cstring options
cpp	YES	0	 string (length-prefixed)
cpp	YES	0	 uint64: low 32 increment, high 32 seconds
cpp	YES	0	 IEEE 754-2008 decimal128 (opaque)
cpp	YES	0	 compares lower than all other values
cpp	YES	0	 compares higher than all other values
cpp	YES	0	 Binary data subtype codes, carried in the byte immediately after the

cpp	YES	0	 DEPRECATED
cpp	YES	0	 RFC 9562 UUID, canonical byte order

cpp	YES	0	 fixed-size blob. Glaze does the same — generation is left to the user.

cpp	YES	0	 the Unix epoch. Users usually prefer std::chrono::system_clock::time_point,
cpp	YES	0	 which the BSON codec auto-maps to this type.

cpp	YES	0	 'm' multiline, 's' dotall, 'u' Unicode, 'x' verbose.

cpp	YES	0	   - terminator appears early (length field is larger than the body) →
cpp	YES	0	     we exit the loop via `tag == 0` with `it < stop`.
cpp	YES	0	   - terminator missing (declared length undercounts, or body is
cpp	YES	0	     corrupted so the terminator is consumed as part of an element) →
cpp	YES	0	     the loop exits via `it >= stop` without ever seeing a zero tag.
cpp	YES	0	 Both surface as `syntax_error` with a specific custom message.
cpp	YES	0	 Most plausible cause: no 0x00 terminator in the expected slot,
cpp	YES	0	 so what we read as a tag was garbage and read_cstring ran off
cpp	YES	0	 the end of the document looking for the key's null byte.
cpp	YES	0	 Marker / hidden / skip / includer fields are never
cpp	YES	0	 written, so any matching key here came from
cpp	YES	0	 foreign input. Silently consume the value.
cpp	YES	0	 --- Reflected struct / glaze_object_t -----------------------------------
cpp	YES	0	 --- Map with string keys ------------------------------------------------
cpp	YES	0	 BSON keys are cstrings; non-string map keys are unreachable on the wire,
cpp	YES	0	 so reading into such a map is rejected at compile time to match the
cpp	YES	0	 writer's static assertion.
cpp	YES	0	 --- Arrays / vectors / ranges -------------------------------------------
cpp	YES	0	 Encoded on the wire as a document with integer-string keys; the keys are
cpp	YES	0	 not validated against the sequence order — matching MongoDB's tolerance
cpp	YES	0	 they appear in the document.
cpp	YES	0	key
cpp	YES	0	 Fixed-capacity container (e.g., std::array): fill by index.
cpp	YES	0	 --- glaze_array_t (tuple-like) ------------------------------------------
cpp	YES	0	 Public entry points
cpp	YES	0	 BSON documents are length-prefixed (int32 header = total bytes). The core
cpp	YES	0	 reader consumes exactly that many bytes, but would otherwise silently
cpp	YES	0	 ignore anything trailing the top-level document. Enforce exact-fill at the
cpp	YES	0	 masked.
cpp	YES	0	 Skip a single BSON value given its element type byte. Used by the struct
cpp	YES	0	 and map readers to drop over unknown keys, and by the deprecated-type
cpp	YES	0	 fallbacks (undefined / dbpointer / symbol / code_w_scope) that we can read
cpp	YES	0	 but choose not to materialise.
cpp	YES	0	 Read a little-endian int32 without advancing (used for length prefixes
cpp	YES	0	 when the consumer needs the length before deciding what to do with the
cpp	YES	0	 body).
cpp	YES	0	 Advance `it` past a null-terminated cstring. On success, it points just
cpp	YES	0	 past the 0x00 terminator.
cpp	YES	0	 BSON skip: the type byte is supplied by the caller (the document/array
cpp	YES	0	 reader) because BSON values do not carry a self-describing header — the
cpp	YES	0	 element tag lives outside the value.
cpp	YES	0	 The length prefix *includes* itself. Skip the rest, plus
cpp	YES	0	 the trailing null byte that the prefix already accounts for.
cpp	YES	0	 Minimum: 4-byte length + 0x00 terminator.
cpp	YES	0	 One-byte subtype follows, then `len` payload bytes.
cpp	YES	0	 String (length-prefixed UTF-8 + null) + 12-byte ObjectId.
cpp	YES	0	 Total int32 length includes itself, the string, and the scope
cpp	YES	0	 document. Skip the whole thing in one go.
cpp	YES	0	 BSON writer — https://bsonspec.org/spec.html
cpp	YES	0	 BSON's top-level container is always a document:
cpp	YES	0	     int32 total_length | element* | 0x00
cpp	YES	0	 where `total_length` counts itself and the terminating null byte, and each
cpp	YES	0	 element is:
cpp	YES	0	     type_byte | key cstring | value bytes
cpp	YES	0	 Because the document length precedes its body, the writer reserves 4 bytes
cpp	YES	0	 up front, emits the body, emits the null terminator, then patches the
cpp	YES	0	 reserved slot with the computed length. Arrays are encoded as documents
cpp	YES	0	 whose keys are the decimal strings "0", "1", "2", ...
cpp	YES	0	 All multi-byte integers and floats on the wire are little-endian.
cpp	YES	0	 Caveat on cstring fields (BSON spec prohibits embedded 0x00):
cpp	YES	0	   - std::map<std::string, T> keys
cpp	YES	0	   - bson::regex::pattern and bson::regex::options
cpp	YES	0	 Strings passed in these fields must not contain an embedded NUL; otherwise
cpp	YES	0	 the resulting wire bytes are malformed and a downstream read will terminate
cpp	YES	0	 the cstring at the first NUL and fail with a syntax_error when the trailing
cpp	YES	0	 bytes no longer parse as a valid element stream. Struct field names are
cpp	YES	0	 safe by construction — they come from reflected identifiers.
cpp	YES	0	 Caveat on nested optionals: std::optional<std::optional<T>> loses the
cpp	NO	0	 outer/inner distinction on the wire. Both `nullopt` and `optional{nullopt}`
cpp	YES	0	 encode as a single null element, so reads cannot tell them apart. This is
cpp	YES	0	 inherent to the tagged-null encoding (same limitation in JSON, CBOR, etc.).
cpp	YES	0	 --- Little-endian byte writers -----------------------------------------
cpp	YES	0	 On little-endian hosts (x86, ARM64) a std::memcpy of the native integer
cpp	YES	0	 is already in wire order. On big-endian hosts we byteswap first.
cpp	YES	0	 Patch a little-endian integer into a previously reserved slot without
cpp	YES	0	 advancing `pos`. Used to backfill document lengths.
cpp	YES	0	 --- Raw byte writers ----------------------------------------------------
cpp	YES	0	 --- Document lifecycle --------------------------------------------------
cpp	YES	0	 Reserve 4 bytes for the int32 length field and record the starting ix.
cpp	YES	0	 Emit the terminating null byte and backfill the int32 length.
cpp	YES	0	 --- Element prefix: type_byte | key cstring | 0x00 ---------------------
cpp	YES	0	 --- BSON string value: int32(len+1) | UTF-8 | 0x00 ---------------------
cpp	YES	0	 The length field stores byte count of the UTF-8 payload PLUS the
cpp	YES	0	 trailing null byte, per spec.
cpp	YES	0	 --- Array key emission: decimal string of index, null-terminated -------
cpp	YES	0	 For small indices a static string table is used; larger indices fall
cpp	YES	0	 back to std::to_chars. Each element is a null-terminated C string
cpp	YES	0	 suitable for a BSON e_name. 1024 covers nearly all real-world array
cpp	YES	0	 sizes at ~5KB of .rodata, keeping the hot path branch-free.
cpp	YES	0	 Returns the key bytes for the given index as a string_view over a
cpp	YES	0	 caller-owned scratch buffer or the precomputed table. The returned
cpp	YES	0	 string_view does not include the null terminator.
cpp	YES	0	 --- Skip logic (ported from JSONB) ------------------------------------
cpp	YES	0	 Dispatcher — routes top-level writes through to<BSON, T>::op.
cpp	YES	0	 Value-only writers: to<BSON, T>::op writes just the value bytes (no type
cpp	YES	0	 byte, no key). Each specialization also exposes a static constexpr
cpp	YES	0	 `type_code` member giving the BSON element type byte for that T, which
cpp	YES	0	 the enclosing document/array writer emits before the key and value.
cpp	YES	0	 For types with runtime-varying type codes (std::optional, std::variant),
cpp	YES	0	 `type_code` is not defined; the member-element helper dispatches those
cpp	YES	0	 cases explicitly.
cpp	YES	0	 BSON has two integer element types: int32 (0x10) and int64 (0x12). We pick
cpp	YES	0	 based on the C++ type's range, not the runtime value, so the encoding is
cpp	YES	0	 deterministic from the schema alone.
cpp	NO	0	   int8/int16/int32, uint8/uint16           → int32
cpp	YES	0	   uint32, int64, uint64                    → int64 (uint64 overflow → error)
cpp	YES	0	 uint32 goes to int64 because UINT32_MAX exceeds INT32_MAX; emitting int32
cpp	YES	0	 would silently truncate values in 2^31..2^32-1. This differs from the
cpp	YES	0	 MongoDB shell default (NumberInt for anything 32-bit wide), so drivers or
cpp	YES	0	 tools inspecting the wire output will see int64 where they may expect
cpp	YES	0	 int32. The round-trip is lossless and the encoding stays type-driven.
cpp	YES	0	 BSON has only `double` (type 0x01). `float` promotes without loss.
cpp	YES	0	 Always emitted as the underlying integer. `Opts.reflect_enums` is
cpp	YES	0	 intentionally not honored — JSON (which does honor it and emits the
cpp	YES	0	 reflected name as a string) and BSON will therefore produce different
cpp	YES	0	 wire shapes from the same shared `opts`. This is a deliberate interop
cpp	YES	0	 choice, not a spec constraint: BSON strings (type 0x02) can carry any
cpp	YES	0	 UTF-8 name, but MongoDB and other driver ecosystems expect integer-
cpp	YES	0	 backed enums on the wire, and emitting names here would silently
cpp	YES	0	 A duration has no calendar meaning, so it is encoded as its bare integer or
cpp	YES	0	 floating-point `rep` count, reusing the BSON mapping of the underlying
cpp	YES	0	 arithmetic type (int32/int64/double). BSON's element model requires a
cpp	YES	0	 per-type `type_code`, so this delegates to the rep type's writer rather than
cpp	YES	0	 the generic cross-format duration specialization in core/chrono.hpp.
cpp	YES	0	 Implementation-defined epoch, so encoded as the bare count of the time point's
cpp	YES	0	 duration since epoch (same rule as a duration). Like the duration writer above,
cpp	YES	0	 BSON needs a per-type `type_code`, so it delegates to the rep type's writer.
cpp	YES	0	 BSON string value layout: int32(byte_count + 1) | UTF-8 bytes | 0x00
cpp	YES	0	 BSON timestamp wire format: low 32 bits = increment, high 32 bits = seconds.
cpp	YES	0	 BSON spec requires regex options be stored in alphabetical order.
cpp	YES	0	 std::sort works on the raw buffer regardless of element type: char,
cpp	YES	0	 uint8_t, and std::byte all expose ordering (std::byte via its scoped
cpp	YES	0	 min_key carries no value bytes.
cpp	YES	0	 max_key carries no value bytes.

cpp	YES	0	 Subtype 0x02 (binary_old) is spec-required to wrap the payload in

cpp	YES	0	 --- glz::uuid → binary subtype 0x04 -------------------------------------
cpp	YES	0	 --- std::chrono::system_clock::time_point → datetime --------------------
cpp	YES	0	 Member-element writer: emits a complete (type_byte | key cstring | value)
cpp	YES	0	 element for a named member of a document. Handles the runtime-dispatched

cpp	YES	0	 BSON keys are cstrings; non-string map keys are rejected at compile time
cpp	YES	0	 to avoid silent loss of fidelity.
cpp	YES	0	 Encoded as a BSON document whose keys are "0", "1", "2", ..., matching
cpp	YES	0	 the MongoDB convention. The document framing is identical to a struct.
cpp	YES	0	 --- glaze_array_t (tuple-like fixed array) ------------------------------
cpp	YES	0	 BSON's wire format requires the top-level value to be a document. Allow
cpp	YES	0	 reflected structs, maps with string keys, sequence containers (encoded
cpp	YES	0	 as integer-keyed documents), and glaze_array_t. Primitives are rejected
cpp	YES	0	 at the call site — they have no valid BSON document encoding on their

cpp	YES	0	 BSON → JSON converter.
cpp	YES	0	 Output uses MongoDB Canonical Extended JSON v2 conventions for types that
cpp	YES	0	 have no native JSON representation:
cpp	YES	0	   - object_id  → {"$oid":"<24 hex chars>"}
cpp	YES	0	   - datetime   → {"$date":{"$numberLong":"<int64 ms as string>"}}
cpp	YES	0	   - timestamp  → {"$timestamp":{"t":<sec>,"i":<inc>}}
cpp	YES	0	   - binary     → {"$binary":{"base64":"...","subType":"XX"}}
cpp	YES	0	   - regex      → {"$regularExpression":{"pattern":"...","options":"..."}}
cpp	YES	0	   - javascript → {"$code":"..."}
cpp	YES	0	   - min_key / max_key → {"$minKey":1} / {"$maxKey":1}

cpp	YES	0	   - undefined  → {"$undefined":true}
cpp	YES	0	   - db_pointer / code_w_scope → syntax_error (deprecated; rare in practice)
cpp	YES	0	 Asymmetry with the struct-read skip path: when reading BSON into a C++
cpp	YES	0	 skipped — the caller didn't ask for them, so silently advancing past the
cpp	YES	0	 bytes is correct. The converter cannot do the same: callers expect the
cpp	YES	0	 output JSON to reflect the entire document, so silently dropping fields
cpp	YES	0	 would misrepresent the contents. These deprecated types therefore fail
cpp	YES	0	 loudly here rather than being elided.
cpp	YES	0	 decimal128 has no native parser in Glaze, so the 16-byte payload is emitted

cpp	YES	0	 the value for round trip without masquerading as a real Extended JSON

cpp	YES	0	 --- small emit helpers ------------------------------------------------
cpp	YES	0	 exclude the trailing NUL
cpp	YES	0	 Emit `n` payload bytes as a lowercase hex literal (no quotes, no prefix).
cpp	YES	0	 --- value / document / array dispatchers ------------------------------
cpp	YES	0	 len includes the trailing null byte.
cpp	YES	0	 Spec: 0x02 wraps the payload in a redundant inner int32

cpp	YES	0	 Trailing bytes beyond the advertised document length are silently

cpp	YES	0	 consume the whole buffer (matches read_bson's exact-fill behavior).
cpp	YES	0	 GLZ_DISABLE_ALWAYS_INLINE can be defined to disable forced inlining,
cpp	YES	0	 reducing binary size and compilation time at the cost of peak performance.
cpp	YES	0	 Enable always_inline when optimizing (-O1 or higher) or in release builds (NDEBUG)
cpp	YES	0	 __OPTIMIZE__ is defined by GCC/Clang when any optimization level is enabled
cpp	YES	0	 IMPORTANT: GLZ_FLATTEN should only be used with extreme care
cpp	YES	0	 It often adds to the binary size and greatly increases compilation times.
cpp	YES	0	 It should only be applied in very specific circumstances.
cpp	YES	0	 It is best to more often rely on the compiler.
cpp	YES	0	 Low-level buffer write primitives (dump functions)
cpp	NO	0	 ================================================
cpp	YES	0	 These functions write directly to the buffer WITHOUT bounds checking for bounded buffers.
cpp	YES	0	 Contract:
cpp	YES	0	 - For resizable buffers (std::string, std::vector): Auto-resizes when Checked=true (default)
cpp	YES	0	 - For bounded buffers (std::array, std::span): Caller MUST call ensure_space() first
cpp	YES	0	 - For raw pointers: Caller assumes responsibility for sufficient space
cpp	YES	0	 The Checked template parameter ONLY enables auto-resize for resizable buffers.
cpp	YES	0	 It does NOT enable bounds checking for bounded buffers - that would require ctx for error reporting
cpp	YES	0	 and would duplicate the ensure_space() logic. The padding model (ensure_space checks for
cpp	YES	0	 ix + n + write_padding_bytes) guarantees sufficient space for subsequent dump calls.
cpp	YES	0	 Characters to integer parsing
cpp	YES	0	 - We don't allow decimals in integer parsing
cpp	YES	0	 - We don't allow negative exponents
cpp	YES	0	 These cases can produce fractions which slow performance and add confusion
cpp	YES	0	 as to how the integer ought to be parsed (truncation, rounding, etc.)
cpp	YES	0	 This integer parsing is designed to be straightforward and fast
cpp	YES	0	 Values like 1e6 are allowed because it enables less typing from the user
cpp	YES	0	 and has a clear integer value
cpp	YES	0	 Valid JSON integer examples
cpp	YES	0	 1234
cpp	YES	0	 1234e1
cpp	YES	0	 1e9
cpp	YES	0	 Invalid for this atoi algorithm
cpp	YES	0	 1.234
cpp	YES	0	 1234e-1
cpp	YES	0	 0.0
cpp	YES	0	 The standard JSON specification for numbers and the associated rules apply
cpp	YES	0	 *** We ensure that a decimal value being parsed will result in an error
cpp	YES	0	 1.2 should not produce 1, but rather an error, even when a single field is parsed
cpp	YES	0	 This ensures that we get proper errors when parsing and don't get confusing errors
cpp	YES	0	 It isn't technically required, because end validation would handle it, but it produces
cpp	YES	0	 much clearer errors, especially when we don't perform trailing validation.
cpp	YES	0	 Turn off MSVC warning for possible loss of data: we are intentionally allowing well defined unsigned integer
cpp	YES	0	 overflows
cpp	YES	0	 Exponents at or beyond this magnitude are out of range for every integer width, so the exponent
cpp	YES	0	 accumulators clamp here rather than growing without bound. Sits far above the largest accepted
cpp	YES	0	 exponent (19, for uint64_t) and low enough that a clamped value cannot overflow uint32_t.
cpp	YES	0	 Consumes the run of exponent digits starting at `c` and returns its value, clamped at
cpp	YES	0	 exponent_clamp. Clamping is what keeps the result meaningful: a narrow accumulator wraps mod its
cpp	YES	0	 width, which aliases an out-of-range exponent onto an accepted one. Every digit is consumed so
cpp	YES	0	 that leading zeros reach their true value -- JSON forbids a leading zero in the integer part but
cpp	YES	0	 permits any run of digits in the exponent, making "1e007" a valid spelling of 10^7 -- and so the
cpp	YES	0	 caller resumes past the whole exponent rather than mid-number.
cpp	YES	0	 Requires *c to be a digit and the buffer to be terminated by a non-digit (the null terminator
cpp	YES	0	 counts); this scan is bounded by the input, not by a digit count.
cpp	YES	0	 Written as a select rather than a branch: the clamp only ever engages on absurdly long
cpp	YES	0	 exponents, so a branch here would be a mispredict risk on the path that matters.
cpp	YES	0	 Computed overflow checks - used instead of lookup tables to save 4KB+ of binary size
cpp	YES	0	 Uses adjusted threshold for branch-free single comparison (7-12% faster than bitwise approach)
cpp	YES	0	 When digit > last_digit, effective threshold is one less
cpp	YES	0	 This is branch-free and faster than bitwise OR/AND approach
cpp	YES	0	 For negative: max magnitude is max + 1 (e.g., -2147483648 for int32)
cpp	YES	0	 slow emulation routine for 32-bit
cpp	YES	0	 compute 64-bit a*b
cpp	YES	0	 ARM64 has native support for 64-bit multiplications, no need to emulate
cpp	YES	0	 But MinGW on ARM64 doesn't have native support for 64-bit multiplications
cpp	YES	0	 _umul128 not available on ARM64
cpp	YES	0	 Test before multiplying. The previous guard multiplied first and then compared the
cpp	YES	0	 already-wrapped value against max/10 - 10, which only caught wraps that happened to land
cpp	YES	0	 below that threshold: "300" wraps to 44 for uint8_t and sailed through, as did most
cpp	YES	0	 out-of-range values. would_overflow_positive is the same branch-free check the signed
cpp	YES	0	 path above already uses, so the two paths now reject on the same rule.
cpp	YES	0	 An exponent past the width's limit overflows any non-zero magnitude, but zero stays zero
cpp	YES	0	 however far it is scaled, so "0e19" is in range for every width. Testing the magnitude
cpp	YES	0	 here rather than ahead of the dispatch keeps it off the hot path: it only runs once the
cpp	YES	0	 exponent has already failed the range check.
cpp	YES	0	 As in the unsigned overload: only a non-zero magnitude can overflow, so "0e19" and
cpp	YES	0	 "-0e19" are in range for every width. `v` is already the signed mantissa, and negative
cpp	YES	0	 zero compares equal to zero, so both spellings land here with the value they should keep.
cpp	YES	0	 Scale in a width the product cannot wrap, then range check before narrowing. Scaling
cpp	YES	0	 inside `utype` truncated first and checked afterwards, so an out-of-range magnitude
cpp	YES	0	 aliased onto an accepted one: "13e2" read as 20 for int8_t and "5e9" as 705032704 for
cpp	YES	0	 int32_t. The widest case here is a 4-byte magnitude scaled by 10^9, which stays well
cpp	YES	0	 inside uint64_t. The unsigned path already widens the same way.
cpp	YES	0	 Bound the magnitude directly rather than subtracting the sign from it: a negative
cpp	YES	0	 zero makes `scaled - sign` underflow, and the old narrow expression only survived
cpp	YES	0	 that because it promoted to int. A negative value may reach one past the positive
cpp	YES	0	 limit, which is exactly INT_MIN's magnitude.
cpp	YES	0	 Scale the sign-stripped magnitude `i`, not the two's-complement bit pattern of `v`:
cpp	YES	0	 64-bit integer written with an exponent ("-1e2") overflowed and was rejected. The
cpp	YES	0	 narrower branches above already scale `i`.
cpp	YES	0	 Compare the full 128-bit product. Narrowing it to 64 bits first would let an
cpp	YES	0	 out-of-range magnitude alias onto an accepted one, e.g. 9e36 truncating into range.
cpp	YES	0	 Increase by 8 to support exponentials
cpp	YES	0	 The number of characters needed at most for each type, rounded to nearest 8 bytes
cpp	YES	0	 We copy the rest of the buffer, or buffer_length bytes, into a null terminated buffer. The
cpp	YES	0	 trailing byte is never written by the copy, so the null-terminated atoi below always halts
cpp	YES	0	 inside the array even when the input fills it: the exponent scan stops at a non-digit rather
cpp	YES	0	 than after a fixed digit count, and a value-initialized array alone would not terminate a
cpp	YES	0	 copy that covers every byte.
cpp	YES	0	 Reaching the end of a truncated copy means the number was cut off: parsing halted on the
cpp	YES	0	 terminator this buffer supplies rather than on a character of the input, so what parsed is
cpp	YES	0	 a prefix and its value is not the number's. Only zero padding can stretch a number this
cpp	YES	0	 far -- no in-range integer needs buffer_length characters -- but a caller that ignores
cpp	YES	0	 trailing content would otherwise take the prefix's value as the answer.
cpp	YES	0	 maximum number of digits need is: 3, 5, 10, 20, for byte sizes of 1, 2, 4, 8
cpp	YES	0	 we need to store one extra space for a digit for sizes of 1, 2, and 4 because we avoid checking for overflow
cpp	YES	0	 since we store in a uint64_t
cpp	YES	0	 digits[i] = 0; already set to zero
cpp	YES	0	 Clamp instead of wrapping: a uint8_t accumulator turns "1e256" into exponent 0, which
cpp	YES	0	 aliases an out-of-range magnitude onto an accepted one ("1e256" decoding as 1). The old
cpp	YES	0	 `exp < 128` guard could not catch that, since the wrap happened before the test, and it
cpp	YES	0	 also left `c` parked mid-number once it did trip.
cpp	YES	0	 a value of n == N would result in reading digits[N], which is invalid
cpp	YES	0	 Disable copy and move semantics
cpp	YES	0	 Ensures that release is called exactly once per acquired object
cpp	YES	0	 Use an aliasing constructor with a handle that will return the value
cpp	YES	0	 to the pool
cpp	YES	0	 indices of available values
cpp	YES	0	 Emplace a default-constructed value into a nullable type so the inner value can be parsed into.
cpp	YES	0	 Handles std::optional, std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr, raw pointers (when Opts/ctx permit
cpp	YES	0	 allocation), and any other nullable_like type exposing emplace() or a glz::meta constructor.
cpp	YES	0	 Returns true on success; on failure, sets ctx.error = invalid_nullable_read and returns false.
cpp	YES	0	 Default integer to ascii conversion
cpp	YES	0	 Uses 400 bytes of lookup tables (char_table + digit_pairs)
cpp	YES	0	 For maximum speed with 40KB tables, use itoa_40kb.hpp instead
cpp	YES	0	 2-digit character pairs table (200 bytes) - cache-line aligned
cpp	YES	0	 2-digit uint16_t table for direct 2-byte memcpy (100 × 2 = 200 bytes)
cpp	YES	0	 Generated at compile-time with correct byte order for target endianness
cpp	YES	0	 128-bit multiplication for efficient division by 100000000
cpp	YES	0	 Modern compilers optimize regular division the same way, but this ensures it
cpp	YES	0	 ==================== uint32_t implementations ====================
cpp	YES	0	 Note: We use `buf + N - lz` offsets instead of `buf -= lz` followed by `buf + N`.
cpp	YES	0	 Forming a pointer before the start of an array is undefined behavior in C++,
cpp	YES	0	 even if the pointer is never dereferenced. `buf -= lz` when buf points to the
cpp	YES	0	 start of an allocation and lz=1 violates this. GCC _FORTIFY_SOURCE with LTO
cpp	YES	0	 correctly detects and aborts on this.
cpp	YES	0	 The compiler optimizes `buf + N - lz` identically (single sub, then offsets).
cpp	YES	0	 val / 100
cpp	YES	0	 val / 10000

cpp	YES	0	 aabb / 100

cpp	YES	0	 aabbcc / 10000

cpp	YES	0	 Fixed 4-digit output (no leading zero handling)

cpp	YES	0	 5-8 digits with leading zero handling

cpp	YES	0	 Default integer to chars (uses 400 bytes of tables)

cpp	YES	0	 ==================== Small integer types ====================
cpp	YES	0	 Optimized for 8-bit and 16-bit integers with compact code paths
cpp	YES	0	 The 40KB digit_quads table doesn't help for these small ranges
cpp	YES	0	 uint8_t: 0-255 (1-3 digits)

cpp	YES	0	 A variant read is speculative: an alternative is parsed to find out whether it fits, and a
cpp	YES	0	 rejected one is rewound and the next tried. Nest that -- a variant whose alternatives contain
cpp	YES	0	 variants -- and the re-parses multiply, so a failure at the bottom of an ambiguous nest costs
cpp	YES	0	 branching^depth. Measured at ~4.3x per level, which turns 189 bytes into 55 seconds.
cpp	YES	0	 The bound is on total work rather than on nesting or attempts, because the honest measure is
cpp	YES	0	 how many bytes get parsed more than once. A wide document (many variants side by side, each
cpp	YES	0	 rejecting an alternative first) re-parses each element once and stays near 1x its own size,
cpp	YES	0	 exhaust the budget stop speculating and report the failure they already have -- which is the
cpp	YES	0	 outcome of a cascade anyway, since it only runs when nothing fits.
cpp	YES	0	 ...plus a floor, because the factor alone is the wrong shape for small inputs. Resolving a
cpp	YES	0	 genuinely ambiguous NESTED variant -- alternatives that differ only in a late member, so the
cpp	YES	0	 rejected one parses most of the subtree before failing -- costs exponentially more per level
cpp	YES	0	 even when the document is valid and the read ultimately succeeds. Glaze has always been like
cpp	YES	0	 correctly in 9 ms would now fail, which is not an improvement. A megabyte of speculative bytes
cpp	YES	0	 covers that shape to 18 levels, and gives up at 20, which is where the unbounded behavior was
cpp	YES	0	 already taking a quarter of a second and doubling every two levels. The adversarial case costs
cpp	YES	0	 a constant ~8 ms at any depth instead of 55 seconds at depth 12 and forever beyond that.

cpp	YES	0	 Concept to detect streaming-capable context at compile time
cpp	YES	0	 Automatically removes cv-ref qualifiers for convenience
cpp	YES	0	 Re-derive the window's edge after handing the input to another reader.
cpp	YES	0	 parse<Format>::op takes `end` by value, so a reader that refills partway through leaves the
cpp	YES	0	 caller holding an edge from the window the parse started in. `it` moved with the refill, and
cpp	YES	0	 the two stop describing the same span -- offsets taken from them then run past the buffer.
cpp	YES	0	 Release everything up to `it` and pull more input into the space behind it. Both iterators
cpp	YES	0	 move, since a refill relocates the window.
cpp	YES	0	 This is mechanism only: when to refill is the calling reader's decision, because only it knows
cpp	YES	0	 where one value ends and the next begins. Calling this anywhere else -- in the middle of a
cpp	YES	0	 value -- invalidates every pointer the reader is holding into the window.
cpp	YES	0	 `it` is clamped to the window rather than trusted. A reader can leave it past `end` on an
cpp	YES	0	 error path, and a variant alternative resolved by shape rewinds it, so an unclamped
cpp	YES	0	 subtraction underflows the byte count handed to consume(); the buffer's size then wraps and
cpp	YES	0	 the next refill memmoves a garbage length.
cpp	YES	0	 A context with no streaming state -- every buffered read -- compiles this away to nothing.
cpp	YES	0	 A streaming read advances by refilling its window in place, so a view pointed into that window
cpp	YES	0	 addresses bytes that a later refill overwrites. Nothing at runtime can catch it: the pointer
cpp	YES	0	 stays inside the buffer's own allocation, so it stays valid, compares equal to whatever now
cpp	YES	0	 occupies those bytes, and the parse reports success. Nor does a larger window fix it -- it only
cpp	YES	0	 changes which values happen to survive.
cpp	YES	0	 The check belongs on the readers that alias the buffer, not on the destination type. A reader
cpp	YES	0	 knows it is about to hand out a pointer into the window and knows from its context whether that
cpp	YES	0	 window moves, so it catches the case wherever the view sits -- behind a tuple, a map key, a
cpp	YES	0	 custom setter, or ten structs down -- and never fires on a type that merely looks like it holds
cpp	YES	0	 one. Every reader that aliases the input places this next to the assignment that does it.

cpp	YES	0	 Variant tagging representation
cpp	YES	0	 How a discriminated variant is laid out on the wire is a property of the *variant type*, not of
cpp	YES	0	 whichever alternative happens to be active. Choosing it per alternative -- emitting a merged tag
cpp	YES	0	 has no single schema, and lets two tag-less alternatives that share a shape be confused for one
cpp	YES	0	 another on read. So the representation is decided once, here, and every alternative obeys it.
cpp	YES	0	   internal (glz::meta `tag` only)
cpp	YES	0	      {"type": "circle", "radius": 5}
cpp	YES	0	      The discriminator is one more member of the alternative's own object. Nicest shape, but it
cpp	YES	0	      only exists for alternatives that *are* objects.
cpp	YES	0	   adjacent (glz::meta `tag` and `content`)
cpp	YES	0	      {"type": "vec", "value": [1, 2, 3]}
cpp	YES	0	      The discriminator sits beside the value under a second fixed key. Works for every
cpp	YES	0	      alternative type -- objects, arrays, maps, scalars, null -- at the cost of one nesting
cpp	YES	0	      level. Under `structs_as_arrays` this projects to the two element array [id, value].
cpp	YES	0	 Declaring `tag` alone for a variant that has an alternative internal tagging cannot represent is
cpp	YES	0	 a static_assert rather than a silent degradation: that combination is exactly the code that is
cpp	YES	0	 quietly producing unreadable output today.
cpp	YES	0	 The object type an alternative presents to the serializers: memory objects (smart pointers,
cpp	YES	0	 std::optional of a struct, ...) tag through the type they point to.
cpp	YES	0	 A unit alternative carries no data at all: std::monostate, std::nullptr_t, std::nullopt_t.
cpp	YES	0	 Internal tagging renders it as a discriminator-only object -- exactly the object an empty struct
cpp	YES	0	 alternative already produces -- so that every alternative of an internally tagged variant is an
cpp	YES	0	 object carrying the tag. Writing it as a bare `null` instead, which is what Glaze did before,
cpp	YES	0	 left one alternative of the union with no discriminator on it for no reason anyone chose: the
cpp	YES	0	 `null` writer simply predates the tagging machinery. Untagged variants still write it as `null`,
cpp	YES	0	 and both readers still accept `null` for it so existing data keeps parsing.
cpp	YES	0	 An alternative can host a merged discriminator only if it serializes as an object whose members
cpp	YES	0	 Glaze itself emits, so one more member can be spliced in, or if it carries no data and can be
cpp	YES	0	 rendered as the discriminator alone. Maps and pairs are objects on the wire but no writer merges
cpp	YES	0	 a tag into them, and scalars and arrays have nowhere to put one.
cpp	YES	0	 A custom-serialized alternative is taken at its word: the JSON writer merges the tag into
cpp	YES	0	 whatever body the user's serializer produces. BEVE cannot do the same because its objects are
cpp	YES	0	 length-prefixed and the member count of a custom body is not knowable in advance -- the BEVE
cpp	YES	0	 writer static_asserts on that combination rather than silently dropping the discriminator.
cpp	YES	0	 An empty reflected object, used to consume the body of a discriminator-only object on behalf
cpp	YES	0	 of a unit alternative. Routing through it reuses the object readers' key handling, unknown-key
cpp	YES	0	 policy, and terminator consumption rather than duplicating them per format.
